subtopic: MR. THATCHER    ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION FROM C.C.F. PARTY

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: MR. THATCHER    ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION FROM C.C.F. PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I crave the indulgence of the house for a moment to speak on a matter of personal privilege. On three different occasions I have been elected to this parliament as the standard bearer of the C.C.F. party. During those years I have appreciated the privilege of working with C.C.F. members of parliament and with the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
However, I regret to say that recently there have been growing differences between myself and my colleagues on matters of major public policy. At one time I had hoped these differences could be resolved. However, the present session of parliament has convinced me that such a hope is futile. Therefore, in fairness to my leader and in fairness to my colleagues and in fairness to myself I feel that I have no alternative but to resign from the C.C.F. party.
This is not the time to deal in detail with our differences, but I shall take an early opportunity in the house to explain the reasons for my action. For the remainder of the present parliament I propose to represent the constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre as an independent member. I shall not apply for membership in any other party. I shall continue to support those measures and motions which I believe to be in the best interests of the people who elected me, no matter from what quarter they are advanced.
Under these circumstances I must ask you, sir, to allocate to me a seat in another part of this chamber.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. Has the minister received a telegram from Glace Bay with regard to the reported closing of Dominion No. 1-B colliery? If so, has he any statement in regard to the matter, or any statement in regard to the situation there from the point of view of employment?

speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext: I have received several telegrams relating to the announced closing of No. 1-B colliery. Most of those telegrams cited the loss of markets as the reason for closing. My understanding is that the real cause of the closing is the high cost of production. That problem has been clearly understood by both management and labour for some time, and I believe the announcement of the closing of the mine has been made after very careful and serious consideration by both management and labour.

maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext: Has the minister given any consideration to the possibility of appointing a group of experts, either from his own department or from outside, to examine the opportunities that may present themselves to make other uses of this colliery, if necessary, in view of the very substantial dependence of a large number of people in that area upon that operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not quite understand what the Leader of the Opposition means by "other uses". There can be only one use of a colliery, and that is to produce coal. For the last two years the problem has been given very careful consideration by the dominion coal board, management and the unions. Only recently a representative of the Nova Scotia government was in Ottawa, and a plan was suggested by me to that representative. He was to take that plan back to the Nova Scotia government, the mining company and the unions. As yet I have had no further report as to how that suggestion was received. It is my intention to get in touch with the president of the company today to see if the suggestion is considered to have any merit.

maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext:
This is not in any way by way of a debate, but since the minister said that he did not know what I had in mind in suggesting other possibilities, may I say I was thinking, for instance, of the fact that in other countries there have been cases where mines which became uneconomic, from


the point of view of ordinary operations, became very economic from the point of view of the development of electricity right at the mine head. I had that in mind, and other similar possibilities, in view of the substantial dependence of a large number of people upon this operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, you just cannot produce electricity economically with $11 coal at the pithead.

maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext: May I ask the minister a supplementary question? Is it correct to say that in so far as the government is concerned, jurisdiction over this matter that the Leader of the Opposition is inquiring about is in the hands of the provincial government? Second, I should like to ask the minister whether the provincial government of Nova Scotia has made any representations to his department with respect to relinquishing control of the industry in order that the federal government might take some action?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: REPORTED CLOSING OF NOVA SCOTIA MINE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 20, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget debate so far has proven, among other things, that the Conservatives are bankrupt of ideas. Certainly, there is a marked resemblance between the amendment that they proposed to the speech from the throne and the amendment they moved in this budget debate. I also note that the leader of the socialist party, the C.C.F., did not at this time propose any socialistic means by which he could cure the ills of the nation. That certainly is a step forward.
The Minister of Finance is a charming man, but he is a Conservative wearing a Liberal mantle. His budget is a palliative, not a cure. It reminds me of an injured man who is given a cane and who is so badly injured that he requires a crutch for support.
Finance in this country today is a sick man, and I would say that it needs the full treatment. Time and conditions will prove that the Minister of Finance might have been the emancipator of all time. Instead of that, I think we shall have finally to record that he is just another tax collector. Instead of throwing caution to the winds, he has decided to follow the Conservative caution that I spoke of earlier. I am almost led to believe that he read some of the budgets that were brought down in the late Prime Minister R.
B.	Bennett's regime, for certainly he has nothing further to offer than was offered at that time.
The Budget-Mr. Hahn I may say that I have always admired the new Minister of Finance. I have always thought of him as a man of vision. Instead of that, I find him a man of revision. He has merely revised the tax structure that has been in existence for some time. I hope the minister will be at the proposed dominion-provincial conference. I would suggest he will find in the discussions at that conference that some of the ministers of finance from the far western provinces will propose new techniques and new principles which might be able to straighten out the affairs of this country. What we require today are alternatives, not remedies. In his first budget he has failed to relieve those who need it most. The man on the low fixed income is the man who gets the least. The man on the small superannuation and on the small annuity gets nothing. I find the budget does nothing for the old age pensioner, or for the war veterans allowance man who is unable to obtain casual earnings. It does relatively little for the blind and disabled. To my way of thinking, their plight is worse than it was a year ago. It does nothing for those who are on old age security. The budget reminds me of the biblical story. When the rich were putting their gifts into the treasury a widow put in two coppers, and our Lord said that she had put in more than all of them. The same widow is still putting two coppers into the treasury, and putting in more than all the others.
It is not my intention to treat the budget with derision, but I say that it is an orthodox conservative budget. It does not go far enough. I congratulate the minister upon the tax concessions and the tax cuts that he has made. It is the purpose of the opposition to offer constructive criticism, not just criticism that will tear down the house that we have built. The leader of my group gave some constructive criticism, methodically and well. It would be presumptuous of me to review all the information that he gave. Before going on with that, let me say that the tax cut now given is too little and too late to cure depressed industry and relieve the unemployment situation as it exists at this time. The situation will deteriorate still further unless additional action is taken by the government.
What we need is an injection of more purchasing power. We must have a balanced economy. We must balance the purchasing power within the nation with the productive capacity of our workers. It is most important that this injection of purchasing power should be made where it will do the most good.
Studying the matter I would say that the quickest way to create work today would be
3072	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Hahn to create a demand for the goods in connection with which we have the heaviest turnover, such as food, clothing and automobiles. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) took care of the automobile matter to some degree with his 5 per cent reduction in the excise tax, but putting money into durable goods at this point is not of as great value from the point of view of creating immediate employment for people now unemployed as other methods would be. It will not cure the problem which is quite likely to continue and grow.
The greatest market for non-durable goods is to be found among the people who have no money, those who do not pay income tax, those who do not buy automobiles. The removal of the sales tax on clothing and textiles would create an increased demand for those particular goods and this demand would be set up almost immediately. It is quite possible that it would help in offsetting the unemployment which is prevalent today in the textile industry. If we had taken the sales tax off textiles we would have done more to create jobs in this country at this time than is being done by the reductions in the income tax. It certainly would have made the dollars which these poor people have go considerably further and would have created a demand for the goods which they require so badly.
It would be better still to inject purchasing power into the hands of these people themselves. This group consists of unemployed employables, war veterans on disability pension, those who are in receipt of annuity or superannuation payments and those who cannot make money by casual work because they are handicapped or because there are no jobs available. We could create purchasing power by increasing the old age pensions paid to our senior citizens. We could increase purchasing power by giving larger old age security payments.
We could also assist materially by putting dollars into the small annuities, into all annuities for that matter, and making them worth what they were when people first purchased them. You will possibly remember, as I do, the days when we saw large signs in our post offices and banks telling people to prepare for their old age by buying annuities or pensions of one kind or another. The people who bought those annuities some years ago were led to believe that if they bought a $20, a $30, a $40 or a $50 annuity it would be worth that amount of money when they needed it most.
However, the opposite is true today. The $50 annuity is worth approximately $25 today. Let us reward these people for their


thrift and foresight ih. investing in post office annuities and.-other forms of annuities by putting dollars back into the annuity fund.
I do not intend to spend any great amount of time discussing the budget, but I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the excellent way in which my leader drew attention to the relationship between agricultural production, labour and national income in the United States. I believe it was discovered that when you have a maximum of labour, farm income and production the ratio is 1-1-7. I commend my leader's address to the minister's careful attention because it is quite. possible that in this lies the key to an economic formula for full employment.
I listened with considerable interest to what the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) had to say during the course of the debate about a guaranteed annual wage. It is not my intention at this time to discuss the guaranteed annual wage because I think we can do a better job and be able to speak at greater length when the estimates are before us. However, I was struck by one point in his speech. I think he gave an excellent discourse, but then he tried, not with the same success, to make out a case against it.
There was one thing that did stick in my mind, that is his suggestion that if the auto workers were not continuously employed in building automobiles under a guaranteed annual wage they might turn to the making of cuckoo clocks. I wondered what was to happen to those who were already employed in the building of cuckoo clocks. Possibly they would be busy building something else of which somebody else had already produced too much.
As I said earlier, I would refer the minister to the address of my leader and his reference to the plight of the farmers. We have noted from time to time the fact that our labour problem depends largely on farm production. Whatever the labouring man creates is quite often the direct result of what the farmer has produced and what he has received therefor. I do not intend to debate this problem because, as I said before, there has been so much said about his plight and the effect of what he produces upon the nation as a whole.
There are other groups that could be dealt with at this time. There is the case of the old age pensioner, the blind person, the disabled person and the men and women who are receiving old age security. I am quite satisfied, as is possibly every hon. member in this house, that this problem is not being adequately dealt with today. We should spend more time studying what can be done for

these senior citizens. With automation and the fact that jobs are becoming fewer, these people have not the funds to carry on, and we must find some way of looking after them. Their plight can and will probably be discussed at the appropriate time on the estimates.
However, there is another group in regard to which I have checked the estimates carefully to see whether I can include it in the discussion on the estimates; but I cannot. Therefore I propose to tell you something about their difficulties. They play a most important part in the economy of the community and they are a most important economic group in the business of the nation. They are the forerunners of the metropolitan areas, they are the financiers of the community, and they are the hardest hit in times of depression. I refer to the small retail shopkeepers. What drew them to my attention was an article in the dominion bureau of statistics "News Notes" of April 1, 1955, from which I quote:
The number of commercial failures under the Bankruptcy and Winding Up acts increased 37 per cent last year from 1,657 in 1953 to a post-war peak of 2,278. Defaulted liabilities jumped to $53,142,000 from $32,818,000, average liability per failure increasing 18 per cent.
Now I know that this refers to commercial failures and does not necessarily include all retail merchants. However, it does include the retail merchants. They, as I said earlier, have played a most important part in the building up of our community and of our nation, and I feel that they have not been given the consideration which we are capable of giving them. The small shopkeepers in this country do approximately 60 per cent of the nation's business; the chain stores in comparison do 40 per cent.
Let us examine the significance of the statement which I have just read. It means in effect that there are 2,278 families who have become financially destitute. It means that those employed by these commercial enterprises are temporarily unemployed. It means that we are going to add all these people to the unemployed list. It means in effect that our employable unemployed list has grown by 2,278 families plus all the people whom they have employed.
That is a most discouraging state of affairs. Here we have people who have lost their life savings. They have no compensation; they have no unemployment insurance; they are destitute. They have given their all to the growth of this country and to the growth of their small communities. They are probably the greatest philanthropists within the nation, and yet there is not a place where we find we can discuss their plight. It is a tragedy of our 50433-195
The Budget-Mr. Hahn economic system that these builders of our community life should finish their business careers in this way.
There are certain factors which cause these failures. Some of them are of a personal nature over which we as a parliament have no control. However, I am not interested in their personal shortcomings. I am more interested in what we have done and what legislation we can pass in order that we might see that these continued failures should not be with us in the future, especially if they are not due to their own personal shortcomings. I speak of the economic aspect over which the small merchant has no control and all the legal technicalities which might be involved in giving him assistance.
The first of these items which I have listed is the fact that buying in quantity means that we should be able to purchase at a discount. I do not know whether hon. members are aware of what buying in quantity actually means. It means to some companies that if you buy one case of goods you are not buying a quantity but if you buy five cases of goods you are buying a quantity. Most people have the impression that one has to buy a carload lot of goods before one is buying a quantity. Does the hon. member have an observation to make?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are selling a fine bill of goods.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you. I hope to continue selling it too. Most people have the impression, as I said, that in order to buy a quantity one must buy in carload lots or at least in multiples of ten. Such is not the case. I am thinking of a particular item which you would be buying in quantity if you bought five items; but you have to buy ten to get a further increase in discount. If you buy 25 you are buying actually at carload lot prices. A particular firm may have 25 different items, and does not care which one of the items you buy. You can buy one of each, which means that it takes just as much bookkeeping and there is just as much trucking involved to pick up each one of the 25 items. You are supposedly buying in quantity, but in effect you are not buying in quantity in the true sense of the word. However, you are getting the advantage of a 25-case purchase. That is one of the reasons why we find that chain stores are possibly able to undersell these smaller retail merchants who are trying to be competitive with them. The man who is helping to build the community contends, and I contend, that buying in quantity should mean certainly buying more than one item, or one per article, not
3074	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Hahn 25 items each of one different article, especially when the same amount of bookkeeping and the same trucking and so forth is involved in carrying out such a transaction.
To illustrate my point further with respect to the sales made by the small retailer as compared with the chain store, I would say this. If the chain stores were to purchase all their goods from the one wholesaler and were to get the chain store price, the wholesaler would in all likelihood go bankrupt. Today the small merchant is in effect subsidizing the chain store. The small merchant is buying 60 per cent of the wholesaler's product, as against 40 per cent by the chain store. In effect it means this. For purposes of illustration, we will use a lot of 100 cases of goods which are sold on the national basis of 40 to a chain store and 60 to the small retail merchant. If each of those pieces of goods is worth $7-assuming it is the net cost-the net cost of that parcel of goods would be $700. If the wholesaler is willing to sell that commodity to the chain store at 10 cents less than cost and to the small retailer at 10 cents more than cost, the price will then be $6.90 to the chain store and $7.10 a case to the small retailer. The 40 cases of goods which the chain store buys at $6.90 would return to the wholesaler 40 times $6.90 which would be $276. The 60 cases of goods which are sold to the small retailer at $7.10 would, in effect, give the wholesaler $426. That would be his net return. The wholesaler then, adding those two figures together, would receive for his goods $426 plus $276 or $702 in this transaction.
In effect what has happened is that the wholesaler has sold his commodity for less than cost to the big chain store and for more than cost to the small retailer, and has still wound up with a $2 profit on the whole transaction. That is something that is being done. For that reason I say that the small retailer is subsidizing the chain store today.
I contend that that is not fair business practice. I contend that we in this parliament should take action to see that no commodity is offered for sale, unless it is on a clearance basis, at a price less than wholesale to any particular group of merchants or individuals. The small merchants of this country should not be discriminated against.
A second factor in this matter is the unethical practice of coupon disposal. I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that each hon. member from time to time has seen the coupons that are offered by certain firms in this country and that are put out as an introductory offer. In one instance I am thinking of a soap firm in the city of Edmonton. I think it was called Soapone. Those people issued thousands


and thousands of coupons to the merchants in western Canada. Then after the merchants had given the 10 cent value per coupon, they failed to recover them. The firm went bankrupt.
A coupon is a form of money and its use should not be permitted in that particular sense. If those companies are willing to sacrifice 10 cents per box as an introductory offer, I would say they should be compelled to issue box lots or case lots to the merchants at a discount sufficient to enable them to quote their price 10 cents below what would be the normal price at a later date. That would be the fair way of doing things instead of what is being done now where, because some particular lady happens to bring along her coupons or because she has an accumulation of them from her neighbours who do not use that particular brand of soap, she has an advantage over the other ladies. That part has nothing to do with the actual merchandising of it. The fact remains, though, that here we have coupons being given to the merchants who take them in good faith and, having taken them, find that they cannot recover their money from the firms in question because they have either gone bankrupt or are unwilling to accept responsibility for the issuance of those particular coupons.
Then there are other unethical practices in respect of this coupon letting. I remember a particular instance-and it also took place in western Canada-in which the small merchants were going to be the outlet for a new brand of soap. The purpose was to introduce a new type of soap of one of the larger soap companies. In this instance the merchant was approached by the supervisor of the soap company and it was proposed that if he bought, let us say, five cases of soap, which would be 60 packages, he would be given 60 coupon cards. On each one of those cards he would have to put the name of one of his customers. Then it had to be sent through the mail to this particular customer. The customer in turn was to return it to the storekeeper and it could be retrieved on that basis.
What it was, in effect, was a grandiose scheme to force the small merchants to buy cases and cases of soap that they did not require. I had occasion to go into one merchant's store subsequent to the offer of this particular deal. Two years later he still had that particular soap in the warehouse. Because he had 500 customers, he obtained 500 boxes. But the soap men knew full well that only about 10 per cent to 15 per cent of these coupons are ever recovered. By this means they were able to get rid of their commodity, get the finances from the merchant who was obliged to pay for this product, and the result was

that the merchant became, in effect, an unloading centre for the manufacturer of this particular soap product.
Then there are certain other unethical procedures that are being followed in today's merchandising. We have deals between manufacturing firms and particular chain stores whereby a chain store is given a certain sum of money for a display in their store. The offer is this: If you give us this particular spot-let us say in a window-for advertising purposes, you will get $2 from our firm. But no little merchant is given the advantage of that same deal. He is never given the same offer. If he inquires about it, he is merely told that it is not open to everybody. Mr. Speaker, if it is right for a chain store to be given this particular treatment-and I call it unfair treatment as far as the small merchant is concerned-then the small merchant should be given the same treatment. We should have the same treatment for the chain store and the small merchant if we are going to keep our equal tenor of good feeling in the business world today.
I also find that if you take five cases of a particular product, possibly you get less in the way of advertising allowance than if you take ten cases, or if you give them a particular spot near the cash register which seems to be one that most of them want.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is another form of
discount.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is, in effect, another form of discount that the small merchant is not being given the privilege of enjoying. I say that the same offer should be open to the small retailer. I say that if he is willing to devote a space in his small store to the advertising of a particular product, he should be given an equal discount for it. We have the small merchant, in effect, first subsidizing the price to the chain store and, second, subsidizing the advertising of the chain store.
Then there is one other factor-and I think this is a fairly well established one-namely that no cost price is established for certain of the products that are for sale today. If it is established, certainly nobody is aware of it. We have instances were you buy five cases of a particular brand of soap. I am using soap again as an example because it is one of the most culpable in this instance. You buy five cases at a price discount. You devote a certain store space to it. You can just about guarantee that another of their products of a similar line will be down 20 cents a case the following week or even 40 cents a case. Thereby they are setting no cost value or no price value on it. Possibly between the two levels there is a cost, but because the demand 50433-195}
The Budget-Mr. Hahn is less for one product they immediately cut its price in order to increase demand, with the result that they have the small merchants coming and going in trying to arrive at an equalized price. The small merchant is always on the short end of the stick because he never has a chance to become and remain competitive with these large chain merchants who are only concerned with one thing, the elimination of the little man.
I charge that there is virtually a combine among the soap companies. They control the soap business of the country. They control soap supply. I am speaking of Lever Brothers and Procter and Gamble. There should be an examination into their unfair practices and it should be determined whether or not the same rights are being extended to the little merchant as are being given to the big merchant. It should be determined by what form of advertising or other method the soap companies are letting the little people know that the same rights are afforded to them.
This is the type of economic practice that is today killing the small retailer. As I said earlier, the little merchant is subsidizing the chain stores. Canada is today losing a share of income tax from the large wholesale outlets of these chain stores by reason of the fact that we find so frequently the wholesale firm has its own retail outlet with the result that there is not sufficient profit to require the payment of a large amount of income tax. There would be sufficient under ordinary circumstances with smaller retailers because the shareholders would require it. In the case of such large firms as Macdonalds Consolidated, Safeway and others I am not satisfied that a large enough amount of income tax is payable. I am not satisfied that is so in the case of Macdonalds Consolidated at the present time, certainly compared with legitimate wholesalers who do nothing but wholesale.
Business and salesmanship in this country should depend upon service, quality, personality, cleanliness, incentive, initiative and their related factors. It should not depend upon special privileges, agreed charges and unethical practices. The purpose of these big firms appears to be to eliminate competition and ultimately to set up a monopoly. We are unalterably opposed to monopolies. These little men are important to our country, and I say that we should examine the matter and see how we can keep them with us.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this time-honoured debate pertaining to the budget and, coming from the riding of Niagara Falls where we probably have more tourists than any other

The Budget-Mr. Houck place in the dominion, I naturally feel I should refer at the very outset to this type of travel in this great country of ours. In the year 1954 there were 647,948 vehicles of the non-permit class which entered at Niagara Falls and 337,181 of the travellers' vehicle permit class. Somewhat larger figures existed at the port of Fort Erie where we had over a million vehicles entering of the nonpermit class and some 350,000 of the travellers' vehicle permit class. One cannot overemphasize the value of the tourist dollar that is left within the confines of our country.
Expenditures in Canada by travellers from the United States and other countries were maintained in 1954 at a figure close to the peak established in 1953. First estimates indicate that residents of other countries spent some $300 million in Canada during 1954, a decrease of some $3 million or 1 per cent lower than the previous year. Although slightly lower than the record of 1953, the 1954 estimate represents an increase of 9 per cent, or $25 million, over 1952. Compared with a decline of nearly 6 per cent in the volume of entries, available data on expenditure indicate slightly higher averages per visit in 1954 for some types of transportation. Travel receipts from the United States declined some $4 million from the year before but remained well ahead of the 1952 figure. Receipts from overseas countries set a record at $22 million, an increase of 10 per cent over the previous record established in 1953.
Most of the increase in expenditures byresidents of Canada returning from the United States can be traced to the automobile traffic. Canadians returning by automobile spent over $136 million in the United States during the past year compared with $133 million in 1953, an increase of over 2 per cent. Compared with an increase of 3 per cent in the number of automobiles returning, this would indicate slightly lower average expenditures.
Purchases declared under the $100 customs exemption privilege by Canadians returning from the United States in 1954 amounted to $66 million, a decrease of $6 million or an 8 per cent decline from 1953. This would indicate that a smaller portion of Canadian travel expenditures in the United States went for merchandise, a trend contrary to that of the previous year.
The total number of visits to Canada by people from other countries amounted to 26-4 million in 1954, a decrease of 1-6 million visits, or 5'7 per cent fewer than the record established in 1953. It must be emphasized, however, that these visits are made by vacationists, summer residents, commuters, businessmen and all other travellers except

immigrants. They include repeat visits by commuters and others who enter the country many times during the year. Approximately 85 per cent of the visits are for 48 hours or less. Only 15 to 16 per cent of the visits last longer than 48 hours.
I want to say I was very much disappointed the other day to hear the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), in reply to a question from the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), say that no redress would be given the automobile dealers on new units which they had on their hands when the budget was brought down. It is my opinion, and it is a very definite opinion indeed, that they should receive consideration. Naturally I was very happy to see the reduction of 5 per cent on new cars, as I think all automobile dealers were as well, but I think they have a justifiable claim pertaining to these new units.
The automotive industry, through its manufacturing plants, sales agencies and connected trades, garages, service stations, buses, transport, petroleum industry, rubber industry, suppliers such as steel plants, paints, glass, textiles, etc., is reported to provide over 20 per cent of the labour force of our country. So you can see that the automotive industry is a very basic one to our economic prosperity. Anything that tends to restrict the sale of automobiles is bound to show up in reduced payrolls, reduced income and corporation taxes from all the connected industries, and reduced sales and excise taxes in new automobiles, all as a direct result. Hence it is of the utmost importance that automobile sales agencies be kept healthy and working at full capacity.
In my own city of Niagara Falls nine dealers had 209 new units on hand when the budget was brought down. The average reduction in excise tax, from the smallest to the largest car, is estimated to be about $100 per unit. So the total reduction in value amounts in Niagara Falls to an estimated $21,000. On top of that there was an inventory of $370,000 in used cars. It appears that this will drop at least 5 per cent on account of the tax changes. This is another $19,000. Therefore the total decrease in inventory value is approximately $40,000.
Ward's Automotive Reports, which is a publication published in the United States, in the March 21, 1955, issue reported that 38 [DOT] 7 per cent of United States dealers lost money last year, and that the average profit of all United States dealers was three-fifths of a cent on every dollar of sale, before income or corporation taxes. We do not have the Canadian figures yet, but as a rule they follow or parallel the United States figures.

In the long run it will cost the government nothing to return this tax, because I think it will keep many dealers in business who would otherwise be forced to go out, and it will leave many others more solvent and thus able to carry on their business more freely. It will increase taxes from dealerships, factory payrolls and the extra new cars that would not have been sold otherwise, and it would be a further indication that the government really meant what it said when it proclaimed the budget as a job-producing and hence an income-producing budget.
I would also like to point out that any excise tax at all on any automobile is unfair. The government described it as a luxury tax when they imposed it. But certainly automobiles are no longer luxuries for most of their uses. And I also feel that the tax is unfair in the following respects: First, because dealers have to pay the tax when they receive the cars, and are given the extra burden of financing it for the period they have that car. They have to carry insurance on it as well. Then when it is removed the government refuses to return it on the units still in stock. And it is my firm belief that if the government would rebate the tax on the new units in stock they would get it all back in taxes on extra units that would be sold, by way of income tax from increased jobs, and from increased taxes from dealer earnings. It could quite conceivably be that they might lose considerably more than they kept if they do not do so.
The previous tax change policies are not applicable at this time because of two very important reasons, first, that the size of inventories in dealers' hands at the present time is very large. When the taxes were decreased, as we decreased them on previous occasions, dealers' profits were high enough to absorb the loss without its being any serious problem.
And now I have another matter of importance in the Niagara district-and it is very relative to the St. Lawrence development-and it is that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) will have to give due consideration to the traffic through the Welland canal which, naturally, will be increased to a very great extent. We have three or four large corporations along the Welland river and because of the boats which will be coming in to these companies, loaded with materials to be used in the manufacture of their products, I think it is only right that some consideration should be given to this problem of widening and deepening the Welland river so that boats can get through a lock into this territory.
The Budget-Mr. Houck I realize this would of necessity be quite a costly venture, and I do not want to tire hon. members with too many local problems, but I think this one is of prime importance. The difference between the Welland river and the Welland canal at Port Robinson is about 7 feet, which would be the extent to which ships would have to be lifted or lowered. And the distance from Port Robinson to Chippawa is some seven miles, as the crow flies. But any development there would,. of necessity, have to straighten out the Welland river at certain points. There are at least six bridges crossing the river, four of which would eventually require reconstruction but, for immediate use, only two located at Port Robinson would have to be altered in order to bring the ships as far as the Welland Chemical and Noranda Mines Limited. The Norton and Carborundum companies are very greatly interested in such a development since, at the present time, they bring their raw material from South America by boat to New York city and break it for rail transportation to Niagara Falls, Ontario. The present canal system on the St. Lawrence permits boats of only approximately 3,000 tons to go through, and this is an uneconomical amount for them to bring in by boat all the way. If they could bring ships of 5,000 or more tons through the canal system, it brings it within the range of economic possibility and, in the case of Carborundum itself, they have mentioned that they would use at least 25 to 30 boatloads per season.
With the construction of the seaway in the lower St. Lawrence, the Welland canal area becomes the best protected harbour on the great lakes system. It might be an expensive and inconvenient method of docking if slips were cut into the side of the canal, with the added hazard of interfering with up and down shipping. One of the best solutions appears to be the use of the Welland river which gets the boats off the routine traffic of the canal into an area which could be built up industrially and where they can move up and down and turn as they like without obstructing the heavy traffic on the canal.
I recall that last year, speaking in this debate, I referred to the terrible congestion of automobile traffic at both the Burlington cutoff and the Homer bridge at St. Catharines. I can only repeat what I said at that time, that these are two of the worst bottlenecks in the province of Ontario.
I want to be fair in this matter, realizing of course that other hon. members have other traffic problems. But I must point out that at these two points we are receiving tourist traffic. They are entering Ontario and Canada for the first time; and I imagine they get pretty well fed-up, if I may use that
3078	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Houck expression, with the delays they have to endure at certain times. We as citizens in the community-and I include in this the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Cavers), the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) and the members from Hamilton-must be getting sick and tired of this dilly-dallying attitude between the federal and provincial governments as to whose jurisdiction it is to alleviate such problems. I note the Burlington high-level bridge is to be started shortly, but this has been in the offing now for a number of years.
I want to say that in my own experience I have seen traffic tied up from the Homer bridge back to Niagara Falls, a distance of about ten miles, with two-way traffic on both lanes waiting for the bridge to be lowered. And I feel that if we want to treat tourists as well as possible, we will have to eliminate this condition where they run into traffic difficulties within only a few miles from Niagara Falls. I am sure their impression of Canada must receive a handicap at once.
Talking about the tourists' impression of Canada, I again want to pay my highest respects to both customs and immigration officials at the ports of Niagara Falls and Fort Erie. They are the first people that the travelling public come in contact with, and I share with the department officials a justifiable pride in the way these men conduct their offices. Many a time tourists have told me how much they appreciate not only the efficiency but the co-operation and advice of these splendid officials, and I hope that their good work will be recognized by the ministers of these departments, and that soon they will receive wages commensurate with the services they render.
Another suggestion I would like to make, and I make this in all sincerity, to the Minister of Transport, is that it would not cost the government too much money to keep an ice-breaker down on the river where it enters lake Ontario. Perhaps not for another 40 or 50 years will we witness the spectacle of the ice jam we had just a few weeks ago. However, on the other hand it might happen again next winter, and if this ice-breaker were on hand when the ice starts to gather and refuses to flow out into the lake, this boat could be immediately started into operation and keep the channel open before the ice has an opportunity to jam and cause millions of dollars' worth of damage such as was caused in the last few months.
I do not want to be at all critical of the Ontario hydro commission, but I think they could well afford to pay half the cost of this ice-breaker in order to protect their very valuable hydro plants in case we have


another jam such as we had a few weeks ago. If this should go even a few feet higher, we would suffer millions and millions of dollars' damage, not only to their own hydro plants but to our manufacturing concerns, resulting in lay-off of employment because of lack of power. I make this as a very serious suggestion, that I think the Department of Transport and the Ontario hydro commission should get together to alleviate the anxiety we had this winter.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the budget, I join with the rest of my colleagues in this house in congratulating the minister on such a very fine presentation, and with it the encouragement that he has given to the people of Canada. With so much bad news coming from various sources in the world, it is encouraging to know that the Minister of Finance has predicted a good year for the people of Canada and has made a general although modest tax reduction for this year and 1956. I think the minister rightly believes, and we all join with him, that the government, business and the people of Canada must work together to ensure continued prosperity, and we all feel encouraged that he expressed the hope for a steady increase in business rather than an immediate upward thrust. The imagination and the effort of the Canadian people have brought this country to its present state of development and there is no reason to believe that it cannot continue to go forward under a government which permits private enterprise to flourish while safeguarding the nation from any monopolistic or other practices which could prove harmful.
Just a few weeks ago, some outstanding economists met to survey the state of the nation's prosperity. They studied every available index of business activity, and when they had gone over all their charts and tables, and had peered into the future through their crystal slide rules, the consensus among them was that 1955 will not be the best year in our history. It will only be the second or third best, according to their calculations.
Now the prospect of struggling through a year that is only the second or third best and most prosperous we have ever known is not exactly what I would regard as a fate worse than death. Yet if we were to believe even one-half of the alarmist talk, we could only conclude that we are sliding into a terrible depression; that Canada's golden age is past, and that our only chance of salvation is to board the first train for Ottawa and beg the government to run our various businesses for us in the Dominion of Canada.
Well, I for one am not quite ready to give this country back to the Indians, and I think

the time has come when we ought to face squarely up to the fact that most of this depression talk is inspired more by the politics of our present situation than by the economics of it.
If our national supply of common sense has not been wholly exhausted, the Canadian people will take a long, cold look at that primrose path to inflation before they travel it again; for the destination to which it leads is national ruin.
So, instead of trying to read the inscrutable future, let us turn our eyes in the opposite direction and use a little of that 20-20 hindsight with which the good Lord, in His wisdom, has so generously endowed us all.
The success or failure of our economy depends chiefly upon our people themselves, upon businessmen, labourers, farmers, everybody in Canada. The only thing that government can do is to provide a fertile field to work in; but the thing that makes Canada go-and that always has and always will-is the individual effort of 15 million people, all trying to do a little more for themselves, a little more for their families, and a little more for each generation, every fellow trying to improve his own position. The cumulative effect of all that work, by all those people, is the thing that has made Canada what it is today.
Canada today is still undergoing that difficult and sometimes dangerous transition from war to a peacetime economy, and all of us are closely watching every economic index that records a change in business activity. But prosperity, unfortunately, is not a mere statistic. It is primarily a state of mind; and if we permit anything or anybody to destroy the confidence of the Canadian people, or to undermine their faith in the future, neither we nor the government can prevent a depression.
Now it would be wonderful, of course, if our economy always grew at a steady, unfaltering pace, but that never happens in any nation anywhere. To me it has always seemed that our economic progress is a good deal like the waves that break over the beach on the incoming tide. Each one comes roaring in, spends itself, and then recedes, but in doing so it contributes to the volume and the force of the next wave, which always comes in a little farther. Yet those who spend all their time watching the waves can become so obsessed with this process that they never observe the onward movement of the tide itself. And so it is, I think, with many of our pessimists today. They simply cannot see the tide for the waves. Many times, I am sure, there must have been those
The Budget-Mr. Houck who felt that the tide had turned, but of course it never had, and it never will as long as freedom of opportunity and freedom of competitive enterprise continue to exist in this country. So let no one tell us that we have reached the end of our golden age; for this, in truth, is only the beginning. In my opinion, we stand on the doorstep of the greatest era of progress this nation has ever known. The problems ahead are difficult, but they are not insuperable if they are approached by men of good will with vigour and energy and primary dedication to the public interest.
In the state, as in the nation, there are two essentially different ways to administer government. One is to sit back and wait until difficulties become problems and problems becomes crises, waiting for these difficulties, problems and crises to solve themselves, or hoping for some easy solution to turn up. This is the easy way, the expedient way, the political way. It piles up the burdens for later years and later generations. In too many cases, time, instead of solving the difficulties, multiplies them, until they become emergencies. By failing to anticipate the problems and to plan ahead, by complacently refusing to face the facts, the problems can assume disastrous proportions. Then, instead of considered and provident action, emergency treatment becomes necessary.
The alternative way of government calls for frank, fearless and continuous looking ahead to see the difficulties before they grow into crises, and to try to do the things that need to be done to prevent them from developing into an acute stage. This calls for a calm but searching appraisal of the future needs of the people of the state. It calls for intelligent planning of how best to meet those needs, how, for example, to stimulate and encourage the necessary expansion of facilities, production and enterprise, public and private, and, of course, it calls for timely action to carry out this plan. This, in my judgment, is the only sound way of government.
I think, Mr. Speaker, we should consult among ourselves and take counsel to advance the interests of each and all. We should all examine and re-examine how we can best serve our common interests. With this as our goal and with God's help, we can move forward with boldness, with confidence and with faith. Our pride is a badge of unity and a common bond amongst us all. We should not seek to divide ourselves but to unite more closely than ever, and by uniting to knit even stronger the bonds of our common welfare.
I he ve the utmost faith in our Prime Minister, in the Minister of Finance and in

The Budget-Mr. Houck the members of the cabinet that they are steering a proper course for the development of the greatest country in the world.
Much of our future will be of our own making, but some of our success will be made by others who go on and apply the knowledge, the materials and the processes we give them to different, and perhaps greater, uses than those for which they were originally intended. So I think it is with Canada. Here we are, a young nation with a great future. Already we are the world's third greatest trading nation, the fourth ranking industrial power, and the seventh steel producer. Surely, that is a record of which any nation would be proud. But it is only the beginning.
It has been said that the twentieth century belongs to Canada. That is true, but the statement does not do anything by itself. We have to make it become a fact; we have to claim it for ourselves; and believe me, Canadians are doing just that.
Let us look at it in this way. Youth is on our side. We are stepping out with all the vigour of youth into a new era in which we are equipped to choose our own road to success. We have the resources, the skills, the will and determination to do the job. By choosing the way of initiative and enterprise, operating in a free economy, Canada today stands in an enviable position. It is a land steeped in the traditions of political, personal and economic freedoms; enjoying prosperity and standing on the brink of greater things to come; it remains an outstanding example of the achievements of a modern industrial civilization.
The late Senator Taft, a great citizen, a great senator with an illustrious father, of the United States, said just a year or so before he passed away that the financial people in Washington would be well advised to go to Ottawa to study the Canadian financial structure. That is the remarkable statement he made pertaining to the financial structure of this great dominion. I think that was a very great tribute by a great man to a great country.
During the Easter holidays I made it my business to talk to many people about the budget. I did not talk just to Liberals,
I talked to people, of all political beliefs and in all walks of life. Almost each and every one of them said to me, "Yes,'.it was a great budget; we had looked for something like that but we hardly dared to expect so much". So I say to the Minister of Finance, "Carry on, you are doing a wonderful job for the people of Canada".	ii;

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have indeed been interested in listening to the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck). Like all Liberals, he seems to be a disciple of Dr. Coue. There is only one thing that I was impressed with and that is this: the hon. member knows the part he must play as a member of the Liberal party. He is firmly imbued with the idea that he should be ready to talk at all times on behalf of his party and about the great successes and the manner in which this government has handled the affairs of Canada.
The hon. member does not quite realize that a government is composed of two parties. After the election is over the majority that is counted is Her Majesty's loyal government. But the minority is Her Majesty's loyal opposition and they have a duty to perform just the same as the government. We in the opposition are not going to be mesmerized by disciples of Coue who are ready to go up and down this country saying, "We are well; nothing could be better; there is nothing wrong; there is no depression"

I am not afraid to use the word depression; I am not going to call it a recession-"everybody is working". As a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition I have a duty to perform for the people of Canada.
I am not satisfied that a country with all the natural resources which our friends have enumerated, with all the great potentialities that this country has, should be in the position we see outlined in our daily papers of having approximately 600,000 men out of work. On a recent trip to Europe I visited Italy and I was informed that they had approximately 15 million people more than that country could really support, a number almost equal to the population of Canada. They do not produce coal, timber, pulp, iron, metals of all kinds and the country is a poor farming country. Here we have all that. We say that there is unemployment in Italy and the poor people are not getting much to eat. Well, there are 600,000 people in this land about which we heard so much five minutes ago who would like to have jobs so that they could eat on the basis of their being Canadian citizens.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) was appointed to his lofty position I met a gentleman in Toronto who had never had the great pleasure I had of meeting the minister and who said to me, "This fellow Harris must be some man."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I said, "Hear, hear" at the time too, but I lived to apologize and blush

when I heard the budget. After the budget had been out I met this same gentleman and he said to me, "Did that fellow they appointed Minister of Finance think up that budget or was it the Liberal cabinet?" I said, "What made you think that?" He said, "If the cabinet had anything to do with it it would be the mess it is now, but I cannot just conceive of a man whom they would appoint as Minister of Finance, after having that great honour bestowed on him, thinking up a budget as rotten as this one. It must have been entirely the work of the cabinet."
The hon. member for Niagara Falls said that all the friends he had encountered during the Easter recess had said it was a wonderful budget. If they or any other Liberal in this house or anybody else in the country can possibly conceive that an automobile which formerly sold at $2,400 and which is now to be sold at $2,325 will encourage buying of automobiles, in my opinion that would be the greatest stretch of the imagination possible. Any man who had come that near to having the purchase price of $2,400 for a Chevrolet car would not wait until he got the last $75 before buying a car.
If this government thinks that it is any inducement for a man with four children to go out and cut loose, and as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) says, we are all out for it; if they believe that the people are going all out with a 17 cents a week saving on income tax; if they think that that is going to stimulate the progress of this country, then they are doing some thinking.
What this country should have and what it could have had-not a five cent cigar but a twenty-five cent cigar as suggested by the Liberals-is a much better set-up if they had agreed to co-operate with industry, with provincial and municipal governments, with the immigration officials and with financial people across this country. They could have achieved an over-all plan for our economy.
We should be ashamed in this vast country of ours, with its untold wealth, to say that we had 5,000 unemployed from one end of Canada to the other. We should be crying for immigrants to come here and utilize our natural resources. We must hang our heads in shame when we realize our present position. This government is in power. The government is the only body with the necessary power, with any degree of authority to say to the provincial governments, "Forget politics." In Ontario they may have a great Tory government while there is a Liberal government of Canada. This government should have them all meet at a
The Budget-Mr. Ferguson designated spot with the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Newfoundland, Quebec, British Columbia and all the rest. They should do what was done in the war and call in the best financial brains of the country openly and fearlessly and the top men of industry. That should be done before we have unemployment. They should attempt to widen the path of progress; they should be ready to go further along the path of progress. We are not interested in unemployment, we are interested in the development of the natural resources of this country.
What has been done? This is Liberal prosperity which the hon. member for Niagara Falls does not want me to mention as a member of the opposition. We had Liberal prosperity in 1939 when there were 800,000 people on relief. It was the greatest thing that ever happened to the Liberal government when Hitler declared prosperity for this country by calling a war. As late as December, 1939, there were 500,000 people registered on relief in spite of the fact that war had been going on for three months. The mayor of Midland came to Ottawa with a delegation and pleaded with the government to commence the building of ships at the shipyard at Midland. We had the finest shipyard on the great lakes at Collingwood, the town in which I live, and there were only 250 people working in that yard in 1940 with the war on. It took delegations, telegrams and full-page spreads in the newspapers before we were able to obtain the construction of ships for the war.
That is Liberal prosperity. Hitler called the war. Eventually this government was forced, through the war, to turn the wheels of industry. When we could export and utilize everything we could produce in this country we had about five years of prosperity. During the war we could not make automobiles and tires and we could not use many other things before our factories were changed over from war conditions. That took approximately two years. It has taken six years of the eight since the war to replenish the larders of this country with the necessities of life, and today the greatest undeveloped country in the world has 600,000 unemployed. I for one am not going to go through this country and say that we are doing a great job. We have been endeavouring to obtain manufacturing industries for this country. Pray God they do not hear about the actions of the Liberal government, or they will never come here. This is wishful thinking. When you hear these men who represent towns and who sit on the Liberal side of this house representing human beings here in parliament say that
30S2

The Budget-Mr. Ferguson we are well off and doing a great job- shame on them. They get up here and say that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is the greatest that Canada ever had, or that the hon. Mr. So-and-so can never be beaten. They say that he is a Canadian baby and that surely he was never born in a foreign country with intelligence like that. That is the sort of silly nonsense that you hear. The Minister of Finance until recently held the portfolio of minister of immigration. Here is a clipping from a newspaper and I presume that there is some truth in it. Twenty-six Italians entered this country by means of faked passports or forged documents of some kind obtained through government officials, and these men are being asked to return to Italy. They believed that they entered this country in good faith. They are Canadians. I believe that any people who set foot on the shores of Canada, if they are honest, Godfearing and workers, are Canadians. That to me is the mark of a Canadian, not the fact that he is born in Canada; he may be a loafer and not entitled to the name of Canadian. If there is a semblance of truth in this newspaper report and these Canadians came to this country in good faith, they should never be returned to Italy unless they wish to go back to Italy of their own accord.
Coming back from my trip to Europe, I came in to the port of Halifax, but leaving I went via Saint John. I suppose that the previous speaker would expect me to say that this was a great job. When my wife and I entered Liverpool, we left our stateroom at eight o'clock in the morning, we went through customs and immigration with people from all parts of Europe and from Australia. We had our breakfast by ten o'clock, and the boat train left the dock with passengers headed for European ports and Australia, all cleared.
When we left England and went to Europe, we landed in Calais. The Calais boat was packed with people going to various destinations throughout Europe. We went through customs and immigration, and within one and a half hours we were on the ship with passengers leaving for various destinations. On the way back from Europe, it was the same procedure.
When we arrived in the great country of Canada, which has no faults and should not be criticized, having a great government, our luggage was deposited on the docks at Halifax at three o'clock in the afternoon. At nine o'clock I was still standing freezing in the immigration and customs building, which had been built under the supervision of this government. I was there with a whole shipload of people, my overcoat on and my collar 
turned up. There was not a single spot where I could purchase any food, and all these newcomers, as well as Canadians returning to Canada, were suffering the same treatment. My luggage arrived from the dock at nine o'clock in the evening. I could obtain a cup of coffee, with milk and sugar splashed into it without any request. After I stayed 20 minutes in a line and finally reached a door that wide, I had this stuff slopped at me.

speechtext:
Was it in a
trough?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It might just as well have been in a trough. However, I busied myself in trying to obtain cups of hot coffee for new Canadians, particularly women with little children arriving in this country. They had great difficulty standing in that line and keeping control of their children. The little souls were crying for food and were asking for water and coffee. If you can visualize a newcomer to this great Canada of ours holding two or three children and trying to balance three or four cups of coffee in her hand, that is some sight. That is in the immigration hall built by this great government of ours. The people eventually got on a train for different parts of Canada. The train was freezing cold, and every one of them wore their overcoats in the modern railway carriages in this great country of ours. You are going to get some facts, gentlemen. They slept with their coats on in this train. Two superintendents of that railway line got on the train and apologized for the conditions. Before we arrived at about twelve o'clock in Montreal-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not trying to say who is to blame. I want to say what should be done by an inefficient government so that the people of Canada can really progress and unemployment will be relieved. That is all I am trying to do. I am not trying to put my finger on any group. I am trying to tell this government that it is not yet too late to reduce the number of unemployed and to proceed with the prosperity of Canada-to become more like the men who built the
C.P.R. railroad, and the other men who fought for the development of the great Dominion of Canada, the Tories. I am telling the government to try to emulate to some degree the past history of the great Conservative party of this country. If they do

so they will stay in power; if they do not they will go out at the next election, because their sins will find them out.
We arrived in Montreal at twelve o'clock. The train was shunted to the assembly unit. There was no heat in the carriages. Mr. Minister, I will secure for you a list of all the passengers on board the Scythia and send them a copy of this speech, to see whether I am telling the truth or not. They will all say that it is a fact. At approximately three in the morning a spark of heat came on in those cars. Those who were headed for Winnipeg were on the same train as I was. Another train went to Toronto. The Montrealers got off there, and I landed at Ottawa station, in the capital of Canada, with 10 or 15 people. One woman was coming to see her daughter who was married to a man in the Royal Canadian Air Force. She was approximately 70 years of age. There was not a semblance of a pbrter, a redcap or anyone else to take the luggage which they had brought with them for a two or three weeks' visit. That was not any overnight bag.
I searched around the station and found a polite and courteous railroad employee who had nothing to do with helping people to take their baggage to the warmth of the station; but he condescended or consented to take hold of a truck and together we loaded the baggage on the truck and brought the people into the warmth of the station with their baggage. These were people who could not carry their luggage. They were too old to do so. They should not have been asked to do it. That was 6.30 in the morning. That was their greeting in Canada's capital.
If the government does not know about these things, it should know about them. Those are things about which this government should call a conference and co-operate with its railroads. I am not saying which railroad was involved. But if that condition occurs on both our railroads, call them both in so that, if one is to blame, the other will not do the same thing on another occasion. Or if they are calling the provinces together, if this government is to blame, let them take the blame and see that it does not occur again. Do not worry about the premier of one province saying, "Oh, you people are always making mistakes". But the people we blame are those who make mistakes and continue to repeat them. In my opinion this government is continuing to repeat its mistakes, and has done so almost since the day it first came into power; and that is a long time unfortunately for Canada.
Today we in Canada are headed toward the same conditions with which we were confronted in 1939. I heard that the Prime
The Budget-Mr. Ferguson Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said he did not like to hear people talking blue ruin, that conditions were almost normal and that unemployment was seasonal. I say to this government, to any provincial government or to any group of people that can alleviate suffering and create employment that this is one country on the face of the globe that should say, "We need immigrants; we have absolutely no employable person who is out of work." That is the position for Canada to be in.
We cannot be satisfied because we are a little better off than, say, England. As a matter of fact, we are not as well off as England. We cannot be satisfied by saying, "England has 100,000 unemployed and we have only 15,000 who can become employed and want employment." We are in the position where we cannot say we have 5,000 people who want to work and are unemployed, having regard to the vastness of Canada, its wealth and the millions of people who are desirous of coming here and helping us to build.
It is not too late to put ourselves in the position that Canada should be in. We should have industries that we do not have today coming from Europe and establishing here. We should be creating new industries. Our ships should be going back and forth from various parts of Europe relieving those people over there who want to live in a land of plenty, and bringing them in here to do the work that should be done, in order to build this country up in a lifetime not to 15 million but to 75 million. Those are not big figures. That is not nonsensical talk at all.
Here we are a country with 15 million people. Well can I remember my father saying this to me on Portage avenue in Winnipeg, and he was then younger than I am today when he said it. He looked at the excavation for the great T. Eaton Company store on Portage avenue on a Sunday morning and he said, "Son, when you are my age this country will have 50 million people." I am now past the age that my father was when he made that remark. Through the mismanagement of Conservative and Liberal governments, the old dotards of the past, we find ourselves with 15 million people. It will be noted that I say the dotards of the Conservative party of the past also. I am not my grandfather and neither are these men in this government their grandfathers. We are alive and have the benefit of the examples of the past and the experience of the past. Those men in the government should not do the things their grandfathers did. They should have learned that people ought not to sleep in parliament.

The Budget-Mr. Ferguson They should go ahead, relieve unemployment, encourage immigration and let this be the most prosperous country in the world.
It is all very well for us to crow about this being a land of milk and honey. But we find that people coming into this great land of milk and honey are not able to obtain work. They are capable of working irrespective of their nationalities. They are good workmen irrespective of their nationalities. They begged, borrowed or stole their passage money. They are looking for work in this land of plenty. What do they find in the year 1955? They find conditions almost equal to those of 1939. At that particular time there was in power the same government that is in power today. During the election during the war and after the war they shouted about the great Liberal prosperity. As I have said before in this house, this government takes the credit for putting the oil in the ground in Alberta and for putting the nickel in the mines in Sudbury. The Kaiser used to say "Me and God". This government does not include God. The Kaiser was at least a bit honest, but not this government. They talk about the great Liberal prosperity, the growth of Niagara Falls, the immigrants coming into Niagara Falls, Col-lingwood's growth, 1,100 people employed in the shipyards during the war. Today there are 500, and if there is no new work that is not on the boards today, by the end of July the number will be down to 250. There are 800 people registered for relief in the town from which I come which has a population of 8,000.
If the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) thinks he can cow me into being quiet, he is mistaken. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) laughs. He knows that is true. He knows that in the part of the country from which he comes the condition is serious. It is not a matter to laugh over. Maybe I could do so if I were minister of finance. As the hon. member for Niagara Falls said, some people think this is a great budget. But I do not think that any member of the government has any right to crow or to laugh when he knows that a town near where he was born, namely the town of Collingwood, has 800 people on its unemployment rolls today, in this land of plenty. Maybe that is a provincial matter. Maybe it is a matter of co-operation with the provincial government. But let the members of this government stand on their feet and say who is to blame. Let them say that they cannot get the provinces to co-operate. Let them say that the great industrialists will not cooperate or that the financial institutions of Canada will not co-operate. They would not

dare do that because they know it would be a challenge that would be taken up by all those governments, institutions and peoples that I have mentioned. They would come here only too willingly to do what can be done to make Canada grow, with its great wealth, to a far greater extent than it has ever grown under the guidance of this Liberal government up to date. That is my reply to the budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada, living in a desert of Liberalism, have recently witnessed a mirage. It was obvious, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) brought down his first budget, that it was one of the greatest deceits the Liberal government has ever imposed upon the people of Canada. The budget, couched in misty terms, is nothing but a mirage. The minister touted the income tax reductions and pointed out how they ranged from 13-3 per cent for those in the lower income tax brackets to 2-8 per cent for those in the higher brackets, when actually it was a 2 per cent reduction across the board. The minister placed the mirage at a distance in the hope that by the time the people became aware of the results the matters would be forgotten.
Let us examine what this hoax will give the people of Canada. A single person with a taxable income of $1,500 will save $5 this year or $10 in a full year. That is the minister's 13 [DOT] 3 per cent. If he has an income of $3,000 he will save $20 this year or $40 in a full year, whereas an individual with an income of $100,000 will save $4,000 in a full year. A married man with two children having a taxable income of $3,000 will save $7 this year or $14 in a full year. A married man with two children having an income of $30,000 will save $644. Indeed it is nothing but deception to tell the people of Canada they are being given a tax reduction of 13-3 per cent when the tax reduction is 2 per cent and ranges in amount from $5 to $7 to $40.
Had the minister wanted to give tax relief to those in the lower income brackets he could very well have increased the exemptions from $1,000 to $1,500 for a single person and from $2,000 to $3,000 for a married person. I do not think there is anyone in Canada today who can expect to live on the present exemptions allowed by the government. By increasing these exemptions tax relief would have been given directly and in significant proportions to over a million Canadians.
