subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did you take that through the whole scale?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I took it through the whole scale. I would assume that by giving tax relief to those in the still lower income tax brackets you would have still had a figure lower than the $128 million in tax relief that the minister has granted by giving $4,000 to the man with a $100,000 income and $5 to the man with a $1,500 income. In this way tax relief would have been given to that large portion which is so urgently in need of purchasing power in a time of economic difficulty and severe unemployment in Canada. It was pointed out by my leader that if the government had desired to give relief to those really in need of it, that large and significant portion who unfortunately do not make enough money to pay income tax, they could have abolished or at least reduced the sales tax which is now levied at a 10 per cent rate on most necessities of life. The minister could have changed the social security tax so it would have some progressive features.
In looking over the minister's appraisal of economic conditions in Canada, I find that he wandered into his own mirage in assuming that the decline in the gross national product was due almost entirely to the poor wheat crop. I live in a large farming area in Saskatchewan. I do not know a single farmer who has been unable to deliver all the grain for which there has been room. We find we have a carry-over in Canada of 570 million bushels for export. I think the minister should have been aware of the fact that since the beginning of the crop year on August 1 deliveries of wheat from the farm are nearly 100 million bushels below the ten-year average.
Deliveries from the farm this year are 158 million bushels. Last year they were 268 million bushels, whereas the ten-year average is 257 million bushels. I think the purchasing power that would have been given to the farmers by this extra 100 million bushels of wheat, had they been able to deliver it, would have been a significant factor in giving our economy some purchasing power. I think it is significant that not only are deliveries of grain from the farm the lowest since the war but we also have the highest unemployment since the war. I think those are two sides of the same coin. We have deliveries at an all-time low since the war and we have unemployment at well over 600,000.
The Budget-Mr. W. M. Johnson
We find the government showing no particular concern for the plight of the farmer other than as an excuse for the decline in the gross national product. If they were really concerned I think they would be giving more consideration to the final payment on last year's crop which would at least give the. farmers some purchasing power. The farmers in the western provinces have only been able to deliver two to four bushels of low-grade wheat per specified acre. When you consider that the price of some of this wheat is 85 to 90 cents a bushel and figure what two bushels an acre will give a farmer farming on a modest scale, I am sure you can understand the plight in which he finds himself.
We had the assurance from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that the final payment on the crop would be made before seeding. At least, he hoped so, and he expressed himself in such a manner as to remove all doubt. It is apparent that the farmers of western Canada must wait until the Minister of Trade and Commerce returns from his world tour to announce the payment. We will perhaps be lucky if the payment is 5 to 7 cents a bushel, and the farmers will not receive it before seeding. In fact, they will be lucky if they receive it before they start on their second summerfallowing operations.
Anyone who has travelled through the farming areas of Saskatchewan or who comes from there is fully aware of the hazards of farming. They are aware of the fact that an insect can plague your crop and make it disappear practically overnight or that plant diseases such as the recent rust epidemic can result in total loss. They will realize how the drought of the thirties shrivelled up crops and left nothing in the heads and how excess moisture, on the other hand, can have the same disastrous result. Then there is the damage caused by hail, wind and weather throughout every operation.
When the farmers have overcome the hazards of the weather, harvested their crops, made up their tax returns and paid their tax, they are then confronted with the greatest hazard of all, the uncertainty of the whims and vagaries of the Department of National Revenue. Upon filing your return you are assessed, but the assessment often means nothing. Perhaps you will receive the assessment from the Department of National Revenue within a year, and you will continue to make out your subsequent returns assuming that the assessment made of your revenue was correct.
However, we find that the department can go back six years from the date of the last
3086	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. W. M. Johnson assessment. We find, perhaps in an unusual circumstance, that if the assessment for 1946 were received in 1950, the department can go back six years from 1946. In other words, they can go back to 1940. It is stated in the law that they can go back six years which, in effect, means seven years, since the assessment is usually made in the year after the tax year; and this will amount to eight calendar years.
I do not believe there is so much variation in the cost of production in the various tax areas throughout Canada that it should be necessary to take this length of time to properly assess a farmer's income tax. I should think that in my area of Saskatchewan, served by the Saskatoon office, it would be quite possible to process these tax returns in two years, and give a correct tax assessment.
What do we find happening to the farmer who, as I pointed out, has survived the hazards of the weather? Well, one day he might be confronted by two inquisitive gentlemen who, often without indicating their position, will proceed to question him. The standard practice is for one of them to ask the questions and the other to sit in the background with a pencil and a large notebook.
The typical approach is to ask the farmer what he thinks of the allowance for the cost of living. The farmer, having some knowledge of the cost of living, will say, "Well, gosh, I don't know; things are awfully high". The gentleman will say, "How much does it cost for you to live a year?" The farmer will say "Oh, I don't know, gosh, things are awfully high". "Let's figure it out. How much does it cost to feed your family?" "Oh, I don't know". "Well, we will put down a figure", which they do. "How much does it cost for clothing?" "Oh, things are awfully high". "Would it be about $300?" "Oh, I don't know". So then the second gentleman, who has been writing down the answers, will come up with a cost of living figure of, let us say, $3,000 a year.
Then they will divulge who they are. They will say they are auditors from the income tax branch, and they have found upon checking his returns for the last five years that he has shown a net income of $15,000. But over five years his cost of living at $3,000 a year is $15,000. "Now, what do you know about that? It is obvious that you have gypped us in income tax, and owe us a thousand dollars". Well, the farmer has admitted that was the cost of living. The man was right there writing it down, and they have assessed him on that basis.
Or they might try a different approach. They might ask him, "What car did you buy


in 1946? How much did you sell it for? What did you buy after that?" And sooner or later, knowing how good the average memory is, the farmer will make a mistake. Then the departmental inspector will point out, "Oh, no, you did not get $1,300 for that car; you got $1,900. There is a capital gain of $600", and the farmer immediately becomes confused. He just does not know what to say, or what he should not say. After this questioning the farmer is completely cowed by the brain-washing of the investigator, and in all probability he has been assessed for a figure that bears only a slight resemblance to the true figure.
It is not long before word spreads around the community that the gestapo are in town, cross checking, investigating, intimidating and frightening. And just who are these men? I am not for one moment accusing all of them of doing this with any intent of being deceitful. I think most of the income tax inspectors are trying to do their jobs conscientiously. But under the existing act there are certain procedures they must follow. They are out to collect money, and they are going to collect it.
I have obtained from the civil service of Canada an advertisement asking for auditors of income tax for the taxation division, and I was most interested in what are considered to be the desirable qualifications of those men, who are to receive $4,080 to $4,620 per annum. Their duties, among other things, are to assess farm and small business returns. The applicant must have graduation from a university of recognized standing, with specialization in commerce, business administration, finance or accounting, and at least three years' accounting experience, preferably auditing, in the office of a professional public accountant, and so on and so on.
Nowhere along the line is there any mention of any agricultural experience. They do not need to know what a tractor, or a kernel of wheat looks like. Knowing farming as I do, if you have an old Case tractor, for example, and do not have the carburetor adjusted properly, you can pour three and a half or four gallons of fuel an hour through the old brute without any difficulty. As a result gasoline consumption on your farm will be twice what it should be. If you did not keep every receipt from the company from which you bought your fuel you might be approached by this accountant, a man who might not know a Case tractor from a steam engine. He would say, "Well, you can't do that. According to accounting practice, it is so and so." And if the departmental officials

are not satisfied with the answers given by the farmer they can always ask him to make out a net worth statement.
For those who are not familiar with the net worth statement let me say that in most instances it is a complete reversal of British justice. In this connection I should like to quote from the second edition of the Canadian Encyclopedic Digest where, at page 398, they deal with making the arbitrary assessment on a net worth basis, and say:
An assessment based on the "net worth method" raises a presumption of validity in its favour that must be met by the taxpayer. The taxpayer must establish affirmatively that his taxable income was not that for which he was assessed. It is not sufficient in meeting this onus to establish a possibility that the amounts as shown in the financial statement prepared by the income tax officials are incorrect.
You can see at once the unfortunate position in which the farmer is placed when he is asked to make out a net worth statement. They will assess you arbitrarily for a certain amount and then say, "Prove me wrong." The farmer may be forced to make out a net worth statement for a period of six years, covering his assets for that period of time and contrasting those assets with those of another period of time. It is a fairly complicated procedure and, in many instances, lawyers or accountants making out these returns charge as much as $200 or $300. They are made up at the insistence of the income tax branch, which does not allow the individual to deduct the fee the lawyer charges him.
In connection with the making out of the net worth statement, I have received a copy of a very interesting form the farmer is asked to fill out. It requires information concerning personal expenditures over a period of years, and the document has eight columns. On it there are 25 items one is expected to fill in, so the income tax branch will have a complete estimate of the amount of money he has received.
This is a very interesting document indeed. "Food purchased during the year." "How much food did you buy in 1947, 1948?" and so on. "Food produced". "How much did you spend on fuel?" Well, you might have a record of it and you might not. "Clothing purchased"-and you fill this out for eight years. "How many clothes did you buy in 1946"-or 1947? "Household furnishings; household replacements; bedding; recreation; charitable donations." "Oh yes, I remember going to a show in 1947. There is 50 cents I forgot." How ridiculous can you get? Also "travelling expenses; wedding or funeral expenses."
22, 1955
The Budget-Mr. W. M. Johnson
The farmer is asked to fill out eight columns on this form covering a period of time ranging up to seven or eight years past. I am not certain just how many copies the department asks to have submitted, but the thing I want to point out is the ridiculousness of asking anyone, no matter who he may be, to make out a statement of this kind; because no one, or at least very few, would keep a record of how many wedding gifts he had given in 1947 or 1948. Therefore, why subject the farmers to such a test of their intelligence?
As I mentioned, the farmers receive their assessments year after year, with perhaps only minor adjustments. They, therefore assume that they are paying the correct tax, but five or six years later the department will disallow certain items of depreciation and bill the farmer for perhaps several hundreds of dollars. If it happens in a year like this the Department of National Revenue shows no leniency, because I hold in my hand a garnishee of an entire bank account of $609.39 of a farmer in my constituency, which was collected to pay income tax. The department will argue that the man had made the money and therefore he should pay it. No consideration is given to the fact that the farmer has marketed only two bushels of wheat per acre.
I have another statement which shows that since September 1, 22 writs have been issued by the Department of National Revenue in one of the towns in my constituency. Therefore it is apparent that the department is intent on only one thing, namely collecting money from the farmers of the western provinces. Such an unsavoury mess exists that the farmers would prefer a production tax with all its inequalities and injustices. Recently on the political scene in Saskatchewan the Gardiner machine has seemed to break down. I should like to point out that until they get the McCann machine fixed up, the Gardiner machine will continue to break down.
One of the greatest injustices that existed under the Income Tax Act was the amendment in 1949, which was made retroactive. It will be noticed that in the budget the minister brought down the 2 per cent tax reduction given to corporations was made retroactive, but in that instance the arm's-length clause was made retroactive. In Saskatchewan because of the time the province was settled, many of the farmers are reaching retirement age. We all realize the difficulty of establishing younger persons on the farm; therefore a farmer will decide to give his son the privilege of buying his farm to get him started in the farming business.

The Budget-Mr. W. M. Johnson What do we find? We find that the son gets treatment different from that given an absolute stranger. An absolute stranger can make a bona fide agreement to buy the equipment and buildings and depreciate them at the amount paid. What of the son? He cannot do that. Because of this arm's-length clause the son is not able to depreciate them at any more than the undepreciated value of the machinery as it exists. What is making it particularly difficult-and I wish the minister would look into the manifestations of this clause, because it was made retroactive without notice-is that transactions made in good faith that took place in 1947, 1948 or 1949 are subjected to the arm's-length clause, which did not exist at the time the transactions were made. If a transaction was not made in good faith and was not a bona fide agreement I could see some excuse for the department disallowing the depreciation charged. This factor is making it very difficult indeed for a son to start up and take over where his father left off.
In some instances all that needs to be done is this; and I hope there are enough people familiar with this so they can save themselves the difficulties that others have been subjected to. If it is a transaction between a father and a son, what the father does is take out the machinery and haul it into the machine agent and say, "I'll give you $5 if you will buy this machinery and sell it all back to my son at the same price." The son then takes it back to the farm. In that way he can get away from the arm's-length clause and the transaction is perfectly valid.
We find another aspect of the departmental work that is particularly annoying to the farmers in the three prairie provinces is its inefficiency. I recall a case that was brought to my attention. The farmer pointed out that he had filed his return and in a few days received a refund of $100. The department said, "You paid us too much; you did not owe that much." Well, the farmer was quite pleased, but in three months' time he received a registered letter from the department saying, "We made a mistake; you did owe us the $100. Pay it back with interest." I found that quite interesting and I asked the farmer to give me a little more information. He said, "Gosh, no; I don't want to get into any trouble with those fellows."
The officials operating under the Income Tax Act have put the fear of the Lord, or the fear of something, into the farmers of Saskatchewan. As I pointed out, they are able to deal with the weather but they are not able to deal with the various rulings made by the departmental officials. I recall 
another instance where a farmer had a building destroyed by a cyclone. He had just built it. He was forced to build it, as a matter of fact, to house his grain, and was just putting the roof on when the cyclone came along and blew the whole thing down. Had it not been blown down he could have depreciated it at 5 per cent over its useful life; but since it was blown down and no longer existed, he is allowed no depreciation and is out $4,600.
While I am on this matter of depreciation may I say that it is most unfortunate that over the past years, when we have had congestion on the farms, consideration has not been given to the rightful claims of the farmers to be given accelerated depreciation for granaries constructed on the farms. I realize that we must have a certain number of granaries to store the crops. In some instances farmers have had to build granaries to store twice the crops they would normally store, and as this congestion wears off they will have empty shells sitting on the prairies waiting for a cyclone. It will not make much difference, because they get so little depreciation now, they might as well get none at all.
If the department do not feel they should give the complete depreciation I wish they would consider giving an accelerated depreciation on a certain percentage of the buildings. Suppose accelerated depreciation were given to the farmer on all the grain storage built in addition to that required to house two-thirds of the average yield on two-thirds of his cultivated acreage. He could have the normal depreciation on anything up to that limit. Naturally, the space he would require over and above that should be depreciated in three years.
I am also interested, Mr, Speaker, in another feature of farm income tax. It will be noticed that in the United States farmers are permitted to charge off soil and water conservation against current income up to 25 per cent of the gross farm income. A very significant change has been made in the United States income tax legislation making this allowance. In Canada this is deemed to be a capital gain. You might on occasion have a deep gully washed out in your land, and might have to pay $50 to have it filled in to restore the land to its Drevious condition. But that is considered to be capital gain and you cannot deduct it for income tax purposes.
There is another very interesting aspect to income tax as it operates in Canada, and that is the tax paid by farmers in the various provinces. I should like to place on record the figures for the 1952 income tax year,

which are the latest we have and which come from the tax statistics. They are as follows:

We find that in Ontario and Quebec there are 3,024 farmers per assessor whereas in the western provinces the number is 1,973 farmers per assessor. We find that in Quebec there are 9,595 farmers per assessor as compared with 2,036 in Saskatchewan. If the minister thinks I believe the farmers of Ontario and Quebec are not paying their share of income tax he perhaps would not be too far wrong, but what I want to point out is that it is stated in the Income Tax Act that you must maintain books and records. I believe it is the function of assessors to go around to make sure the farmers are keeping books and records. I have a copy of a letter from the income tax department which points out the necessity of keeping books and records, and it concludes by asking the farmer to advise when he has complied with the above request. It would appear that the 14 income tax assessors in the province of Quebec will require additional help if they are going to call on 134,336 farmers and ask them to keep proper records.
These are some aspects of the manner in which the income tax department has been operating. I think you will agree that there are some changes and improvements which could be made. As I pointed out, the farmers have been intimidated by the departmental officials, and it is very difficult to get statements from them. They refuse to give you information. I would like the minister to see what he can do about correcting some of these most flagrant injustices.
In conclusion I should like to state that I am in wholehearted support of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as all hon. members had an opportunity during the Easter recess to return to their constituencies and consult with those whom they represent in this house, I am sure those of us who support this government returned very much encouraged by the public acceptance of this budget. I am sure that hon. members opposite do not come back to take part in the budget debate in any way aided or comforted in the task before them.
In the debate this afternoon the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) in the course of his remarks referred to experiences which he underwent on his return from Europe a few weeks ago, when he landed at the port of Halifax. I am not going to deal in any great detail with what the hon. member had to say, not having been there at the particular time to which he referred. I am unaware of the actual facts involved. However, I do know that the building to which he referred mainly in his remarks is not only newly built but is a building which at the time he was there was, and indeed still is, under construction. I would point out to the house that the inconvenience and difficulties which he experienced were obviously the result of the upsetting and unusual conditions which always exist when a building is required to be used for its normal purposes while it is in the course of construction or substantial renovation.

I can assure the hon. member and the house that so far as the treatment of immigrants and other passengers landing at the port of Halifax is concerned, the evidence I have seen is completely contrary to the evidence that was given in this house this afternoon by the hon. member. I have on many occasions been present when large numbers of immigrants and other passengers were being handled by the immigration facilities at Halifax. I have seen the facilities provided there for them, the speed and courtesy with which the necessary formalities of customs inspection and other matters are carried out, and the general satisfaction shown by those who go through the normal procedure of landing at that port. I have seen many completely unsolicited letters written to individuals and officials at the port of Halifax thanking them for the extreme courtesy and care that has been shown in dealing with newly-arrived Canadians, particularly, and the general public as well.
Mr. Speaker, my real purpose in entering this debate is to deal with a question which is, I think, of considerable importance and interest to this house and to the Canadian people. Statements have been made in this debate by several hon. members opposite, and indeed they have been made outside this house by the same members and others, to the effect that we in this country export an undue proportion of our natural resources in the raw and unprocessed state. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), particularly, in the last day or so have made assertions of this kind in contributions to this debate. The well-worn phrase, "the hewers of wood and drawers of water" has been used. The suggestion has been made and the impression left that government policies are at fault and that there exists a situation which is unhealthy and not in the best interests of Canada.
I want to deal with this matter on a factual basis, to try to point out just what is the real situation and then deal with some of its implications for the Canadian economy and the Canadian people. First of all I should like to make two or three preliminary points. The first is that Canada is the greatest trading nation in the world on a per capita basis. This trade and the resultant Canadian prosperity has been built up in the only way that was possible, namely by producing the things we can produce and which can be sold on
The Budget-Mr. Dickey the world market, and producing them better and more cheaply than they can be obtained from other sources.
The second point is that if we take a narrow point of view it is possible to say with truth that to manufacture completely in Canada the raw materials we produce would provide to Canada, in the form of income and employment, the maximum return which can be achieved from those particular materials. However, in my view it is not true to argue from that particular statement to the general statement and say that it follows that the maximum benefit of resources development in Canada would accrue to us by insisting upon complete manufacture of all our raw materials before they leave this country. Our experience and, I believe, that of other countries, seems to me to prove that a sound program of resources development cannot be built on such a narrow foundation. What is perhaps even more important, I think our experience proves that a broad program of resources development creates the only possible basis on which any substantial development of secondary industries can be built.
The third point I should like to make is that we ourselves are dependent on imports of raw materials. I do not think it is generally recognized or understood that we in this country are, in fact, net importers of industrial raw materials. We hear a great deal about Canada being a great storehouse of natural resources and that the world is becoming increasingly dependent on Canadian raw materials. Those statements are true. But what Canadians do not realize is the fact that we are a net importer of the raw materials that go into our industrial production.
For example, in 1953 our exports of industrial raw materials amounted in value to some $300 million. These included nickel, pulpwood, iron ore, asbestos, copper, zinc and other similar products. Our imports of industrial raw materials in the same year amounted to about $550 million, covering such things as crude petroleum, coal, raw cotton, iron ore, raw wool, crude rubber, etc. Hence we are a net importer of industrial raw materials to the extent of about a quarter of a billion dollars.
What is the explanation of our dependence on these imports? Canada has a rapidly growing industrial economy which requires raw materials which we do not produce or which we have not in this country, but which we are obliged to go out and buy, sometimes at extremely high costs. We believe in buying

The Budget-Mr. Dickey in the cheapest markets in the world, and we get our imports from the cheapest sources. But the point I want to make is that those who are critical of our exports of raw materials would do well to recognize and keep in mind the dependence of our secondary industries on imports of essential materials which we ourselves do not possess.
Let us look at the facts of our trade. I am going to use 1953 because that is the last year for which final figures are available. The principal raw materials we export are agricultural and vegetable products consisting mainly of food; animal and animal products, which also are to a large extent food; non-ferrous metals; non-metallic minerals and their products; and wood and wood products. In 1953 the proportion of our total exports which were raw materials was 32-2 per cent. The proportion of our total exports that were partially manufactured or semi-processed was 28-9 per cent and the proportion of those which were fully manufactured . was 38-9 per cent.
The first point of importance to recognize in these figures is that the largest segment of our export trade is in fully manufactured goods. The second is that the value of our exports of fully manufactured goods was $1,600 million in round figures. The value of our raw material exports was $1,328 million. In spite of all that has been said by hon. members, opposite and others, the first fact to remember is the preponderance of fully manufactured goods in our export trade. The second is that adding the proportion of semi-manufactured goods in our export trade, the total amounts to 67-8 per cent. In other words, two-thirds of our export trade consists of fully manufactured and semi-manufactured goods, combined with only one-third left for the export of raw materials.
A closer examination of these figures brings out some even more striking facts. Of our total raw material exports, approximately 80 per cent are agricultural and vegetable products, wheat, feed grains and various kinds of food products. These things are exports which must almost inevitably leave this country in their raw state because they are designed for either human or animal consumption. If we add to these agricultural and vegetable products the category of animal and animal products the proportion rises considerably more, in fact to over 85 per cent. In other words if we were to try, as was suggested by the hon. member for Broadview, to make some extreme, and I think impractical, efforts to reduce the proportion of our exports which are in the category of raw materials, we would either have to stop


exporting wheat and feed grains and that sort of thing or try to work on a mere 15 per cent of our total export trade.
One result of the speeches and statements that have been made on this subject by hon. members opposite has been, I think, to create in the minds of the Canadian public an idea that our resources development industries are in some way in the category of poor relations in the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, I think nothing could possibly be further from the fact. Canada's resources industries in 1953 provided jobs for 1-6 million Canadians, or 31 per cent of Canada's total labour force. Thirty-four per cent of Canada's national income of $19 billion was earned by Canadians working in these industries, and 564 per cent of the Canadian investment program undertaken by business, amounting to $34 billion, was devoted to the development, the growth and the extraction of our natural resources from our lands, our forests and our waters.
We all recognize, Mr. Speaker, how important to the Canadian economy has been our great investment program, amounting to over $5 billion last year, and I think it would be most unfair to that great segment of our economy, the resources development industry, not to recognize that almost two-thirds of that investment program arises out of that particular industry.
I should like as briefly as I can to cite some of the reasons our resources industries are so important to Canada and to the Canadian economy. First of all there is the contribution we make to international security and prosperity. Industrial raw materials, fuels and food are the three basic economic ingredients which a free world requires in its endeavours to increase international security and prosperity. We in Canada not only have an abundance of these resources but we are developing them in an efficient manner and at a rate that is hardly matched by any other country. Therefore a broad resources base makes Canada one of the strongest natural allies in the cold war for the United States and the other countries of the western alliance.
The second matter to which I should like to draw attention is that the expansion of our resources industries is balanced with a growth of secondary industries. Our resources development in Canada has gone hand in hand with the expansion of secondary industries. Both these developments have taken place in response to long-term demands, and there has been little if anything in the way of forced or specially induced expansion in Canadian resources development or in secondary industries. The sole exception is certain

developments during and after the war for defence reasons. Notwithstanding the recent renewal in the house and elsewhere of the cry that we are the hewers of wood and drawers of water, our production of food and raw materials continues to be looked upon not only by Canadians but by our allies as very respectable occupations, and we are interested in an economic expansion that is well balanced but which will have to be on the basis of resources development as well as the industrial front.
The third point I should like to make has to do with the diversification that we have been able to achieve in our resources development, which has lessened our economic vulnerability. Canadian resources development, as a result of the program that has been carried on over the last few years, is now much more broadly based than it ever was before. In the fuel field, coal and hydro power are supplemented by the newcomers, oil and natural gas. In the mining field our traditional resources of nickel, copper, lead and zinc have been supplemented by uranium and titanium. Further, resources industries, which were of minor importance before the war, have become major factors in our industrial raw material development-for example, aluminum and iron ore. This broadening of our natural resources base has undoubtedly removed some of the vulnerability of the Canadian economy, which was inclined to suffer when world demand dropped for certain particular commodities.
The fourth matter to which I should like to refer is the contribution that resources development has made to strengthening regional economies within Canada. Our resources development program has made an important contribution to Canadian regional economic diversification and to the opening up of new land for settlement. For example, the prairie provinces used to depend primarily on agriculture for their prosperity. Now we have important oil and natural gas developments in Alberta, uranium mining in Saskatchewan, and nickel and copper mining in Manitoba, with processing and refining industries located in these regions in increasing numbers. More recently the development of mining prospects in the maritime provinces and Newfoundland is having an increasing effect. The Kitimat aluminum project, the Lynn Lake non-ferrous metal mines, the Labrador iron development, all mean the building of new railway lines into these regions and the opening up of new areas of virgin northern country.
The fifth point is the effect that the development of our resources industries has had
The Budget-Mr. Dickey on improving our balance of payments position. We have been selling as much of our raw materials resulting from these great developments that could not be used in Canada at excellent prices on foreign markets, and this has had a very beneficial effect on the Canadian economy.
The final point is the general one of the contribution to general economic stability. Canadian resources located in inaccessible regions, or difficult to prove up or extract on an economic basis, could in most cases only be developed by the making of large capital expenditures. In the post-war period substantial and for the most part increasing amounts have been invested for this purpose in this country. High capital spending for resources development has been one of the most dynamic and vital factors making possible a continuing rise in Canadian economic activities. In fact, but for the very large and diversified resources program, Canadians could not have avoided the consequences of the so-called inventory recession in 1949 in the United States to the extent we did.
Having dealt with our resources development industry, I should like to come to the vital question of whether we should process more of our industrial raw materials before export and, if so, how it should be done. This is a problem that has been given consideration for many years. When the alternative was between leaving the resources unused or selling them abroad in unprocessed form, initially at least, the answer given in this country in most cases has been, let us go ahead with the development of these resources. But this problem has remained how to increase processing at home and how to convince our customers that it is in their own as well as in our long-term interests for them to take more raw materials in processed form when they can be produced in Canada more efficiently than or at least as efficiently as in other countries.
What progress has been made in this regard? With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on Hansard two tables taken from the government publication "Trade of Canada". These tables show the total exports of Canada for 1929 and 1953, both in percentage and value terms, broken down as between raw materials, partially manufactured goods, and fully manufactured goods.

I am putting on the record in these tables the total proportions for 1953, and the same information is given in the table for 1929. These figures show that since 1929, by reason of natural development, we have made significant progress in increasing the proportion of natural resources products being exported in processed form, either fully or semimanufactured. The table will show that there are four main groups of exports which show substantial declines in the proportions shipped abroad in raw form in 1953 as compared with 1929. Three other main groups show somewhat smaller increases. The main decreases took place in the classification of non-metallic minerals and their products, which were down one-half, from 70 per cent in 1929 to 35 per cent in 1953; in fibres, textiles and textile products, down from 18 to 7 per cent; in non-ferrous metals and their products, down to 23 per cent from 36 per cent in 1929.
If hon. members will study these tables I believe they will see a very clear pattern emerge. From this I submit that it does not appear that we are shipping an unduly large amount of our natural wealth out of this country, in its raw state, to supply factories in other countries. It is true that we do export considerable quantities of natural resources products in their raw form, especially foodstuffs, but their relative share of our total exports is declining, and the great bulk of our non-food raw material exports is processed to varying extents in Canada.
The belief has been expressed that if Canada insisted that all her natural resources products be completely processed before being exported, unparalleled prosperity would result. Unfortunately it is not nearly as simple as all that. For example, to begin with, any attempt to compel foreign buyers of Canadian products to alter the form of their purchases would lead quickly to serious losses of our world markets. There are alternate supplies and substitute materials for most of our natural resources products, and undoubtedly other countries would utilize these in the face of any such Canadian restrictions.
Second, any such action would invite retaliation. Other countries would follow suit to Canada's ultimate detriment, as we are on balance, as I pointed out earlier, a heavy net importer of raw materials of the industrial type. If the inward flow of these raw materials were interrupted our steel mills, our textiles mills, our natural rubber and aluminum smelting industries would suffer severely. The aluminum smelting industry would be especially vulnerable, since it

depends entirely upon imported bauxite and imported cryolite, with Canada's main contribution being abundant low-cost hydro power.
In addition, some of our exports of raw materials are really part of an exchange trade based on the economies of transportation or on the interchange of complementary products. Both these factors operate in the two-way flow of iron ore, with the totals being almost in balance in 1953, when exports were valued at about $31 million and imports at $28 million. For similar reasons of economy it may turn out that when Canada achieves a large measure of self sufficiency in crude petroleum supplies it will be done by large exports balancing large imports rather than by processing all our own crude oil.
I should like now to deal with the extent of industrialization that would be required in Canada to process all the natural resources products we are capable of producing. This may be gathered by looking at the iron and steel picture. It is expected that within a few years Canada's iron ore capacity will have expanded to 25 million tons annually. The question arises, why do we permit the export of this raw material rather than require its conversion in Canada into steel and steel products?
Superficially that is an attractive suggestion. But besides the necessity of finding markets for that steel production, there is the rather difficult problem of finding $5 billion in capital investment which would be required to create in this country that kind of steel capacity. Without assured markets I am very much afraid that we would not find capital ready to risk itself in that way.
In summary, if I may just list the reasons for the present state of our trade in raw products and manufactured goods, and the reasons for the developments which have taken place since 1929, I would say, first, that Canada is a low-cost producer of a number of raw materials for which there is a world-wide demand in their natural form, and has become an important source of supply for many of the countries which need these raw materials.
Second. Canada's domestic market for most of these materials is small, and frequently such resources would not be developed at all except for the export market. For example, the nickel developments at Sudbury would never have been made to meet the requirements of the Canadian plating industry.
Thirdly, it is usually more economic to produce in larger quantities; and selling in wider markets reduces the cost of production, which

benefits the Canadian consumer and the Canadian manufacturer who also uses these raw materials.
Fourth, the development of natural resources often contributes to regional economic development, as I have pointed out.
Fifth, the development of Canada's natural resources for the export market usually paves the way for the setting up of domestic industries to process the resulting materials for home use, and eventually for export as well. Certainly that has been our experience in a number of fields.
Finally, the export of raw materials is a part of Canada's economic structure and any drastic reduction, whether due to restrictions on exports in raw form or not, would upset the whole economy. Any upset in the balance of payment pattern could mean large trading deficits for Canada, and eventually even the curtailment of essential imports.
Therefore I think that in respect of this, as in many other problems, the correct view is the balanced view based on the facts. I submit that the generalized and unsupported statements made very frequently on this matter by hon. members opposite have not been contributions to clear thinking in respect of the Canadian economic position today or its future prospects.

to see that those empires will be set up under conditions and in locations that will be in the best interests of Canada as a whole.
I feel that there are three main departments of our government that would be economically affected by planning of this kind. The first department is that of transport. Indications are that our railroad systems have been operating at a tremendous deficit for the last year. In fact we know that in the year 1954 the Canadian National Railways had a deficit of $28,758,098. They find that some of this deficit arises from the fact that quite a number of their branch lines are not paying. I feel that if industry, which is being centralized in our metropolitan areas, could be distributed throughout the entire width and breadth of our country it would naturally give more business and bring more revenue to our transportation systems. I also feel that if many of these branch lines are discontinued the possibility of smaller communities getting any of these industries will become practically nil.
Another department that is involved is the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources which, through co-operation with the provincial departments of planning and development, should take some steps to see that great industrial empires do not encroach on our very valuable agricultural lands. I speak particularly of the lands in southern Ontario, where we have been endowed by old mother nature with fertile soil, a moderate climate and all the natural attributes to make that one of the most productive fruit and vegetable districts in the world. Man can never replace these natural resources which have been given to us, and there are many districts where soil and natural conditions make it impossible to carry on agriculture economically, yet where it would be feasible to build manufacturing plants.
Then we have one other department of the government which is directly involved, namely the Department of National Health and Welfare, which has the task of promoting and developing civil defence. We hope and pray that these tense periods will pass and there will not be another great war, but we know that we must look upon this matter with a sense of reality when all the great nations of the world are doing their utmost to keep ahead in the creation of new weapons of destruction. To this department falls the task of looking after the safety of the citizens of our country in case of attack.
When so many people are gathered together in great metropolitan areas the task of protecting or removing them from these areas becomes well-nigh impossible. We shudder to think what could happen. We have seen

The Budget-Mr. W. M. Howe it happen before when our weapons of destruction were many times less devastating than they are today. Had more thought and planning been given to this situation the expensive projects that we find in our larger centres to relieve traffic congestion, such as subways and through expressways, might not have been necessary. I feel that if more direction were given, many industries could settle in smaller communities to the mutual advantage of both the industries and the communities. Today we find that people living in those smaller communities are demanding and getting all the facilities provided in more thickly populated areas. If they had more supporting taxpayers the burden of municipal taxation on property owners would be less oppressive.
The second matter I wish to speak about is also one that has been given considerable publicity in this house, but it is also one about which I feel not too much has been done. I refer to the condition of the farming industry in our country. When one looks over the budget one finds that as regards the farmers as a whole very little relief has been given to alleviate the trying circumstances in which they find themselves. It is true that the average farmer may pay a few cents less in income tax, though when I spoke to a couple of my constituents during the Easter recess I found that one indicated that his reduction in revenue from the sale of his hogs over the past year was $2,500, while in the case of the other the reduction was $1,500. Therefore I think they will find that their reduction in income tax will be very small this year because a lot of them will not have to pay any tax. The farmer may get his tires a little cheaper. If he has a car to turn in he will likely pay a little less for a new one than he did before.
A survey by Dr. MacFarlane, of the Macdonald agricultural college, indicated that according to the bureau of statistics a year's work by an agricultural worker was worth only $3,600, while a year's work by workers in other occupations was worth almost $5,000. The explanation is that while the prices of farm products have been steadily declining for several years, the prices being charged for other products have been going up. In other words the producers of our agricultural products are not getting an undue share of the national production.
I am sick and tired of the fanfare and headlines that follow declines in agricultural prices. So much has been said about our high-cost economy that when beef prices drop, when hogs, poultry, or any other agricultural products go down in price, headlines proclaim that according to the index of the bureau of
[Mr. Howe (Wellington-Huron) .1

statistics the cost of living has dropped. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that when it is caused by only one segment of our economy it is too much to shout about, and I feel it is a very selfish way of looking at this question.
No part of our national economy can live unto itself today. If farm prices drop, the things the farmers buys are fewer, and believe me, he is willing to buy when he is making a profit on his operation. He is willing to buy such products as farm implements, clothing, electrical appliances, automobiles and many other ordinary commodities of everyday life. When the farmer stops buying the manufacturers of all those commodities find that production soon catches up with the demand and there are lay-offs that are not all caused by the dumping of commodities by other countries where labour costs are lower. They are caused partly by the falling off in the purchasing power of one of the basic industries of our country.
I say that part of the fluctuation in the farmers' prices and in our agricultural returns results from the fact that today we have no definite, genuine market on which we can depend from year to year. The United States of America has from time to time been a good customer, but under ordinary circumstances and in an average year the United States produces more agricultural products than she herself can use.
The budget gave no indication that there would be any increased promotion of trade in agricultural products with other countries. There was a time when we enjoyed access to and even preference in the British markets where, because of their tremendous population, there are approximately 30 million people to be fed every year, and which is one of the most permanent and stable markets in the world for agricultural products. There was a time when our cheese ranked first in demand by the people of Britain. How do we know that the newer generations who have grown up and who have developed an appetite for this product from other countries will have the same preference as the rank and file of British people?
In those days not only did our cheese go to Britain, but our butter, our pork and our heavy steers went to that market. We do not send any beef today, and in that connection it might be interesting to note that Britain buys 70 per cent of the beef produced in the world. I feel that a great deal of the uncertainty in our agricultural economy is due primarily to the loss of this market.
This great Liberal government tells us that one of the reasons we had to give up the

British market was that Britain did not have the dollars with which to buy the products of our farms. But did this government leave no stone unturned to see that every possible dollar's worth of defence production was spent in Britain? The report of the Department of Defence Production, January 1 to December 31, 1954, indicates that materials purchased in the United States in the period April 1, 1951 to December 31, 1954 totalled $493,731,000, whereas those purchased in Great Britain amounted to only $104,255,000. Had more dollars been spent in Britain she might have had dollars which could have been used to stabilize our agricultural economy.
This government has been telling business, which has been in straitened circumstances for years, that they are faced with another buyer's market. This applies not only to business in Canada but to business in the international field. If the farmers of our country felt that there were adequate markets for their products and that when they were ready for market there would not be a surplus they could produce more than they are producing of cattle, hogs, poultry, butter, cheese, etc., and their cost of production would be reduced while our gross national product would be increased.
In the face of continued drops in agricultural prices there is one other thing I should like to mention, a phase which was applicable not only to my own riding in 1954, but because of excessive rainfall during the harvest season applied equally to many districts, particularly in southern Ontario. It is true that last year the western provinces had an unusually wet crop year, but the farmers there have the facilities of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to help them when needed. The farmers in southern Ontario depending on late crops such as flax, white beans, soybeans and sugar beets to get extra money to pay taxes and many other yearly debts that accumulate, particularly in these days of high production costs on our farms, found there was no assistance available to them.
I maintain that what is good for one section of this dominion in time of economic strain should be applicable and within the reach of every farmer who needs it. I should like to endorse the suggestion made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that we recommend the development of an adequate scheme of crop insurance with costs to be borne jointly by the federal and provincial governments and the producers.
In closing I should like to say a few words about education, a matter which I understand will be brought up before the coming dominion-provincial conference. We have no 50433-196J
The Budget-Mr. Herridge greater asset in our country than our youth, and we should leave no stone unturned to see that everything possible is done to fit them to take their place in the world of today. Most municipalities are trying to do this, but with the limited means of taxation at their disposal they are finding it well-nigh impossible.
I feel that the federal government, which now takes over 75 per cent of the tax dollar, must do more to assist this very important function of government at all levels. This was the conclusion arrived at after a research program carried out by the Canadian school trustees' association under the direction of Dr. M. E. LaZerte, a distinguished Alberta educationalist. This report indicates that to ensure equality of educational opportunity for all Canadian children the dominion government should designate special grants to the provinces for the specific purpose of assisting education.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

I have learned them since that time. Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment and the subamendment. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) expressed the collective views of this group so far as major criticisms of the budget are concerned. I do not intend to weary the house by a repetition of his explanations. I merely want to re-emphasize and deal with a few matters of particular concern to working people in this country generally, and to bring to the attention of the minister a few matters of particular concern to some of my constituents! which they have asked me to raise during this debate on the budget.

The Budget-Mr. Herridge
The minister made provision for a percentage reduction of the corporation tax and a percentage reduction of personal income tax. On first hearing it sounded rather good, but on later calculating it did not look so good. I am of the opinion that it would have served the interests of the lower income groups much better if he had accepted the suggestions that have come from this party-in recent years, that he increase the basic exemption for single persons to $1,500 per annum and for married persons to, say, $3,000 per annum. The present proposals of the minister merely mean a saving of a few cents a day, and in fact afford no actual relief to the low income groups.
I suggest that the loss of revenue that would be occasioned by increasing exemptions could be made up in other ways. We in this group recognize the fact that a certain amount has to be raised by taxation. Taxes are required to pay for the things we advocate; we do not back away from that. We in this group point out what we consider a fair distribution of the tax burden in this country. In our opinion there was no necessity at all at this time for a reduction of the income tax for corporations. That would be one way to meet the loss of revenue occasioned by increasing income tax exemptions.
We think there should be the imposition of a capital gains tax, which we believe would bring a considerable sum to the treasury of this country. We think that if the minister removed the 20 per cent tax credit allowed on dividends from Canadian corporations his revenue would be considerably increased. We believe the policy we have suggested would be sound and would cover the loss of revenue occasioned by extending the exemptions to lower income group people.
We believe the minister could have assisted the lower income groups by removal of the 3 per cent floor on medical expenses. If the minister considers it proper to reduce the income tax for corporations. That would the time has come to give effect to the wishes of the House of Commons that have been expressed in this respect. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and other members of this group have advocated the abolition of the 3 per cent floor for some years, and we hope that, even before this debate is finally concluded, the minister will again consider the proposals coming from this side of the house.
Now I should like to deal with a few matters which are of particular concern to some of my constituents and which, as I said before, they have asked me to bring to the


attention of the minister. There are many working people in Canada, both salary and wage earners, who because of circumstances are required to live some distance from their place of employment-in my constituency it is a matter of between five and thirty miles-not because they wish to live that distance away from their employment but because in many cases they are forced to live that distance away in order to obtain satisfactory housing accommodation and so on; as for instance the employees of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. This is a large corporation operating in my constituency, and I think the circumstances are typical of those existing in many other parts of Canada. There are thousands of those employees who have to travel from five to thirty miles a day to and from their employment. These expenses are considerable. They vary from $10 to $35 a month. They are all unavoidable expenses incurred by these salaried and wage-earning people.
I believe other members of this group agree with me that if the minister can allow the travelling expenses of a commercial traveller who goes around the country selling bubble gum or something as unnecessary as that, surely he could give consideration to allowing these salaried and working people an exemption on account of these abnormal travelling expenses. I am not suggesting that the ordinary expense of 10 or 25 cent street car rides to work should be exempted for income tax purposes, but I do think there is a sound case for consideration of those who have to spend from $10 to $35 a month travelling to and from their employment day after day. I urge the minister to give this representation consideration.
I noticed that when the minister was speaking on the budget he made some reference to special incentive provisions for certain companies. I find on page 2738 of Hansard the following:
Our tax laws contain special incentive provisions for the oil, gas and mining industries. It has been the policy in the past few years to review these provisions each year and annually to grant an extension of them. There are certain advantages in this procedure but, on the other hand, it carries with it some uncertainty for the future. In the past few months I have been giving considerable thought to the operation of these incentives and to the importance of these two industries to the future of Canada. I believe these special tax provisions have clearly established their value in promoting expansion and I now propose to make them a permanent part of our law.
I think the minister is quite correct in stating that this provision has been a special incentive in the exploration for these natural

resources. In my opinion there is some justification for giving consideration to these corporations in this respect because they are endeavouring to develop natural resources, and I think we should promote such development.
However, once again I should like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that I believe the farmers of this country should get similar consideration. If these incentive provisions are justified for these corporations which are expanding production by developing natural resources, then ethically speaking, and by the same token, I think the farmers of this country are entitled to similar consideration. Every new acre cleared, drained or irrigated increases production in this country and this increase performs the same function as does the development of natural resources performed by these companies to which I have referred. I think the farmers of this country who are increasing production by doing the things I have mentioned are entitled to exactly the same consideration as these corporations which are carrying on exploration for the development of our natural resources. I again urge the minister to give consideration to our pleas from this side of the house on behalf of the farmers of this country.
I must say in passing, Mr. Speaker, that I was pleased to note that the minister has decided on the reduction or elimination of tariffs on brooders for farm animals, certain components of feedstuffs, sweet potato seedlings, poultry eviscerating equipment and other machinery connected with agricultural production. I am pleased indeed to see that statement. While in the reading of the paragraph this announcement might not mean a great deal to some members of the house or to other people not acquainted with the circumstances, I know personally that it brings a measure of relief to some of our poultry producers and some of our farmers. I am pleased that the minister has seen fit to do this. I am glad that the representations of the farm organizations and of members of this house in this respect have received favourable consideration by the minister.
We are all pleased with the repeal of the excise tax on tires and tubes, regardless of their use, and with the 5 per cent reduction in the excise tax on automobiles. I am sure that step is welcomed by employers and employees in the automobile industry, and by a good many purchasers of cars in Canada. However, I think that the decision of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) not to allow claims for refunds arising out of tax reduction in respect of goods upon which taxes have been paid
The Budget-Mr. Herridge occasions some injustice. In that respect I have had representations from automobile dealers in my constituency. I know a good number of these smaller dealers very well indeed and I think there is some justification for consideration of their protests and their claims.
The implementation of the budget places some of them in quite a serious position. To illustrate the effect this decision of the Minister of National Revenue has on their businesses, I am going to read one letter I have received, and it is typical. I think it illustrates the position of the average small automobile dealer. My correspondent has this to say:
In connection with the reduction in excise taxes on new vehicles, we understand that no provision has been made in the budget to take care of new vehicles in dealers' stocks prior to bringing down the budget.
This places practically every dealer in the country in a very awkward position. Every used vehicle on our lots has to be reduced proportionately, which we are quite ready to assume, of course. This is a large item in itself, as any larger dealer has in the vicinity of $50,000 worth of used cars for sale.
My firm's stock of new vehicles on hand on April 5th totalled 20 units, on which we had paid $6,315.80 excise tax. In effect, without any rebate from the department, we stand to lose $2,105.27, in addition to the revision in our used car inventories.
The argument seems to be that the last time they raised the excise tax they did not assess stocks in dealers' hands at the time. However, if I recall correctly, there were practically no dealer stocks in existence at that time-and certainly there was no request from the dealer organizations to be excused from collecting the additional tax.
We automobile dealers are responsible for the collection of vast amounts of taxes for the government-which we pay in advance long before most of the sales are actually made.
May we respectfully request you to make a serious plea to the honourable minister to implement ways and means of rebating dealers for stocks on hand as of April 5th?
I think there is some justification for the complaints of these automobile dealers, particularly the smaller ones, who will be quite seriously embarrassed by the application of the law according to the decision of the Minister of National Revenue. I urge that he give their representations further consideration.
There are one or two other matters I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. The first is one that I have brought to the attention of the house repeatedly throughout the last six or seven years. I have a number of constituents who practice forestry conservation. Some of them have wood lots; they might be termed large wood lots. Some have small timber holdings and some have holdings which are somewhat larger. But they are men who throughout the years have attempted to conserve a certain area of timber varying all the way from 100 acres to, in some cases, 5,000 acres. They have

The Budget-Mr. Herridge built roads. They have built trails. They have done thinning on their properties and they have made provision for easy access to the forests in case of fire.
In some cases these men have been doing this for 50 years. They have been conserving cutting from these natural resources throughout the years, and I know several who at the present time have more timber today than they had the day the first axe was swung in those timber holdings.
For persons who are practising conservation policies with respect to the management of timber I suggest that some opportunity should be allowed for certain income tax deductions, such as those that are allowed in the United States, for moneys expended directly in practising these policies. I know that the larger lumber companies are enabled to charge up to operations the cost of roads and certain other costs in developing large timber holdings. I think those arrangements are made with the income tax department. I have never been able to get to the bottom of that deal, as a matter of fact, but I am quite sure that a good many of the smaller timber holders are not able to take advantage of these provisions.
I believe some arrangement should be made for these smaller holders.
In our country there is going to be a much greater development-and I am very keen on it myself-of the woodlot and the smaller managed timber holding of anywhere, as I said before, from 100 acres to 5,000 acres. These people who are providing for the maintenance of the supplies of forest resources should receive some compensation for capital expended now on which in many cases they will receive no return in their lifetime. I know men who today are spending considerable sums of money in building roads and trails and practising forest management principles who will never receive full benefit from the expenditure during their lifetime. It will possibly be 50 years before the results of these conservation policies are fully effective.
I ask of the minister in his budget proposals consideration of some arrangement for these persons who can prove, by inspection or by certificate from the British Columbia forest service or something of that sort, that they are conserving our natural resources and that they are investing money for the future, so they may have an opportunity to deduct a percentage of these expenses from their income tax.
There is no question, Mr. Speaker, but that unemployment is our major domestic


problem. I am not going to rehash the unemployment debate in my brief remarks this evening but in that connection, like my leader and all other members of this group, I regret that the budget does not provide for a long-term public investment program to meet this urgent need now and in the days to come. We are very sorry about that. We believe the budget should have contained proposals for a long-term investment program in low-cost housing, a national conservation policy, improved highways, trans-Canada pipe lines, irrigation projects, power development, hospitals and grade crossing improvements. All these things are sadly needed in the country. We are sorry the budget does not make provision for at least the commencement of such a long-term program.
I must say that we welcome the announcement that the government intends to establish a royal commission to examine carefully our potential economic prospects. This is all to the good and from our point of view a very necessary step for the planning of the proper development of our natural resources. Apparently the seeds sown by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in this respect are beginning to sprout. His speech of March 2, in which he urged the government to adopt a public investment program and to adopt a 100th anniversary committee, has been recognized and considered by the government.
At that time he urged the government to consider a committee to deal with a public investment program, so that when we celebrated our 100th anniversary we would have many things about which we could be proud. The hon. member placed a resolution on the order paper on March 17 asking for the establishment of such a committee to deal with the development of a public investment program over the years and coming to fruition at the time of our 100th anniversary. We are very pleased indeed to learn that the voice of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been listened to by the minister and the government at this time.
I should like to refer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as the Sir Stafford Cripps of the House of Commons. He is no Greek Adonis to look at, but he is certainly a good one to listen to. There is no question about it in this case, as on former occasions, the government has listened to his suggestions and advice, and we are very pleased that they have done so.
So far as the personnel of the commission is concerned, I hope it will be thoroughly representative. Naturally you have to have very well qualified persons to act in a satisfactory manner on such an important commission. I do think that, among others, there

should be qualified representatives of the working people, the farmers and the veterans of the country. There are certain aspects of this problem which these three large groups would wish considered, and I am sure that qualified representatives could make a most valuable contribution to the investigation and report by the royal commission.
However, it will take some time for the commission to complete its studies, and what is required at the present time is immediate action to meet the unemployment situation. I do not think we can ignore the fact that owing to various technological and other changes that are occurring in Canada and other countries at the present time, we are faced with the problem of a considerable amount of unemployment unless we take special measures through government action, federal, provincial and municipal, to overcome it. We believe that action should be as the result of planning, co-operation and co-ordination of activities among all levels of government.
I must say I find it very difficult to follow the policy of the Progressive Conservative party so far as their criticisms of the budget are concerned. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), if I heard him correctly and if his television interview was correctly reported, suggested that deficit financing is not a good thing. I think the hon. member for Greenwood was expressing his personal conviction. 1 judged from his speech that he considered deficit financing a poor thing. I listened to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), and I am quite sure anyone can fairly say that his proposals would mean a great increase in deficit financing so far as the government is concerned. Therefore I am not quite sure just what is the policy of the Progressive Conservative party with respect to deficit financing.
Personally, while small deficits may not be of serious concern, I do not think a government or a country can be run for long on very large-scale deficit financing. I think a better way is to provide for a public investment program because-
