Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to offer a few general remarks on the budget and the economic situation of our country. It would be presumptuous on my part to attempt to give a detailed analysis of either the budget or the economic situation, but perhaps I can offer a few remarks which will have some value or which, if they have no value, will at least give me some satisfaction.
There is one feature about budget debates and the consideration of budgets that has always interested me, and that is the attitude taken by newspapers, people in public life and the general public, when they seem to consider the budget of any public body as something to be considered by itself. To my mind a budget should always be associated with the work it is trying to do. All too often I find newspapers, and the public in general, either going into ecstasy or despondency over whether a tax rate has been raised or lowered; and a finance minister or a secretary-treasurer is either praised or condemned in the light of how much more or less he is providing to be spent in the conduct of the public business for which he is responsible.
This matter has puzzled me for a long time. If I were not afraid of disclosing my age I would say that as far back as 1934, when I happened to be making a speech on the budget of that time in the legislature in Saskatchewan, the same thing puzzled me. On that occasion I said it was as necessary for the people of a country to be tax conscious as to be conscious of a malady such as cancer, tuberculosis or some sickness of that nature. It has always been a puzzle to me to find that people consider expenditures or the providing of funds as something in, as it were, a separate room, apart altogether from a consideration of the things the expenditure of tax moneys is to provide.
The fact is that the two things go hand in hand. If one is fair, then he must consider it in that light, and in that light alone. The balance sheet must be looked at from both angles. To my mind the budget of a public body is much the same as the budgets we have in our own private lives. We see that we have so much money to spend, and that we have so much earning power. Consequently we decide what we are going to buy- what kind of car, what kind of radio, and all those things we wish to provide for ourselves.
When we begin talking about either reducing or increasing taxation we must emphasize in our own minds, and keep it as a background in the consideration of any budget, a clear picture of those things we desire to have.


In the budget now presented to us we must follow a similar procedure. While home during the Easter recess I interviewed a good many people. I called on municipal officials, on elevator agents, on reeves and councillors, and talked to people on the street, and I found the reaction to this budget was very favourable indeed. The impression I gained- indeed, it was told to me in so many words- was that the budget was considered honest and realistic, that it was facing the facts with which we are confronted, that it did not go off into an inflationary program but that it did the best it could to meet the prevailing situation.
People realize that we do not want any reduction in those services which, during times of prosperity, we have built up for ourselves. Those people do not want to give up any of their old age pensions or war veterans allowances. They do not want to deny themselves any of the public services that, as taxpayers in Canada, we have purchased for ourselves. Furthermore they felt that if we were to enter into an extensive program of public works the government would be acting as the agent of the taxpayers to hire those who are unemployed. It was felt that to hire
600,000	people at a time such as this would present some difficulty to the taxpayers.
These were the thoughts that appeared to be in the minds of the people. I was happy with the reception the budget received, particularly so because we in the west, where money is short, as it may also be in some other parts of the country, felt that the budget was facing up to the situation as it exists. The government in office is responsible for the carrying on of the public activities we want, those things for which in many cases we have asked and petitioned. We do not want to have them reduced. We know that moneys have to be provided for these purposes, and therefore we could not expect any great reduction in taxation.
In 1953 our national economy did not suffer greatly dollarwise. The figure, one we hear often repeated, was something over $24,500 million. According to the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce it had dropped last year to $24 billion. Since I am a grain grower and come from the prairies, it interests me very much to know that both in the budget and in the speech from the throne it is emphasized that the lack of production with respect to grain, particularly in western Canada, has had a serious effect and is indeed partly responsible for the drop in Canada's national output. To me this is very interesting, because it emphasizes the great importance of the three prairie provinces in our economy. Indeed, they are at

least the stone on the side of the keystone in the economic arch of Canada. I noted particularly the emphasis on that phase of our economy.
We did suffer last year. In the province of Saskatchewan there are places where we grew 20, 30, 40 and 50 bushels of wheat to the acre the previous year. Last year we grew 2, 3, 4 and 8 bushels of wheat to the acre. My constituency of Qu'Appelle is practically all under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That means that a great part of it yielded fewer than 4 bushels to the acre and nearly all of it yielded fewer than 8 bushels to the acre. This made quite a dent, shall I say, in the economy of our area, as it did all through Saskatchewan.
We are very appreciative of the help this act has given. Naturally some of us would like to have had more; who does not want twice as much, if he can get it? But we do appreciate and have appreciated the consideration that has been given to the west by this government over the years it has been in office. We do appreciate what it has done to solve western problems and the help it has given to meet them.
I have mentioned previously some of the things this government has done, which we greatly appreciate. Of course we westerners must be forgiven for some of our impatience, because we are so young. Some of our grandfathers saw the buffaloes roaming there. Our grandfathers and fathers took over the raw prairie from the Indians, the gophers and the buffaloes. That is in the memories of men still living there. We all know that the young are very impatient. That can be seen from the political performance of the twin provinces of western Canada, Alberta and Saskatchewan, who are celebrating their fiftieth anniversary this year. I do not know of any two political parties that are more opposed to each other than those two facing each other across the Saskatchewan border. One province' is Social Credit and the other is socialist at the present time.
It will not be that way all the time, of course. That is partly owing to their youth. I hope other members from other parts of Canada who are pioneers, not of the west but of Canada itself, will understand that. I think at once of the oldest and yet the youngest province of Canada, namely Newfoundland. I have been told that in that province today there are roads that were laid 350 years ago. It makes me feel very humble and very appreciative of the fact that we are young, and because we are young we make demands and requests, sometimes in very violent fashion. That is one of the reasons we do it in that way.
The Budget-Mr. Mang
We are short of cash throughout western Canada at the present time. It is not at all hopeless, however. The situation is that we bought a great quantity of goods during our prosperous times. We are just like the worker in a factory. If he gets an increase in wages he spends it the day after tomorrow, and very often it is spent on a new television set or on a new commodity of some kind that he wishes to have.
We are far from bankrupt in western Canada. Indeed, our wealth is quite substantial. A good deal of our money has been sent to Windsor, Toronto, Montreal and Oshawa. We do not regret that because we do not care so much for money out there. What we care for are goods, which are the true wealth of any land. We want a new combine; we want a new truck or a new car, and that sort of thing, but at the moment we are short of cash. If those wheat payments can be hustled along a little we shall appreciate it. I do not threaten as some people do, by shaking a finger or a fist at our very efficient Minister of Trade and Commerce. That does not make the stenographers work any faster, and it is not physically possible to get the payments out any faster. We are going to be patient. We are very patient people out in the west. We have acquired that virtue because we have learned to depend chiefly on the weather and the soil for whatever we have.
In spite of the handicap of a socialist government from which we suffer out there-I shall not mention the other government, because it does not concern us at the present time. They are getting along very well, but they are also getting help from sources outside their own borders and, of course, oil and gas-we are hoping that with the help we are getting from this government in various ways, with the other payments coming in, and with the grain moving again, we shall not have to ask the house for any special consideration.
The matter of trade has been emphasized over and over again. It has been said that we must expand our trade. The loss of some of our markets has been deplored. Of course the loss is regrettable. I was interested in the discussions on unemployment and trade. Employment in any country depends upon trade, both domestic and foreign, but that trade depends upon the consumer. Unless someone buys the thing you make, it just lies there. For example, you can have combines standing in Toronto by the acre, or trucks standing in Oshawa by the acre. They do not do anybody any good until someone starts to use them. As soon as the products of labour are brought into use you have wealth, and not before that.

The Budget-Mr. Mang
The consumer has not been emphasized enough in our discussions here. The consumers of this country, or of any country with which we trade, call the final tune. The consumer is the one who decides whether he will or will not buy. May I point out that we, as western farmers, have always tried to be reasonable in the marketing of our grain. May I give this illustration. Every manufacturing concern in the economy of Canada should consider it very carefully. When we formed the wheat pool through which we hoped to market our grain, one of the objectives of that farm organization was to try to keep the price of our grain in a reasonable relationship with what the consumer was able and willing to pay. With the exception of 1929, when many people in this country, the United States, and throughout the world for that matter, misjudged what the consumer was going to do, we have followed a policy in our sales of grain of always considering the ability and willingness of the consumer to absorb our product.
Without going into detail on that point but just to bring it into focus I would point out what happened last year, and I do this to indicate what I think industry should do. Perhaps I should not say "should do", as it is up to them, but this is what the wheat board did. First of all we recognized that the markets of the world were becoming highly competitive, and that if we were going to sell our product we would have to maintain our competitive position. We all heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce make that statement when the price reduction was announced.
This is what happened in western Canada last year when we tried to adjust ourselves to the competitive situation that had developed in the international grain market. I should like to quote a short paragraph from the Canadian wheat board report dealing with price which illustrates how we have tried to meet the international competitive situation with regard to the sale of our wheat which, as I said a few moments ago, forms such an important part of our national economy, as was recognized in the budget speech and the throne speech as well. Referring to the international wheat agreement the report had this to say:
From the agreement level of $2.03 per bushel at the start of the crop year board quotations for No. 1 northern wheat basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur declined through the course of the crop year to a level of $1,704 per bushel on July 30. 1954, representing an over-all decline of 324 cents per bushel for the year.
That was done in order to meet competition in the markets of the world. I ask industry,


which would consist of the investor, management and labour, what they have done to remain competitive in the markets of the world. In western Canada the budget resources of the farmers have shrunken, not only because of yield but because of price adjustments. When we come to consider the purchase of a new truck, a new combine or a new machine produced in eastern Canada in the centres I have named we are faced with the fact that the cost of labour has risen and profits have increased.
We in the west cannot see how our commodity is going to take the adjustment when on the other hand industry, consisting of the units I have mentioned, is permitting its returns to go up all the time. We hear of less work, more wages, better holiday arrangements and more fringe benefits. The cost of all these items is built into the price of the combine, the truck and the car which we must have to run our business of producing wheat.
I am not telling anyone what to do; I am simply posing the question. That is one reason I was glad to have it announced in the budget speech that a commission is to be appointed to look into the whole economic picture of Canada. Some hon. members have indicated that they think this might take a long time. I do not know, but if the right men are appointed and they get busy I do not think it will take too long. The Prime Minister will know more about this because he was on the Rowell-Sirois commission, which had a somewhat similar duty to perform.
I suggest that the commission should consist of responsible men. It should look into the reasons for our high costs of production which I have hinted at, and the relative influence those matters have upon our high-cost economy which is making it so hard for us to compete in a highly competitive world against West Germany, Great Britain and Japan, three of our chief competitors who within the past few years have come up by leaps and bounds. As a matter of fact, as their employment figures have increased and as their production has been poured onto the markets of the world, to that extent have our unemployment figures here in Canada increased.
This commission should make a thorough survey of company profits, investor returns, labour and transportation costs. The cost of transportation is quite an item in the wheat and pulp and paper industries. Last year it cost the pulp and paper industry something like $250 million in transportation costs alone, and we could easily figure out the cost of transporting wheat, a most vital

factor in our high-cost economy. And then there is taxation to be considered.
This commission will be able to establish facts in a way that we cannot establish them in this House of Commons. In this chamber we might be able to assess the economic situation in Canada in relation to the five points I have mentioned, but our duties are different. One group has the responsibility of conducting the business of the country; another group has the responsibility of criticizing the way in which that business is done; others offer suggestions, and so forth. The net result is that the poor public are very much confused as to what is the actual situation.
I am pleased that this matter is to be dealt with by a royal commission because above all else it will provide information to the people of Canada which is unbiased and not coloured by the political expediency of any party, or entangled with certain matters which should not enter into it at all. I would not undertake to indicate the personnel of this commission, but I was highly impressed by Mr. Graham Towers at committee meetings last year. Then there should be two representatives from the manufacturers' association, one from management and the other from the investors' side. I would certainly have representatives of labour sitting on the commission. Such institutions as banks should be included, and of course farmers, one farmer from the east and one from the prairies.
The reason I would like all these people represented is this, that they would share the responsibility for that report. You could go out into the country and give the people a factual presentation of the situation as it is, uncoloured by political bias. It would do away with the confusion that is brought about at the present time in the way these economic facts are presented to the public who are responsible for the membership of this house.
There is another point I should like to mention because it comes up so often. It came up again tonight. That is the question so often asked, if we can so regulate our economy during war that there is no unemployment, and if we can get all the money we want during a war, why not in peace? I have puzzled over that for quite a while, but I have answered the question, to my own satisfaction at least, for some time past. I do not remember much about 1914-we had no radio then-but you will remember that on the eve of the declaration of war in 1939 we had a marshalling of all the political forces of this country within one hour. I think it was from seven to eight o'clock out west, when the then prime minister, Right 50433-1974
The Budget-Mr. Mang Hon. Mackenzie King, spoke, telling the people of Canada what was happening and what had happened. Then the premier of every province spoke on the same program. The result of this was a marshalling of the minds and the will and, as a result of that, the resources of this country to one purpose. That is the first reason you can do certain things during wartime which you cannot do in peacetime. I challenge anyone to suggest that such unity could be attained even if you had a million unemployed today.
The second thing is this. With the marshalling of all those forces of the mind, of the will and of the resources, both human and natural, you have the government immediately going into action with respect to the regulating of the economy, and you institute a rigid economy to accomplish that one aim in which we all unite. You have the invoking of the War Measures Act, you have the national registration, and you have the wartime prices and trade board. You marshal the human resources, and that is why you can do those things about which the question is so often asked: if you can get all that money in wartime why can you not get it in peacetime? That is one of the reasons. You can get that kind of unity and you can solve your problems as easily as that. But you would never get it, even if you had a million unemployed, today. That is the way I answer that question for myself. Others may answer it as they wish.
The other matter concerns the profits of corporations. We live in a free enterprise economy. That of course is a term which has been kicked around almost ad nauseam, "free enterprise" or "private enterprise". Many people mention it and do not even know what it is. It simply means that a person in this country will produce the most when he is seeking his own happiness; when he has his own way of working and is using his own skill for his own profit. He may have great ambition or little ambition; he may have initiative or not, and that depends on each individual human being. A great deal is made out of so-called big business. I sometimes wonder whether it is to the advantage of the people themselves-never mind the business or the economics-to indicate to them that somebody is trying to rob them all the time. It creates a spirit of leaning on somebody else to accomplish the things which the individual actually wants to accomplish. Let us look at some of the figures. This is perhaps just one example, but it applies to others in a greater or lesser degree;
The British Columbia firm of MacMillan and Bloedel Limited, one of the world's greatest enterprises in forest products, records gross receipts

The Budget-Mr. Mang of $142 millions in 1954. Of special significance is the disposition of profits. To 4,582 shareholders there went a total of $4,189,000 in dividends.
Coupon clippers, I presume.
To governments (federal, provincial and municipal) there went taxes totalling $14,490,101. To 8,648 employees there went salaries and wages totalling $30,023,649.
. . . the owners of the business-the shareholders- got less than one-third of what went to governments in taxes, and about one-seventh of what went to workers in salaries and wages.
I am not condemning labour, those who work with their hands or work with the pen or work with their brains in management, for wanting a fair share and keeping the bulk of what comes out of that particular business. But the point I am trying to make is that we should not condemn a business as such just because it is making profits. We are all sharing in those profits, particularly today, because in the last 30 years at least the corporations have taken on a different form. The public itself is a shareholder. General Motors corporation has something like 500,000 shareholders, and you could name others.
I do not want to go into details at the present time, but the point I am making is that labour prospers to the extent that businesses prosper; it gets its share out of those profits. Remember this. In this house the Minister of Finance through his taxation powers can reduce those profits by taxation if they should get beyond all bounds or if they injure the economy by taking too much in profits out of the production of goods. The Minister of Finance and the government in that case will use those profits and redistribute them, as he is doing now.
I know there are other sides to the argument, but the point is, what is the alternative? The alternative is, of course, state ownership and state control of the means of production and distribution. If you are going to switch from this economy you will have to go to some alternative. I question very much, and I have always questioned, whether the people of Canada are of the type who want to have their private initiative controlled and governed by a body that is perhaps not endowed with any more wisdom than the average man in the land. Looking at it fairly, before we condemn the system we have and try to substitute another one therefor, we should look at some of these angles in a realistic way.
There is one more matter on which I wish to give my own view. In this house we have had mentioned very often-indeed we hear it every day-our great natural resources of forests, lands, streams and rocks. Those four basic natural resources have been mentioned.


It has been contended that because we in Canada have such an abundance of these natural resources, and an extremely energetic people, there should be no unemployment, and that all this is wealth.
I think I pointed out previously in this house, in my own immature way, of course, that these natural resources are not wealth until they are turned into something usable, and that until it gets into the hands of the consumer it is nothing. Otherwise you might as well leave the resource for the artist to paint or for the fisherman to enjoy.
To make the example more extreme, consider these combines and trucks that you see standing around that have not gone into consumption. Until they go into consumption they are not wealth. If you try to monetize them after they are built and bring them into consumption in that way, I just am not condemning the idea but I am wondering whether that is feasible or possible. Those combines and trucks might just as well have been left in the ground, as far as wealth is concerned, until some farmer buys the combine or somebody buys the truck. The combine or truck is not wealth until it goes into consumption. It can go into consumption only when an individual uses his brain and his brawn to get some purchasing power through his own efforts. Then he can turn this into wealth and something usable.

Perhaps you do not get my point. I have not time to go over it again. So we have these natural resources, but we must have the application of the stored-up wealth that we have in the form of money and the desire or the ambition and the energy-particularly the initiative and the ambition-of the individual Canadian to go out and get something for himself if we are going to keep the economy alive and build it up. If you are going to bring these products of your ambition, energy and initiative to the consumers you must bear in mind what the consumer thinks he can pay you for the service you have rendered.
We in the wheat business are trying to do that. I urge the rest of the people of Canada -particularly the labour unions, management and investors-just to take a good long look at the matter. I therefore think this suggestion of the Minister of Finance with regard to appointing a commission is a good one, together with my suggestions as to personnel. By this means I think we can bring the economic problems into focus.
It has often been stated that the twentieth century belongs to Canada. It was repeated

this afternoon. That prophecy was made at the beginning of the twentieth century. It was made by a son of old Quebec from which the original white Canadians came. By a peculiarly strange stroke of fate, in the middle of the twentieth century we have from that same province a Prime Minister who is charged with the responsibility of making a reality that vision of 50 years ago. I think we are well on the road to that progress if each individual and each section of Canada will assume his and its share of responsibility rather than throwing the responsibility on somebody else, or more particularly loading upon the government of Canada alone the responsibility for prosperity and well-being in this land.

Mr. Speaker, on looking quickly over the budget speeches over the years, I have found that one thing is noticeable, namely that the question of tariffs looms less important now in the budget speeches than it did a number of years ago. I suppose this situation is due, in part at least, to the fact that tariffs are not now looked upon as a source of revenue to the extent they were at one time.
I realize that I am running the risk of committing the sin of oversimplification but it would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that generally speaking the items on which we might have tariffs fall naturally into three classes. First, there is the class of items which we are forced to import, which we do not produce in our own country. In that category, of course, fall such things as citrus fruits, spices and many other things.
It would seem to me that those items as a class should be free of duty, because any duty imposed on them is imposed merely as a source of revenue; and if duties are imposed they increase the cost of living by that amount. I think there are some items in this classification which are not duty free but which might well be. For instance, I believe there are tariffs on some such items as fruit juices, citrus fruits and items of that sort which there is no hope of ever producing in this country. I realize that there are other fruit juices that might be considered to be competitive; nevertheless I think that, generally speaking, there is a large class of goods which should remain duty free.
Then on the other end of the scale there are other items in which this country is pre-eminent and as to which there is no worth-while competition from other countries. In that group you might place nickel, asbestos, perhaps wood pulp and many other things. We do not normally import these articles anyway, because our own national industries can compete effectively with any
The Budget-Mr. MacLean imports. In these cases it would seem that duties are unnecessary. That leaves, of course, the great group of products which are produced in this country and with which imports compete. That, of course, is the group that gives us the biggest problems when it comes to deciding what items should be protected and what items should not be protected.
In connection with changes in the tariff, I am pleased to note that certain things which are used in the agricultural industry have had the tariffs removed. I refer to such things as agricultural spraying equipment and items of that sort. I feel that is a welcome move to Canadian agriculture and the Canadian people generally. I am also pleased to know that it is intended to refer the question of the tariff on potatoes to the tariff board. To my way of thinking it is a matter of pressing importance that some protection should be given to the Canadian potato grower if at all possible.
The question of arriving at what is a suitable tariff for various imports is further complicated by the fact that our country falls into four different economic areas, the Atlantic provinces, central Canada, the prairies, and British Columbia. A tariff set-up which will please one section and stimulate its economy may not be satisfactory for the others. I suppose the only way you could make everyone happy as far as tariffs are concerned would be to have the reverse of a customs union. You would have to balkanize our tariff system so that it coincided with out naturally balkanized economy. That of course would not be practical.
Therefore the only solution that remains is to try to bring the economy of all parts of the country more into balance. In this connection I think it is fair to say it would be easier to devise a tariff structure that would meet with the approval of all if industry were spread across the country, and if our industrial areas were not so dependent for agricultural products on far-away sources. I was very interested in a brief reference to a certain subject made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. As found at page 2730 of Hansard of April 5, he said:
There should also be an increase in construction activity in the season now beginning. Indeed, it is clear to all of us that alongside the pushing back of the physical frontiers of our country there is also taking place an expansion of urban facilities which is simultaneously making Canada a land of large cities. This trend toward metropolitan development creates special problems of its own . . .
I am very pleased that the minister recognizes that this trend creates problems. I think it is perhaps one of the most serious trends that has taken place since the war.

The Budget-Mr. MacLean If it is allowed to continue and the policies are maintained which permit it to continue, this dangerous and shortsighted program may well lead ultimately to the very destruction of civilization in this country.
If we do a little basic thinking about the matter we will realize that centuries ago, or even up until quite recent times, large cities were a necessity. They were a necessity for defence reasons in early times. In medieval times you had to put a wall around a city. It was necessary to have the people living in a very small area. Cities were necessary for purposes of communication. In those days means of communication were very crude and slow, and you could not communicate rapidly over great distances. There was also the problem of transportation. Everything had to be carried by man, animal or boat.
All these problems have now disappeared. In this connection I should like to quote from a speech delivered at Harvard University in 1930 by Alfred North Whitehead. He said in part:
Throughout the whole span oi civilization up to the present moment, the growth of condensed aggregates of humans, which we call cities, has been an inseparable accompaniment of the growth of civilization. There are many obvious reasons: the defence of accumulated wealth behind city walls, the concentration of power in the form of human muscles and, later, in the form of available heat energy, the ease of mutual intercourse required for business relations, the pleasure from a concentration of aesthetic and cultural opportunities, the advantages of a concentration of governmental and other directing agencies, administrative, legal and military . . . But, if we examine the trend of technology during the past generation, the reasons for this concentration are largely disappearing. Still more, the reasons for the choice of sites for cities are also altering. Mechanical power can be transmitted for hundreds of miles, men can communicate almost instantaneously by telephone, the chiefs of great organizations can be transported by aeroplanes, the cinemas can produce plays in every village; music, speeches, and sermons can be broadcast. Almost every reason for the growth of cities, concurrently with the growth of civilization, has been profoundly modified . . . the effect of new technologies on the sites of cities, and on transformations of cities, is one of the fundamental problems which must enter into all sociological theories. . .
There are, on the other side of the scale, very important reasons why this trend toward a few large cities in Canada should be reversed. In this atomic age large cities can be wiped out almost instantaneously by H-bombs. It would take very few of them to paralyse a very high percentage of the production and population of the country if present trends are permitted to continue. Transportation also is being complicated by the congestion of our larger cities. At the present time we have the contradictory situation of it being necessary to spend millions of

dollars in Toronto, and probably in Montreal, for the construction of underground railroads, while at the same time we have applications from our national railways before the board of transport commissioners requesting that services be discontinued in many of the outlying parts of the country because of lack of traffic.
These, Mr. Speaker, are a few of the reasons, but there are many more. I could refer at length to the many complications created by the fact that our population is concentrated in a few centres. For example, it has been calculated that the workers at the A. V. Roe company spend $12,000 a day just getting to work. It has also been calculated that traffic delays in the city of Montreal cost $30 million a year. These are figures which alone would give one reason to believe that we should contemplate doing something about the growing tendency for our industries and our population to congregate in a few large centres.
Ex-mayor McCallum of Toronto was reported in 1949 as saying that he thought his city should grow no larger, but that only senior government action could prevent it. I think that was a true statement, and that it behooves this government to give a lead in the dispersal of industry and population more evenly across the country. I do not mean by this that it would be necessary to uproot present industries, wherever they may be, and transplant them to new areas. But the continued trend to construct new industrial sites around our larger cities definitely should be discouraged.
In other countries something is being done about it. In 1940 the government in Great Britain appointed a royal commission to look into this very problem, as a result of which the new towns act was passed; so that now in Great Britain there are under construction 16 garden cities ranging in population from
30,000	to 80,000.
In the United States the problem has received government recognition. In 1948 the national security resources board issued instructions in industrial locations advocating that no new factories be built adjoining centres of more than 50,000 people. After that report was made, and perhaps partly because of it, only about a third of the new plants built in the United States since 1940 have been located in places with populations over 100,000. So it appears that in that country a concerted effort is being made to deploy the economy and the industry of the country evenly throughout the whole area.
In this connection I should like to quote briefly from an article which appeared in the

Community Planning Review for November, 1952, regarding a conference held just prior to that time. It says:
The theme of the presentation, made by members of our council to the federation of mayors last July, was that the major cities of Canada, and indeed major cities all over the world, have grown beyond the point where they are efficient in terms of industry and commerce, and also beyond the point where they provide happy and satisfactory living for those who must spend their lives in, or in close proximity to, these larger metropolitan areas.
In that connection, in 1946 a survey was taken in the United States by, I believe, Fortune magazine, when it was found that two-thirds of the people living in American cities having populations of over 100,000 were dissatisfied with the environment in which they were forced to live.
I think it should be agreed that this is an important problem about which up to now this government has taken no action. It is a problem which is becoming increasingly acute, and it is a trend which as time goes on it will be more difficult to reverse. I intend now to turn briefly to another subject, but I must say that the one I have just discussed is one I would like to hear debated in the house when the subject of civil defence is under consideration, if indeed it cannot be approached from some other point of view.
I turn now for a few moments to government accounts and to the budget, as such, presented by the minister. During his budget speech he had this to say, as reported at page 2730 of Hansard:
Assuming normal crops, and if no unforeseen adverse events occur, I would expect our gross national production in 1955 to exceed 1954 by 5 or 6 per cent; that is, it should reach $251 billion or perhaps just a bit more, and on that figure X shall base my revenue forecasts.
A little later on he had this to say regarding his predecessor's budget speech of a year ago:
In his budget speech last year my predecessor projected a scale of expenditures and revenues that almost exactly balanced. He made it clear, however, that his projection was based upon two assumptions, normal crops and an early resumption of our normal rate of industrial expansion. He said explicitly that if these conditions did not materialize there would be a deficit of 2 or 3 per cent. Well, as hon. members know, we had a poor wheat crop, the poorest in 17 years, and the resumption of a normal rate of industrial expansion has been slower than we had hoped. As a consequence we have a deficit equal to 31 per cent of our expenditures.
My reason for offering these quotations is to remind the house that during the last ten years at least we have been in a period of rising prices. Or, to say this in another way, we have been in a period when the value of the dollar has been going down constantly
The Budget-Mr. MacLean in the matter of purchasing power. Under those circumstances it is or should be easy indeed for any government to balance its budget, for the simple reason that it pays its commitments in dollars having less purchasing power than dollars had when the commitments were made.
In a period of rising prices, of course, all debtors benefit because their commitments in terms of purchasing power go down. That is a happy situation for any government to find itself in. But, like most benefits of that kind, the old rule that one gets nothing for nothing comes into play; and there will come a day when the situation will be reversed and all debtors, including the government, will find themselves obligated to meet their commitments in dollars with a purchasing power equal to that of the dollars current at the time the commitments were made.
Relatively speaking it has been a simple matter for this government to meet its commitments to the recipients of family allowances and old age pensions in dollars which have only a little more than half the purchasing power of the dollars existing when the commitments were made. The same applies to the interest on the national debt, and all other commitments of government. But from now on there is a strong possibility that this trend will not be so great, and that it may even be reversed.
Under those circumstances the minister admits that the budget will not be balanced. He places his estimate on a very optimistic outlook, so far as gross national product is concerned, measured in dollars. It seems to me that when the inflationary trend stops the actual gross national product may continue to go up as far as goods are concerned, but it may decline as far as dollar value is concerned; and after all it is on the dollar value that the budget is based. So we may be entering a time when it will become increasingly difficult for this or any other government to balance its budget.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I maintain that this is a time when every effort should be made to reduce unnecessary expenditures and see to it that the taxpayer gets 100 cents in value for every dollar he is forced to spend. If prices continue to rise in a spiral the cost of living will continue to rise, and that would not be a good thing. We could quite easily reach the inflationary point of no return. Already the cost of living is so high that many Canadians find it difficult to exist.
Not only is the cost of living high under this government; even the cost of dying is very high, and no change has been made in that regard. I note with regret that the Minister of Finance did not see fit to remove

The Budget-Mr. Ellis
the sales tax from such items as coffins, hearses and even flowers, which one places on the graves of deceased persons. It strikes me as almost ghoulish that the government should see fit to enhance its revenue at the expense of those who have been recently bereaved. In most families death is a catastrophe from the financial point of view, even leaving the sales tax on coffins out of consideration.
Some minor reductions have been made in the income tax, and they are welcomed. I regret that no relief whatsoever has been given to the large group of Canadian citizens whose entire tax burden is borne in the form of indirect taxes. I also regret that no relief has been given to the municipalities. The least that could have been done was to make purchases by municipalities exempt from sales tax. I should have liked to see a budget which gave more consideration to the primary producers of this country. It is those who produce goods who cause our standard of living to rise in a material sense. Too much emphasis can be placed on services. Services may be a very convenient thing and in many instances are necessary and contribute to production; but if the accent continues to be placed on services, we may as a nation get to the point where we are trying to be well off and reach prosperity by, if you carry the argument to its logical conclusion, taking in each other's washing.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the most important thing to consider in a debate of this kind is the role which we assign to the budget in our modern-day society. There may have been a time in our history when the budget was considered merely as the instrument by which the government raised moneys to carry on the day to day activities of government. But I believe today we have to consider that the budget is also an instrument of social and economic planning. It is a means of dealing with the

major economic difficulties facing the nation. It is on that basis that we ought to consider the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance, and judge whether or not it contributes to a solution of the outstanding problems facing Canada at the present time.
Before dealing with the broader aspects, I should like to make a very brief reference to a number of specific provisions or perhaps omissions in the budget. Great emphasis was laid on the reduction in the personal income tax but I wish to draw to the attention of the house the fact that there are a great many people in Canada who do not pay income tax, for the simple reason that they have never earned sufficient money to become liable for taxation. I checked the latest figures available, and I must say at the outset that they are 1952 figures. I do not believe percentagewise there is a great deal of difference between the figures of that year and the figures of last year.
I found that in Canada in 1952 there were over half a million Canadians, some 594,980 to be exact, who had incomes of under $1,000; there were over 403,000 Canadians earning incomes of from $1,000 to $2,000; there were some 251,000 Canadians earning incomes of between $2,000 and $3,000; and some 20,000-odd earning between $3,000 and $3,500. These figures give us a total of some 1,276,610 Canadians who, during that year, were not liable to income tax simply because their incomes did not make them liable for such tax.
Bearing these figures in mind we have to ask ourselves this question. What has the budget done for this great number of Canadian citizens? It has given them no tax relief whatsoever, and I remind the house that these are the people in greatest need. I suggest that when the government is bringing in some measure of tax relief it should be directed toward those who are in greatest need. If the government has operated on that principle there would have been a different sort of tax reduction provided for in this budget.
We have to ask ourselves, what has the budget done for our senior citizens on old age pensions? What is in this budget in the way of tax relief for our blind pensioners, for those on war pensions and war veterans allowances, or for the vast number of Canadian citizens who are on small pensions of one kind or another, such as former railroaders, for example, who are seemingly trying to exist on pensions as low as $25 a month? There is no tax relief for these people in this budget.
When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget and there was a tremendous amount of desk-thumping by supporters of

the government, it seemed to me that it was an indication of an attitude of mind. They were pleased with the budget even though it had overlooked the needs of the great number of Canadian citizens who are not earning enough money to pay income tax, and in 1952 there were over 1,200,000 Canadians in that category. As I pointed out, there is no tax relief whatsoever in this budget for Canadian citizens in the greatest need. I remind those supporters of the government who were so enthusiastic the night the budget was brought down that this budget has shown a callous disregard for the plight of many of our citizens.
I would call attention to the deceptive manner in which the government tried to get this across to this house and indirectly to the people of Canada. A great play was made on reductions in the income tax, and we were told that the income tax deductions were going to vary according to income. We were told that those in the lower income brackets were going to get a tax reduction of 13-2 per cent, and then we were told in the next breath that those in receipt of high incomes were going to get a tax relief of only 2-8 per cent.
I wonder who the government thought they were fooling with that sort of subterfuge. No matter how you figure it out it means a 2 per cent blanket reduction across the board. The government brought this in in a deceptive manner and tried to convey the impression that there was some fairness and equity in the manner in which these reductions were being made, when all the time there was plain evidence that the income tax reductions amounted to a flat 2 per cent reduction across the board.
There is no justice or equity in that sort of tax relief. A 2 per cent reduction across the board means a lot more for the big fellow than it does for the small fellow. When we look closely at the figures we find that a married man with two children having an income of $3,000 will get tax relief this coming year of $14. On the other hand the taxpayer who is in receipt of an income of $20,000 will get tax relief amounting to $354. Is that the Liberal concept of equity and fairness in a tax program, that the person who needs help, the person with a low income, gets a niggardly $14 reduction in income tax while the man earning $20,000, who certainly is not on the verge of being poverty stricken, gets tax relief amounting to $354? I ask, is that the Liberal concept of fairness and equity in a tax program?
If the government had wished to do something to reduce the tax load on the people of this country who most need relief they could have done that by reducing the indirect
The Budget-Mr. Ellis
sales tax. I would venture the opinion that the average family in Canada in the lower income groups, perhaps those at the lowest level of liability for income tax purposes, will pay about twice as much in sales tax during the year as they will pay in income tax. So if the government had been anxious to give tax relief to those who are in greatest need they would have brought about a reduction in the field of indirect taxes.
There are not too many figures available with respect to this problem in Canada, but I have noted a survey and study prepared for the United States congress in 1941 entitled "Who Pays the Taxes?" This report reveals that in the United States indirect or consumption taxes took from 16 to 20-6 per cent of the income of those receiving incomes under $3,000. For the income group earning from $10,000 to $15,000 indirect or consumption taxes took only 9-9 per cent of income. In the case of those earning $15,000 up to $20,000 the indirect and consumption taxes took only 8-8 per cent of income, and in the case of those earning more than $20,000 the indirect or consumption taxes took only 5-7 per cent of income.
Therefore it is quite obvious that the indirect tax bears most heavily on the low income group. The figures supplied in this study would indicate that indirect taxes bear about four times as heavily on the lower income group as they do on the higher income group. The reason is quite obvious. A person on a low income must spend all of his income on consumer goods, whereas the man with a higher income can afford to put money aside in savings. Therefore the lower the income the greater the amount of money spent on consumer goods.
I repeat that if this government had been anxious to provide a measure of tax relief for the lower income groups of this country they would have gone about reducing the indirect taxes.
On motion of Mr. Ellis the debate was adjourned. '

Mr. Speaker, this is a rather unusual motion for the production of papers. I say that because the Auditor General informs me that a similar motion for the production of papers was moved by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) on January 28, 1953. The Auditor General states that that was the first time in his experience that correspondence of the Auditor General

Motions for Papers
had been called for. At that time the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated, as reported on page 1398 of Hansard:
The Auditor General is always available to appear before the public accounts committee when his presence is desired, and it is open to any hon. member to address to him any question he may see fit to put to him directly.
The committee on radio broadcasting is sitting and I suggest that the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) would have the same opportunity as was indicated on that former occasion to go before the committee on radio broadcasting and ask any questions which he might desire to ask with reference to what he has in mind.
The Auditor General is presently in New York at the United Nations where he acts in the capacity of auditor, but he has signified to me his willingness to appear before the committee on radio broadcasting at any time and is prepared to answer any questions or not answer any questions which might be put before him. If that is acceptable to the hon. gentleman I make that suggestion to him; otherwise I shall have to oppose the motion.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the suggestion made by the Minister of National Revenue is one which I do not think I can accept as dealing adequately with the situation. To my mind this is a motion which involves the rights and privileges of every member of parliament. The Auditor General is a servant of parliament. I feel that parliament is entitled to obtain the production of correspondence between the Auditor General and departments or agencies of government.
I would point out that in days gone by it was the practice of the Auditor General to include in his report to parliament copies of correspondence which he had exchanged with various departments and officials of departments. I have in my hand one copy of the Auditor General's report in which a number of letters are reproduced. I do not know when this practice was discontinued, but I do suggest that inasmuch as the Auditor General in some cases in his current report refers to correspondence with government departments, and particularly as in this case in connection with the C.B.C. he has reproduced that correspondence in part, it is perfectly within the rights of parliament, whose servant he is, to ask for the production of the full correspondence in order that we may be in possession of the facts.
The public accounts committee has not been set up for this year. I myself am not a member of the committee on radio broadcasting, and I would not consider it proper to suggest that some other member should

cease to be a member of that committee in order that I might pursue this matter there.
I rest my position on the basis that parliament is entitled to the production of full correspondence between the Auditor General, its servant, and any government department or agency.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I do not think that anyone would contest the right of parliament to require the Auditor General to produce any correspondence, but inasmuch as the Auditor General in the discharge of his responsibility to parliament prepares a report I suggest that it would not be in the best interests of proper administration to have him feel that any correspondence he had had with departments for the purpose of preparing his report, which it is his responsibility to deliver to parliament, would itself be subject to publication in the house. It seems to me that if we have, and I think we all have, implicit confidence in the manner in which the Auditor General discharges his responsibility as such we should not establish any practice which might hamper him in the methods he adopts to get the information which it is his responsibility to communicate to the house.
I am sure that when he attaches correspondence to his report he does so because he feels that that is proper in the discharge of his responsibility, and when he does not do so it is because in his best judgment he is otherwise giving parliament all the information which his duty requires him to divulge. I do not think it is a matter of the right of this house to insist that correspondence be produced. The house should determine in the proper exercise of its discretion whether it will make that a feature of the duties of the Auditor General or whether it will continue to leave it to him to discharge, in the light of his oath of office, the responsibility he has to parliament whose appointee he is.
Perhaps the motion could be allowed to stand while the hon. gentleman conferred with the Auditor General, as I know we all do at times. I think we are all agreed that we would have the right to make an order, but what we have in mind is whether it is desirable that this order be made or not.

Mr. Speaker may I say with respect that I think the suggestion of the Prime Minister is reasonable under the circumstances.
I should however say that I myself have not received any communication from the Auditor General indicating that he would have any reluctance to produce the correspondence in question. Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to direct a question to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys? My question arises out of a telegram received from the president of district 26 of the united mine workers, Nova Scotia, and also out of a statement which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald on the 23rd of this month. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my hon. friend for giving me short notice of his intention to ask this question. speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 263, to implement the convention on damage caused by foreign aircraft to third parties on the surface.

subtopic: THIRD PARTY DAMAGE
subsubtopic: PROVISION TO IMPLE- MENT CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I might take a few moments to say that, although it has been indicated to us by the minister we are left in the position of having to accept this legislation and the schedule contained therein in full, it should at least be remarked in passing that there are some serious shortcomings in the legislation. I make that statement notwithstanding the fact the legislation is of a type sorely needed so far as the regulation of air traffic is concerned. I will be brief and will refer to individual points which I think show that in the over-all picture sufficient consideration has not been given to the various items that have been covered.
In the first instance, because of the mechanical requirements set up covering security which must be complied with by the various contracting parties, in order to cover, by insurance or otherwise, damage claims which may arise, we find that we have placed ourselves in the position that a virtual embargo may be placed upon the entry of our aircraft into another country at the whim or fancy of that foreign country. I say that because it appears that the type of security which may be offered may be rejected by any contracting party, and although arbitration is provided in some instances, it would still be possible for that contracting party to refuse admittance to our aircraft. In that respect, I would say that this condition is the same condition as has arisen in connection with some of our trade policies where we bound ourselves under agreements, and at the same time allowed some discretionary power to one of the contracting parties to admit or refuse our goods as they saw fit. In connection with that point, I may say that these provisions are set out in chapter III of the schedule to the agreement.

The second point with which I should like to deal is found in chapter II of the schedule, where we find that the compensation to be paid is tied to the French gold franc. I must say that before the minister explained the meaning of tying the compensation to the French gold franc, I had serious misgivings as to just what compensation parties in Canada might obtain under a valuation of that kind. But even with the explanation which has been given, and even with the tie-up to the French gold franc, we are still left to obtain our compensation on the basis of the amount which may be paid from time to time by the United States for one ounce of gold. Even using that type of valuation, there is nothing to ensure that in the future the number of francs which are provided to cover compensation to an injured party might not be entirely inadequate.
The third point to which I shall refer is that there is no protection afforded to parties on the ground injured as a result of accidents which occur in the use of the aircraft prior to the actual application of power for the takeoff or subsequent to the removal of power upon landing the aircraft on the runway. There is no coverage whatever in those two individual cases, from the time the aircraft touches down until it is at rest at the airport with its engine shut off, nor do we have coverage from the time the aircraft is warmed up on the tarmac and is removed to the runway for full power to be applied for the takeoff. Those provisions are contained in chapter I of the schedule. It seems to me we have been remiss in not obtaining complete coverage for people on the ground from the actual time the ignition switch is turned on in the aircraft until it is turned off after the passengers have alighted.
The fourth point is that, upon examination, we have found there is a continuing liability on the owner of the aircraft for a period of time after the complete legal disposal of title to the aircraft itself. I think perhaps in connection with this point there was the intention to provide the same type of continuing insurance coverage for injured parties as we have now provided in a number of public liability and property damage policies covering the use of automobiles. However, I feel that this provision may present a real obstacle in so far as our own airlines are concerned. As an example, in connection with Trans-Canada Air Lines re-equipment program, there may be disposal of numerous aircraft to foreign countries and we may find our government-owned airline bearing a continuing responsibility notwithstanding the removal of any legal title to the aircraft in question. These provisions are contained in chapter I of the schedule.

My fifth point concerns the question of the procedure used in obtaining execution of judgments which may be obtained in connection with this legislation. The minister has been fair in pointing out that no greater rights are obtained through this legislation than have been available to any private party heretofore in attempting to obtain execution of a judgment in a foreign country. I feel that should have been one of the main reasons for drafting this type of legislation, to ensure that in the execution of a judgment for a valid damage claim no particular impediment might be placed by the country in whose territory the assets or insurance fund lies. These provisions are contained in chapter IV of the schedule. Execution of the judgment may be refused if the judgment concerned is contrary to the public policy of the state in which execution is requested. What public policy may be in any number of South American countries, I would not know. There might be a complete inability to issue execution and obtain repayment of any damage claims.
My sixth point is that there has been a very feeble effort in chapter II of the schedule to provide some type of preference for persons who have personal injury claims. The fund has been divided into two parts, for personal injuries and for property damage. There is a residual clause that if money is available after property damage has been completely paid, that money will go into the personal injury fund. At the same time, that does not definitely cover the situation. I feel there will be numerous claims where personal injuries have been suffered and, because of the division of the insurance fund, the person who has been injured may end up by getting a payment of 10 cents on the dollar whereas someone who has suffered property damage only may receive 100 cents on the dollar.
My seventh point is the usual one. Again we are being asked to agree to proposals which have been contributed mainly by representatives of the United States. As usual, too, we are being asked to ratify the agreement before that country ratifies it. Again the minister has been very fair and has stated that only a small percentage of the actual flights over Canadian territory as of this date are going to be covered by this agreement. Until such time as the United States does formally accept this agreement, then the coverage that will be available to Canadians will be restricted to a great extent. I believe it is the responsibility of the government, in presenting legislation of this type, to see that we are not being presented with the hollow shell of an agreement which reads well but does not afford the protection it is intended to afford.
Foreign Aircraft
Finally, I may say that, on questioning in the special committee on transport, the president of the Trans-Canada Air Lines indicated satisfaction with this agreement but I was very surprised to know that this agreement was negotiated entirely without the benefit of the advice of counsel of our two major operating international airlines. It seems to me that if we are to go out in the future under the guise of obtaining some beneficial result for the Canadian public, giving them protection, which undoubtedly is the chief requisite of this agreement, in view of the thousands and thousands of dollars that are spent on delegations of this kind, we should expect that they would seek, and be glad to seek, the counsel of those airlines in our country that are having to deal with these problems day by day.
If we cannot do better than this in the future, we should call on such advice or it would be better for us to stay at home.

I certainly do not wish to prolong the debate on this measure unduly, but if I may judge from the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, he seems to fail to appreciate that there are manifest advantages in relieving persons on the surface who suffer damage from the necessity of establishing negligence. I take it that the price of not having to prove negligence is the limitation of liability for which the convention provides. As I said in the debate on second reading, I do not think anybody would suggest that this is a perfect convention from every point of view. Particularly, it might be considered that it represents an agreement reached after discussion between some 32 nations in 1952, and that in consequence it is the result of compromise on the part of those who participated in the discussion. I have no doubt it was the best agreement that could then be made.
The hon. member also referred to the fact that the compensation was expressed in gold francs, and complained that if there were a fluctuation in the price of gold, there would thereupon be a fluctuation in the limitation of the liability. Well, that may be a perfectly valid criticism, but it would have been more valid if the hon. member had indicated some means by which the amount of the compensation could have been fixed by some standard other than that which is provided for in the convention. It ties it to the gold franc consisting of 65 grains of gold of fineness 900.

Foreign Aircraft
The hon. member then went on, in expressing two or three criticisms of the convention, to complain that it did not provide for the situation where damage occurred before takeoff or after landing. I find that a little contradictory because, after criticizing the convention, he went on to regret that it did not apply for a longer period than that for which it is to apply. In effect, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member has failed to appreciate the fact that before takeoff and after takeoff there is no limitation on liability whatsoever. The convention does not protect the operator who causes damage to the person on the surface in these circumstances.

Well, I suppose that would depend on whether you considered the airplane itself as something having value or not. If, as is usually the case, and I should like to touch on that in reply to another comment of the hon. member, one bears in mind that these foreign aircraft do come into Canada and that there is therefore the process of executing judgment against planes belonging to the operator who has incurred a liability, it would be wrong to say that there was no security. The insurance security might not be so easily attainable, but the fact would remain that the plane would be there. It could be there, and the judgment could be executed, provided the plane was within the jurisdiction of the court which granted the judgment.
With respect to the question of the continuing liability on the owner if he dispossessed himself of the aircraft, perhaps if the hon. member had been the only person who had anything to say in making the convention it would not have contained the clause which it does contain; but, as I said earlier, this is the result of international negotiations between 32 countries, and I do not think we should condemn the convention solely on the ground of this fact of continuing liability.
The hon. member spoke also of the question of the execution of the judgment. I think it is fair to say that the provisions of the convention reproduce in substance what I would assume to be the general provisions of law in any jurisdiction with regard to the execution of the judgments of some foreign court. I do not think there is anything repugnant in the provisions and I think the

hon. member, if he were advising a Canadian airline, would be rather glad, when he was defending it against the execution of a judgment rendered in some foreign court, if, under the convention, he could invoke the grounds of defence which are mentioned in the convention itself. Certainly, I would feel much happier if I were in the position of defending one of our airlines from such a judgment if I felt I could oppose execution on the grounds set forth in the convention.
As I said earlier, so far as execution of a Canadian judgment is concerned, the house should not overlook the fact that there is always the possibility of executing against an aircraft when it touches down in Canada, not necessarily immediately but on some future occasion.
The hon. member also spoke of what he described as a feeble effort to protect or to give priority to personal claims. I am sorry that he does not seem yet to understand the provisions of the convention. When we were discussing this matter in committee the other night I tried to show him by giving him a hypothetical example of the division of the proceeds of the insurance that when the proceeds were less than the total amount of the claims those who had claims for personal injury had a priority over those who had claims for property damage.

subtopic: THIRD PARTY DAMAGE

speechtext: I had better examples.

subtopic: THIRD PARTY DAMAGE

speechtext:
Well, all I can say is that though the hon. member may have better examples, he cannot find an example anywhere where the property claims would be paid in full without a very substantial proportion at least being paid to those who have claims for bodily injury. At all events, I do not think the convention can stand or fall on this point. On reading the convention one can see that there is no doubt whatever that there is a definite effort, not a feeble effort, as the hon. member said, to give a species of priority to those who have claims for bodily injury.
In conclusion, the hon. member said that the United States of America had not ratified this convention. He referred to the fact that only a relatively small number of flights over Canada were by foreign aircraft. Of course I think that is true. If there is a smaller number of flights there is a decreased possibility of foreign aircraft causing damage to persons on the surface.
I think the convention is a workable document and one which ought to be ratified by

parliament. I would add that both the Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Air Lines have approved the signing of the convention by Canada and I think it will be in the interests of Canadian aviation to have this convention ratified.

Each of the twenty people may put in a claim for $10,000, which would total $200,000. The property damage may amount to $50,000.
If I understand the working of the formula correctly, the fund would be divided into two, $50,000 for personal injuries and $50,000 for property damage. speechtext: I have been trying to follow the hon. member as he went along. I shall give him the figures and he can go back and check them afterward. Those claims to the extent of $150,000 would divide with the claim for property damage amounting to $50,000 the other half of the indemnity, so that the property damage claim would receive $12,500 while the claims for bodily injury would receive $87,500.

This subclause deals with a matter of great importance to the people in my constituency, particularly those who live at Banff. I realize that this legislation will apply to all national parks and will cover Jasper as well as people who live at Banff. May I say first that I appreciate the minister bringing forward this legislation at this time as it is something the people of Banff have been working on for some considerable time.
Both the hon. member for Acadia and I have discussed this with the minister and the departmental officials in Ottawa on a number of occasions during the past year or so and we are pleased to know that the minister is now bringing down legislation which will make available to the people of Banff the general hospitalization plan which is in effect in Alberta. So that hon. members of the committee may know what we are talking about in a little more detail, may I tell them something about the plan which is proposed for Banff. I should like to quote what Mr. Lee Leavitt, the M.L.A. for Banff had to say about this, as reported in the Banff Crag and Canyon. Referring to the $1 per day, it says:
Each patient under this plan pays one dollar for each hospital day. The local hospital district and the provincial government share the remaining cost for the standard ward care on a 50-50 basis.
Then it goes on:
Then there is a separate contract which covers extras, which may be negotiated only if the dollar per day plan is in force. But such agreement is optional. After 25 per cent of the daily set cost of these extras is paid by the patient, the remaining cost is shared again on a 50-50 basis by hospital district and the provincial government.
Proposed new legislation which will be brought before the house-
Meaning the provincial legislature.
[DOT]-this session, will make some changes to these present arrangements. In short, it means that, providing a hospital district will also negotiate an agreement covering special services or extras, the cost of both agreements, as described, will be shared by the provincial government on a 40-60 basis. With the government paying the 60 per cent there will be little difference in costs between the alternative plans. The cost of the dollar per day contract, without extras covered, will continue to be shared on a 50-50 basis. The additional contribution by the provincial government will, I am sure, stimulate interest in this hospitalization plan.
Now, Mr. Chairman, you will see that this hospitalization plan is one of the most progressive of the hospitalization plans in all of Canada. Therefore the people of Banff are rightly concerned in their desire to have the federal government amend the parks legislation so that they will be able to share under this plan. It is going to affect every one of
[Mr. Lesage.l
the citizens of Banff who are taxpayers, and provision is made also for those who are nonresident if they take out a separate contract with the district and the government to share in this plan. Speaking from memory, I think that the cost of this plan is $8 per individual, or $15 per family a year, giving them access to all these services. But the people of Banff themselves feel that they have the right to share in these hospital benefits in the same way as any other person in Alberta. Of course I think that it is only right and proper that they should have it. Again I say that I am glad that the government has seen fit to come to the same conclusion.
The provincial law which exists now makes the province's share payable to the municipal authorities, and the municipal authorities must collect their own share of that revenue; but there is no municipal authority in Banff. Therefore Bill No. 261, which we are presently discussing, is to make Banff parks an eligible area under the provincial law. Alberta is amending its hospitals act to permit park contributions to be levied and collected from the Banff citizens by the parks superintendent or other person or authority appointed by the government authorities here. I want to make it clear that the amendments in the province of Alberta are making it possible for these collections to be made either by the park superintendent or by some other authority named by the government. I think that is quite clearly borne out by what the minister said the other day in the house. On page 2146 of Hansard he had this to say:
Hence the provincial laws are going to be amended to say that in the parks the contributions can be levied from the population by the parks superintendents or persons authorized by the park authorities. Our bill is to authorize the government, through the park superintendent-
May I just point out, Mr. Chairman, at that point that, as far as I can read the bill, it does not authorize the park superintendent only to make the collections.
I am pointing that out to you now because I wish to speak about that further a little later on. The bill, as I understand it, makes it possible for the park superintendent or other authority to make the collections.
Our bill is to authorize the government, through the park superintendent, to receive these contributions paid by people for these hospital schemes which would be established. They could be so established only after a referendum has been taken, according to the provincial acts, in the parks or in the townsites, I am not sure which at this time. It will be easier to follow when I have the bill.
I just bring that to your attention for the purpose which I indicated, Mr. Chairman.

The people of Banff are desirous of having this tax collected by some other authority rather than the park superintendent. Their view-and I shall give it to you categorically in a moment-is generally speaking that, if the park superintendent is one who is going to collect these fees, then of necessity he will be guided, and must be so, by the park regulations, and the people of Banff through their advisory council are of the opinion that they do not relish being under the park regulations, for reasons which I shall give. They do suggest, though, that this collection could be made by the advisory council itself, which is the body chosen by the people in Banff to represent their interests, or it could be collected by the provisional board of the hospital district which is being set up in the Banff area. In that way they contend that it would be more fairly levied and more fairly collected and greater satisfaction would come about all the way through.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that I was going to tell you exactly why the Banff people did not want this under the regulations. This may come somewhat as a surprise to the minister, but I think he will agree with me when he hears my argument that the people of Banff are quite right in what they say. Now, I am reading from a letter dated March 14 from the advisory council. Mr. Shaw is the chairman of the advisory council, and the secretary is Mr. R. E. Edwards, both living in Banff. It says in part-
