The chief reasons for this opposition are (a) The very unsatisfactory administration of the health and welfare tax and the almost certainty that the hospital tax would be administered in a similar manner, (b) The inclusion of the hospital plan in the parks regulations would render it subject to the same unjust penalties that are incorporated in the welfare tax. imprisonment for not more than six months, and as the welfare tax is part of the park regulations the section quoted becomes applicable. Just in case there should be some question as to whether or not that is the actual law, may I just refer to the regulations; and may I say to you that, when I studied these regulations, I was astonished to find the severity with which this matter can be handled. It refers not only to a delinquent in respect of the payment of a welfare tax, or rather not only would it refer to a delinquent in the payment of his hospital tax, but to anyone who violates any part of the act or any regulation whatsoever, no matter how trivial. Just listen to some of these provisions. I thought I was reading something from the medieval ages when I went over this thing. I am going to suggest to the minister what should be done with it in a few moments. I am reading from page 5 of the regulations. It is chapter 189 of the statutes. It says here:

What is astonishing about it is this. It applies to any regulation whatsoever. The minister told me he was going to give me a lesson in fishing. Incidentally, I may say that I am looking forward to that lesson. But I would advise him not to bring along a fish hook that has three prongs on it because, if he does so, that is a violation. I am told that "two-gang" is the word. I am not a fisherman, but I will be one when the minister gives me a lesson. If you had one of these hooks in your possession, or if the police had reason to suspect that you had one of these in your possession, they can come into your house without a warrant and break into your trunk, your dresser, or into your bedroom if the door is locked and search the house, even on suspicion. Then the next heading is this:
Arrest, Search and Seizure
Any constable or any person having the powers of a constable under the provisions of this act or regulations may, (a) on view,-
That is on sight.
-arrest any person found committing an oifence against this act or the regulations or found committing within a park any unlawful act; . . .
It is an unlawful act or it is a violation of the regulations if a person fails to get that old licence for the town cat that I was talking about some months ago. If he fails to pay this $3 licence fee to have a cat in the park, he is subject to a fine of not more than $500 or to six months' imprisonment with hard labour-whoever heard of such a thing?-without even a warrant being necessary. Then part (c) reads as follows:
(c) on view, seize, whether within or without the boundaries of any park, any timber, hay, mineral, fish, mammal or bird, or any part thereof, arms, ammunition, explosives, traps, nets, rods, vessels, boats, vehicles, equipment, outfit, appliance, or any other article whatsoever that he has reason to believe are or have been possessed or used in connection with the commission of a violation of any of the provisions of this act and the regulations.
That means that if I were suspected of having had one of these fish hooks with three prongs on it-that is not the right term but you know what I mean-in the park, the authorities could come into my house in Calgary, without a warrant, and make a search of that house; they could break into any part of it which they desired to break into; and on conviction I would be liable to a penalty of $500 or six months' imprisonment with hard labour.

On a point of order, I do not mind the minister interjecting to answer a question or to try to correct me if I am wrong, but I wish he would wait until I am through to make his speech. He has made a couple of statements that are causing me some concern. He said there was never any question of anything else except a poll tax. The people of Banff have been unalterably opposed to a poll tax. They have understood from the beginning that there was to be an assessment tax. In fact, the provincial government has gone so far as to say this plan could not possibly be put into operation at Banff on any other basis than an assessment tax because everybody else in the province of Alberta is on an assessment basis. The minister and his department know that to be true. I want to emphasize that. Do not say here that the people of Banff have always advocated a poll tax. They certainly have not. The provincial government has also made it very clear to the authorities at Ottawa that it could only be done on an assessment basis.
When he was discussing the matter a moment ago the minister pointed out that the people there wanted such a plan. Of course they want it. There is no question about that. As I said when I started my remarks, we are all grateful to the minister for bringing in this legislation-although it is only his job-and making it possible for the people of Banff to have hospital service. However, the only thing the federal government has to do is to bring in this little bit of legislation, and the people of Banff and the province of Alberta will do the rest.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITHDRAWING LANDS, CREATING NEW PARKS, ETC.
speechtext:
Certainly they would. The people of Banff want it collected either by the advisory council or by the provisional board of the hospital district which is being formed in Banff. Certainly they would do it because, as I have indicated, they do not want to come under these park regulations with these unfair penalties attached to them. In a letter I just read I indicated some of the unfair penalties that have been applied. It is no use for the minister to say that this section has never been applied or that the penalties would not be applied to the hospital plan. Of course they will. They have been applied. If these things are so outdated, why keep them in the act?
I suggest to the minister again that this section should be taken out of the act because it is so ridiculous to think that a person violating any of these regulations should be subject to a $500 fine or six months' imprisonment at hard labour. There may be several reasons why a person could not pay his tax on the date when it was due. There may be several reasons why he had a fish hook with three prongs on it in his house. But is that to say he should be subject to a fine of $500 or six months' imprisonment with hard labour? Of course that is ridiculous. I suggest to the minister he would be doing a service to himself, to the country, and particularly to the national parks of Canada and the people therein, if he would strike this penalty clause from the statute entirely.
At this moment I do not have much more to say. I have pointed out to the minister how grateful the people of Banff are that this amendment has been introduced. I have pointed out to him as strongly as I can why I think there should be certain changes. I have mentioned two very important changes. The first is that the collection of the tax should be allotted by the federal government to the advisory council, the elected body of the people of Banff. The government can do that if they want to without further amendment of the legislation. If not, the collection of the tax should be allotted, to the provisional board of the hospital district. In either case, it should not be subject to these park regulations.
In the second place, the tax, without any question, should be on an assessment basis. The provincial government has made it very clear it just would not be feasible to do it on any other basis, and certainly not by means of a poll tax. That is something that is not done in any other part of the province, and the contention is that the same practice should be followed in Banff that is followed in

other parts of the province. I hope the minister will take the suggestions I have made into consideration. I do not think he has made a definite decision whether or not the tax will be a poll tax or will be on an assessment basis. I hope he will give this matter consideration. In view of what I have said, in view of the fact the people of Banff do not want it on a poll tax basis but on an assessment basis, and in view of the fact the provincial government insists it shall be that way, I think the government should declare quite candidly at this time that the things I have asked for will be incorporated in the act and the regulations.

speechtext:
I am glad to see this amendment to authorize agreements with authorities in a province for making arrangements with hospitals for hospital service. I understand the main reason for introducing this amendment now is to make it possible for the people of Banff national park to come under the dollar-a-day hospitalization plan. I understand also that there is some concern now as to whether or not the sisters at Banff can continue to operate the hospital without financial assistance. On the other hand, they are strongly in favour of coming in under the dollar-a-day plan. I am sure the minister himself would agree that it would be a deplorable situation if the hospital at Banff had to close.
I attended a public meeting in September called under the auspices of the advisory council, to discuss the dollar-a-day scheme. I may say that at that meeting there was a great deal of confusion as to the method by which the money would be collected, and confusion as to the method by which the tax would be levied. Some were under the impression it would be done by a poll tax; some were under the impression it would be by a mill rate levied on property; some thought the province would collect the tax; some thought the superintendent of the park would collect the tax, and others thought the hospital board would collect it. There was so much confusion at that meeting it was decided finally that a member of the advisory council would go to Edmonton and have a meeting with the minister of health. Upon the return of this delegate, another meeting would be called and then a further discussion would take place.
Mr. Shaw of the advisory council went to Edmonton and had a thorough discussion with Dr. Cross, the minister of health, concerning the plan. Then, on October 27, another public meeting was called. At that meeting Mr. Victor Price, the business manager of the Holy Cross hospital in Calgary, was in attendance in order to answer any

questions that might be asked because he had firsthand knowledge of the operation of the dollar-a-day plan. I might mention that Mr. Price was there, not as a representative of any government but purely as a service to the people of Banff in order that they might get firsthand knowledge of the operation of the dollar-a-day plan.
When the meeting was called it was announced that if the plan went into operation it would have to be on the basis of a mill rate tax on assessed property. Perhaps to make this quite clear I should read a letter that was written by Dr. Cross to Mr. R. E. W. Edwards, secretary of the Banff advisory council. The reason the letter was written was that the people of Banff had asked the advisory council to obtain from the minister of health a statement in writing so that there would not be any more conflicting statements. During the first meeting some people said the minister of health had stated this, and others said the minister had said something different. In view of this the people wanted a written statement so that they would know exactly what the proposal was. I will read the letter that was written by Dr. Cross to Mr. Edwards, and which was made available to the people at that meeting:
Dear Sir:-
Re Proposed Municipal Hospital District for Banff National Park
Further to a meeting with a member of your council, Mr. Shaw, last week, this will advise that the only plan acceptable to the department to establish the $1 a day hospitalization scheme is by way of a mill rate tax on all assessed property within the boundaries of the park. This method is in accord with the municipal hospitals act, being chapter 185 of the revised statutes of Alberta, and the plan is in operation today in sixty-nine municipal hospital districts over the province.
We have agreed to amend the municipal hospitals act as suggested-
I should like the minister to pay special attention to this:
-by Mr. R. G. Robertson, deputy minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources at Ottawa, to make any resident of the park assessed for school taxes, a ratepayer under the municipal hospitals act. This will give your council (or park superintendent) authority to levy and collect a tax on the same basis as your school tax at present in effect: then the municipal hospital board will be in a position to requisition your council each year for sufficient funds to carry out an agreement with the sisters' hospital at Banff.
So from then on the discussion that took place in that meeting was on the definite understanding the plan would be financed by a mill rate on the assessment.
Now, Mr. Price wanted to know just how many of the people present at the meeting were ratepayers, and how many were just curious spectators. A show of hands was called, and it was found that 99 per cent of
National Parks Act
the people present at that meeting were ratepayers. When the vote was called an overwhelming majority of the people at the meeting voted in favour of the dollar-a-day hospital plan financed by a mill rate tax, on the assessment of property. I quote from an article appearing in Crag and Canyon concerning that meeting:
Following an explanation of the dollar a day hospitalization plan, a meeting that jammed the auditorium on Wednesday evening voted overwhelmingly for the establishment of Banff national park as a municipal hospital area. A request, therefore, to this effect will be forwarded to the proper authorities.
A show of hands established that over 99 per cent of those present were ratepayers-those whom the plan would most seriously affect. The only plan acceptable to the department of health as a means of financing the scheme is by way of mill rate tax on all assessed property within the boundaries of the park.
I believe that should settle clearly in the mind of the minister that any discussion that has taken place recently concerning the adoption of the dollar-a-day plan in Banff has been on the basis of a mill rate levied on property. The minister has stated it should be on the basis of a poll tax. Personally, I believe a poll tax would be a very unfair method of financing the hospital plan. I have heard it suggested that the minister has been influenced by the Canadian Pacific. I am not making that as a charge. Of course, it was made quite clear at the meeting that the Canadian Pacific would be very much opposed to a mill rate tax on property for the purpose of financing the hospital. Some of the other very large property owners were also opposed. As I say, however, 99 per cent of the people at that meeting were ratepayers and they voted overwhelmingly in favour of the hospital plan being financed by a mill rate tax on assessed property. Let us not have any more discussion as to whether the people of Banff are in favour of the poll tax or a mill rate on assessed property. They are definitely in favour of the mill rate tax on assessed property.
I am hoping that the minister will not now, at this late date, throw a monkey wrench into the works by insisting that the plan be operated on the basis of a poll tax. As the Alberta health department has pointed out, they could only do it on the basis of a mill rate. All the other hospitals are being financed on that basis and they could hardly make an exception for one hospital to be financed on a different basis. I hope the minister will find it possible to agree to something to which his deputy minister has apparently already agreed, namely that it be financed by a mill rate.

I think there is considerable merit in collecting the taxes from those who pay health and welfare taxes because there would be a wider distribution. Approximately one-third of the residents of Banff fall into the class of renters; consequently they would be excluded if a property tax were adopted, unless they came into the scheme on a contract basis.

It is most difficult to decide whether it should be a poll tax or a so-called property tax. As a matter of fact the property is all owned by the federal government and it is leased; but it would be a tax on the interest of the lessee in the property. You may call it an assessment tax if you wish.

Yes, it has already been done for school tax purposes. Therefore, it is a question of deciding whether it should be a poll tax or an assessment tax. Both the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Bow River argue in favour of an assessment tax. May I say again that when I discussed the matter with the members of the advisory council in Banff last summer it 
never entered my mind that it could be anything but a poll tax that they had in mind, which would be levied in the same manner as the park superintendent collects for the welfare services.
I do not want to argue in favour of the poll tax and against the assessment tax at this time because I do not have to make the decision today. I want to study the matter very carefully and discuss it with the authorities of the province of Alberta and with the officers of the parks branch of the department, and also to consider the representations which I no doubt will receive from the residents of Banff. But it seems to me that whenever we discuss welfare measures, we should as a general principle try to have as wide a distribution of the burden as possible.
That was one of the principles which were the basis of the recommendations which were made by the committee on old age security in 1950. Whenever the benefits of a social security measure are universal, be it all over Canada, all over a province, or all over a municipality, the burden should be as widely distributed as possible over the people who will benefit from it. That is one of the principles I have to keep in mind when I make the decision whether it will be a poll tax or an assessment tax. There are other considerations; but one thing is important. It is this. The bill which is before the house now reads as follows in subclause 3, paragraph (q):
Levying taxes on any residents of a park or on the interest of any persons in land in a park in order to defray in whole or in part . . .
It permits either an assessment tax or a poll tax to be established.

He has already indicated that the tax should be applied to the greatest number of the people who are to receive benefit under it. When the minister is considering this matter may I suggest to him that the provincial government could not inaugurate a program of this magnitude without being reasonably sure that the revenue would be forthcoming to carry it out. It seems to me that because the population at Banff is a shifting one the revenue from a poll tax would be very uncertain. On the other hand, an assessment basis tax would be more permanent.
In addition to that, all the people in Banff who were not taxed on an assessment basis would have the privilege of coming under this legislation by entering into separate contracts, and everybody would be covered. It seems to me that an assessment basis would be the most appropriate of all, and certainly it would be the most satisfactory from the standpoint of administration and the security of the people of Banff, who are anxious to have this measure in effect. As the hon. member for Acadia has stated, they have indicated an overwhelming desire that this be as we have outlined it. I hope the minister will see fit to follow the advice of the people who are going to be concerned in this very matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING SALE OF LAND BEFORE SURVEY
speechtext:
The amendment to the Territorial Lands Act provides simply for the repeal of subsection 2 of section 5 of the act.
[Mr. Harkness.l
This subsection required that plans of survey had to be approved by the surveyor general before territorial lands could be sold. It applies to lands in both the Yukon and Northwest Territories. While the intent of the subsection was perfectly sound, it has raised difficulties in practice.
When a person wishes to purchase a parcel of land, he expects to be informed of the price that will be charged. While it has been possible under the present subsection to give a prospective buyer an estimate of the probable cost of the land, no formal agreement of sale could be legally entered into until after the survey had been carried out and approved by the surveyor general. Due to a continuing shortage of qualified surveyors it has usually been a minimum of two years and often much longer between the time a request to purchase was made and the time the survey was completed and approved. During the intervening period the land may well have increased substantially in value, and the original estimate of price would be greatly exceeded when the time came for the formal agreement to be completed.
By deleting subsection 2 the sale of land will be governed by the general clause in the act, namely section 4 which states:
Subject to this act, the governor in council may authorize the sale, lease or other disposition of territorial lands and may make regulations authorizing the minister to sell, lease or otherwise dispose of territorial lands subject to such limitations and conditions as the governor in council may prescribe.
It would then be possible under this general section to enter into an agreement of sale shortly after the request to purchase was made, based on an appraisal of the land in question, with a price fixed on a unit basis and with the total price to be paid subject to the completed survey. Normally the unit price -would be a price per acre. The appraisal would be made by competent officers who would make as accurate an estimate as possible of the area involved so that subsequent adjustments in the total price, on completion of the legal survey, would be kept as small as possible.
It is proposed that regulations made under the act will contain a provision that no letters patent covering the sale of land may be issued until the survey has been completed and approved by the surveyor general, so that the original intent of subsection 2 will be met.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PERMITTING SALE OF LAND BEFORE SURVEY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see this proposed amendment which will repeal subsection 2 of section 5 of the Territorial Lands Act to permit sales of territorial lands to be made prior to survey of the land

and which will permit the price to be fixed at the time the application to purchase is accepted by the department.
In the past, under the present provisions of the act, I know of persons in the Yukon Territory who applied to purchase parcels of territorial land many years ago. They naturally wanted to know the cost under the present act, but officials of the lands division could not tell them what the price would be until such time as the land in question was properly defined by a dominion land surveyor. In certain cases there was a gap of several years between the time of application and the time of survey, a situation which naturally caused considerable dissatisfaction and inconvenience. In other words, under that interpretation a person would not know how much he would be assessed for the land until several years after he had decided to purchase it.
Those now contemplating the purchase of territorial land will welcome the proposed amendment which will enable the department to tell the applicant what the price of the land will be when he applies to purchase it. I am pleased to see this amendment being introduced.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: At present when a man is convicted and his conviction has been set aside on appeal, he has to re-enrol in order to be reinstated. In other words he cannot be retroactively reinstated. We find, as the result of a ruling of the Department of Justice, that there is a break in his service even though, having been convicted, he wins his appeal. This provision will take care of that situation. The practice proposed here is followed in the United Kingdom. Except for this clause the break in his service would affect his pensionable time, seniority, and possibly his position in respect of progressive increase in pay. On clause 3-

speechtext:
The minister might explain this clause. It would seem this is a method of taking back from civilian life ex-members of the forces in order to try

them before a military tribunal. I wonder whether the civil courts could not adequately take care of matters of this kind. I am thinking about the instances of pilfering to which reference has been made. Would the civil courts not be able to take care of people who have returned to civil life?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: A civil court can only deal with civil offences. The law now provides that a man who has been released from the service may still be tried under the code of service discipline for offences committed while in the service although he has left the service. That is the law now. But there is no provision in the present law stating that the man is under service discipline for the period between the time he is charged and the time he is convicted or acquitted. This amendment will mean that a man who has left the service and is charged with a service offence which took place during the time he was in service shall be under the code of service discipline from the time he is charged until the charge is disposed of. It is a purely procedural gap which we are trying to fill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

case that you have to have stand for a very considerable time in order to properly prepare it.

It is my opinion that cases in which it takes the prosecution 90 days to complete its evidence, as a rule, are not the type where a man would be under open arrest. Even if he were under open arrest there is a big difference between being under open arrest and being out on bail in a civil case. In the case of open arrest you are not in the hoosegow, as the hon. member for Nanaimo mentioned, but you are confined to quarters. There is, therefore, a very big difference between being under open arrest and being out on bail in a civil case. It looks to me as though there is an undue hardship on a person who has not yet been found guilty.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

The difference between a man *out on bail in a civil case and a man in the fMr. Campney.]
services who is confined to barracks is that the man on bail can go to his work and maintain his family, while the man in the services is deprived of his pay and allowances during the period he is under charge. I feel that 90 days is a very long time to hold' a man, even under open arrest. I do not believe he would be under open arrest, anyway. My experience with commanding officers is that they generally like to tie you down and keep you where they can get you when they want you.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: I might say that a man under charge, before he is tried, does not lose his pay and allowances. I might give some examples of the need for this clause. We had several cases in Korea where serious offences were charged and we had to bring some witnesses from Canada to Korea. We have had charges of murder in Germany. It is not so easy to find out all the facts in such cases in a foreign country. This power will not be used lightly, but in serious cases it is necessary, and I think it is very necessary to the proper functioning of trials under military procedure. speechtext:
This represents a change in procedural law. At the present time the judge advocate merely advises the court-martial as to what is the law. This provision would extend his duties and his responsibilities to the point where he will decide what the law is. In other words he will be somewhat in the position of a judge with a jury. The lack of this authority by the judge advocate, it is felt, has led to some unfairness to accused persons on a number of occasions where trials within trials on the admissibility of evidence have taken place in the presence of the members of the court. It is not felt that such procedure has been altogether fair to the accused.
Since normally the only official of the court who is a lawyer is the judge advocate, it is felt it would be more in the interests of the accused obtaining a proper trial if the judge advocate were made responsible for directing the court-martial as to what is the law,

and then the court-martial, having taken their law from him, can make any finding they see fit on the facts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: In connection with that section, does the minister see the change in procedure amounting to this. Then the board comes back. Is that the process we see developing here?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: I am getting to be an old man; therefore I am not up to date on these things. If there is assurance of that procedure being followed we can possibly say that this clause is satisfactory. What everyone is concerned about is that the judge advocate does not act both as judge and jury. We have talked about setting it up on the basis that it would be closely akin to the civil process of judge and jury. If it is currently in the act or in the regulations- I have not noticed it-that the judge advocate does not sit in at the time the decision is made, I think we can safely say that we have separated the law from the peers of the accused, which in effect may not be a true statement of military law, but it still does what we are trying to achieve, namely to have the accused tried by laymen.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: This is an attempt to cut down the time and expense involved in appeals under certain circumstances, by reducing the number of appeals. As the law stands now the court-martial appeal board may find an appellant guilty of an included offence or on an alternative charge, but in such a case it cannot impose a greater sentence than that already given. This is to provide that the minister or some other authority which he may appoint can do these two things himself rather than sending the case to the court-martial appeal board. In other words, if he sees or his officials see that a case has gone wrong and the court-martial appeal board will undoubtedly substitute another finding, he can himself do that and avoid the loss of time and the cost involved in an appeal. It is felt that this provision will be in the interests of justice and will reduce the number of court-martial appeals.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext:

The tribunal could on the charge have found the offender guilty under section 120 of that other offence,-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: I should like to make three observations. First, under no circumstances can the minister increase the punishment. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: It is clear that this can be done only with the consent of the accused; the minister cannot substitute a conviction for one offence after the accused has been convicted in error on another. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext:
I realize that clause (a) is a recapitulation, but we are passing it now and it covers a situation where a man has been convicted illegally or where his conviction cannot be supported by evidence. That is

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: The powers under discussion are vested in the appeal board. This is merely a narrow selection of cases where it appeared obvious the minister might properly act. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: I do not understand the phrase in line 13 which reads "if it appears that the service tribunal was satisfied of the facts".

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: When they made a mistake.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: There is no transcript made of their proceedings and observations. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: When a service tribunal comes to a decision, whatever it may be, I think it must be assumed that they are satisfied as a tribunal of the facts on which they have reached a decision. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

This provision if enacted will enable the minister to obviate all the expense and time involved in holding a court-martial appeal board hearing and to come to a decision which is obviously the proper one on the facts. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

speechtext:
Yes. We were all possibly getting a little bit confused with respect to this section. The hon. member for York West suggested that I might prepare an example under each of the subclauses (a) and (b) (i) and (b) (ii) illustrating how we would deal with a situation under each of those subclauses. Under subclause (a) a man charged with desertion may, under the power granted by section 120 of the National Defence Act, be found guilty of absenting himself without leave. If a man is convicted of desertion and, on review, it is found that there is no evidence of intention-something which is, of course, an essential ingredient of the offence of desertion-the minister may, under clause
(a)	, on the same facts substitute a finding of guilty of absenting himself without leave.

If he is convicted of using threatening language and there is not sufficient evidence to establish this fact, there may, however, be sufficient evidence that he behaved with contempt or used insulting language. To come to subclause (b)	(ii), a man
charged with theft and alternatively with negligently failing to account for property set out in the theft charge, might be originally convicted of theft. If it was felt that the record did not support a finding of wilful misappropriation-that is theft-the minister could, under subclause
(b)	(ii), substitute a finding of guilty on the charge of negligently failing to account.

Canadian Forces Act
may in effect quash a conviction where a charge has been laid in the alternative? subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: The thing that bothers me is this. If a man is accused of alternative charges, one the major charge and the other the lesser, I should like to know what the explanation is of the fact that if the court finds him guilty of the lesser charge the minister may nevertheless in effect quash that finding because it is illegal, or because it cannot be supported by the evidence, and find him guilty of the major charge. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext: I am glad of that assurance, but I wonder if the minister could just carry it one step further and point out to me-and I am sorry to be obliged to delay him-the basis upon which he says it works in that way. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext:
Clause 15 deals with amendments to the Defence Services Pension Act, and the first amendment introduced in this clause is to make provision for the common law wife of an officer in the services to receive a pension on the death of the officer with whom she had been living.
It will be recalled that the Defence Services Pension Act is divided into five parts. Part I deals in the main with army officers; part II has special reference to the navy; part III has special reference to the air force, and part V deals with those personnel who entered the service since March, 1946. Therefore this particular amendment deals
[Mr. Campne.v.l
solely with the common law wife of an officer who joined the army prior to March, 1946.
I regret exceedingly that the minister should have even thought that it was desirable to introduce such an amendment. The reason given is that this act is being brought into line with the Public Service Superannuation Act, but I submit that there is all the difference in the world between a gentleman holding the Queen's commission and who is expected to exercise powers of leadership, and an ordinary civil servant.
An officer's character should be unquestioned. I do suggest that if an officer is living with a common law wife then his character might very well be open to question, and he will not be able to exercise the same qualities of leadership as a man whose domestic life is above reproach. We know that common law wives are recognized in many respects, and no doubt they came in during the frontier days when a man had to live under pioneering conditions and quite often would take unto himself a native woman.
While life in the army may be considered in some respects as living on the frontier, especially in our northland, the fact is that there is ample opportunity for officers stationed in the north to return to civilization in order to have carried out the ordinary religious ceremony of marriage. There are in the services today hundreds of chaplains of all denominations, and there would be no difficulty whatever in an officer having a priest or chaplain of his own denomination available to carry out the marriage service.
I think it is fundamentally unsound and unwise to lower the high standards required of an officer who is expected to lead men in battle. I know that sometimes during wartime it is necessary to lower some of these standards, when you have to have a wide expansion of officer personnel; but this is dealing with regular army officers, career men who have entered the services with the idea of setting high standards for others to follow. I cannot believe there are many regular officers who were in the services prior to 1946 who would require this particular amendment.
This pension to the widow is not paid as of right, it is paid as a compassionate allowance and is granted under certain definite conditions. There are limitations as to those who may receive a widow's pension. Section 26 of the Defence Services Pension Act sets out the qualifications. First, an applicant must be in the opinion of the minister worthy of a pension. If in the opinion of the minister the applicant is wealthy she will not

receive a pension. And there are other qualifications. Surely high moral qualities are of more importance than wealth. I take strong exception to this amendment, and I hope the minister will see his way clear to withdrawing it inasmuch as it applies to the regular army officers in peacetime.

The purpose of this clause
probably is not as narrow as the hon. member may be inadvertently suggesting. With the variation in divorce laws, even as between Great Britain and Canada, as well as other parts of the world, we have cases where people have regarded themselves as properly married throughout the great part of their lives. Then the man dies and it is found out that because of the interpretation of the laws of divorce in this country the widow has no pension.
These are not just cases of people living together in defiance of all the laws and conventions of society. A certain number of cases exist such as I have mentioned, where on the death of the spouse the widow finds herself faced with great hardship and difficulty, especially if she is left with a family. I think this principle has been well recognized in our procedure in Canada. It is approved in the Pension Act, the superannuation act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and was also approved in the dependents' allowances regulations.
I think it is well recognized that men and officers serving throughout the world serve under many difficulties, especially abroad, and occasionally find themselves in the position I outlined a moment ago. I would think that a provision of this kind, the principle of which has been well recognized for many years in other acts in Canada, would prove of considerable benefit for officers and men in the services and their dependents.

speechtext:
Sections 8 and 12 of the Veterans Benefit Act, 1954, make available to certain ex-service personnel the benefits of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act and of the Unemployment Insurance Act, respectively. Originally, the reinstatement in civil employment provisions were restricted to those who were specially enrolled for the purpose of serving in the special force, or who belonged to the reserve forces and served on the strength of the special force.
In the case of unemployment insurance the provisions were extended to the same two groups and also to members of the regular forces who served on the strength of the special force in a theatre of operations and were discharged on medical grounds while on the strength of the special force.
In 1951 the benefits of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act were extended to all persons enlisting for service in the regular forces and who did not serve for more than

three years; and in January, 1953, the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act were so extended. It is now felt that circumstances have changed to the point where the granting of these benefits should be restricted to those who have had service in a theatre of operations or who are now members of the regular forces and qualify under the conditions which I have outlined above. The latter are aware that they have this coverage and it is proposed to cover all who will have enlisted before July 1, 1955.
It has never been the policy to consider as veterans those who serve in the regular forces in peacetime and who do so for a career. The other statutes mentioned in the Veterans Benefit Act apply only to veterans who were enlisted for the special 18-month engagement or had service in a theatre of operations.
I might repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the proposals will not affect any entitlement which those now serving may already have under the Veterans Benefit Act.

subtopic: CERTAIN BENEFITS CONTINUED TO PERSONS JOINING REGULAR FORCES BEFORE JULY 1, 1955
speechtext:
Mr. SpeaKer, as I understand it this bill is to be referred to the committee on veterans affairs and no doubt it will be discussed in detail there. As we all know, the Veterans Benefit Act has been amended a good many times. It has been amended practically every year since 1950. As the parliamentary assistant has told us, it was passed in order to allow benefits which were given to veterans of world war II to be given to members of the special force who served in Korea during the Korean war, if we can call it that. I am sure everyone here will agree that this situation is as it should be. Korean veterans should receive and are receiving, we are glad to know, the same benefits as those which were given to veterans of world war I and world war II.
I think it is quite appropriate at this time to mention the fact that these veterans of the Korean war have given a good account of themselves. The last of the troops are now returning from Korea. As a matter of fact I think the last battalion has returned to Canada, and the other troops in Korea will soon be returning home. As we all know, these men gave a good account of themselves, as I have mentioned, in an extremely difficult fighting area, perhaps one of the most difficult in which men have ever had to fight. They have maintained the high standard that Canadian troops have always maintained in war, both in the first war and in the second war.
As to this particular bill-and as I said a moment ago it will be before the committee-there are two outstanding features.
Veterans Benefit Act
One is that it discontinues the benefits under the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act. The second is the discontinuing of the benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. These benefits are discontinued on July 1 of this year. Up to July 1 any man who enlists in the Canadian army will receive the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Those who enlist after July 1 will not receive those benefits. In other words we shall have two groups of men serving in the Canadian army, namely one group of men who will receive benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act-and these are of great value-and another group of men who will not receive those benefits.
On the face of it, Mr. Speaker, I must say that there seems to be discrimination there. A soldier coming back now or being discharged from the army, as I understand it, is entitled to 90 days' benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Hence all these men up to July 1 will receive that benefit. It is my understanding that these benefits will not be available to soldiers who enlist after July 1.
I should like to ask the minister just why July 1 was decided upon as a cut-off date. I should also like to have his comment on the criticism I have made on the score of unfairness. I should like to know whether there is some substitution which is being made for the benefit of these men who enlist after July 1 in order to compensate them in the same way as those who enlist before that date. After being in the army for three years, a man turned loose in Canada even at the present time, when we have considerable unemployment, would have a difficult time to carry on and obtain a job.
The parliamentary assistant spoke about the men serving in peacetime. The peacetime as we have it today is entirely different from the peacetime we have had in the past. Today we have what is known as the cold war. Today a young man who enlists for three years might well expect to be thrown into a hot war in a short time. I think these men might be considered. I believe it would be a good thing to continue the unemployment insurance benefits for the men who are enlisting. It would give them a sense of security after their three years' time was up and they retired from the forces. I should like to have from the minister or the parliamentary assistant some comment on these criticisms I have made.

Mr. Speaker, there is no particular significance with regard to the date

Veterans Benefit Act
of July 1, 1955. I should like to point out to the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) that this date applies with reg.ard to men going into the service. As the hon. member knows, men are being enrolled and enlisted for terms of three, five and seven years. Hence a person enrolled in the regular forces now would still be covered for the next three years. The date of July 1, 1955 was set so it would not be unfair to anybody. Anyone who enrols or enlists in the regular forces up until July 1, 1955, is covered. The date was set far enough in advance so there would not be any unfairness.
As the minister said when he introduced the resolution, and as I said in the statement I have just made, it has never been the policy to consider as veterans those who serve in the regular forces in peacetime and who do so for a career. The other statutes mentioned in the Veterans Benefit Act no longer obtain or apply to people serving in the regular forces. I do not think the hon. member believes that the unemployment insurance statute or the civilian employment statute should so apply. It is on that principle, that people who follow a regular force career should not have the benefit of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act or the Unemployment Insurance Act, that this act is now being amended.

subtopic: CERTAIN BENEFITS CONTINUED TO PERSONS JOINING REGULAR FORCES BEFORE JULY 1, 1955
speechtext: In reply to what has been stated, may I just say that we now have the Unemployment Insurance Act which covers practically all civilians. My point is that a man who serves for three or five years in the army, and that has been his employment, should be treated just the same as the man who is employed in civilian life. In these days, when we are bringing everything up to date, I think we could very well include men in the army under our unemployment insurance scheme in the same way as we try to include our civilians. subtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER 10, 1954

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (for the Minister of Fisheries) moved
subtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER 10, 1954
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 279, to implement a convention on great lakes fisheries between Canada and the United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. Watson MacNaughi (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER 10, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to approve the ratification of the convention on great lakes fisheries between Canada and the United States, and to provide implementing legislation to carry out Canada's obligations arising thereunder. The convention was signed at Washington on September 10, 1954, after prolonged negotiations extending over a period of many years. The fishing interests of Ontario and the government of Ontario were consulted on all aspects of the convention and were represented in the negotiations leading up to the signing of the convention
The purpose of the convention is to improve the great lakes fisheries through co-ordinated action of governmental agencies in Canada and the United States. Over a period of years the decline in some of the principal stocks of fish in the great lakes has been viewed with concern on both sides of the border. The causes of the decline are not adequately known. The sea lamprey has been greatly increasing in numbers and threatening some of the valuable fisheries. The lake trout in particular have suffered from the deprada-tions of this parasite.
At present research in the great lakes area on the Canadian side is being carried out by the federal government and the government of Ontario. On the United States side the federal government and eight state governments are engaged in similar research activities. One of the principal aims of the convention is to co-ordinate all these activities and direct them to common purposes.
The minister made a very thorough and complete statement at the resolution stage, and I do not believe I can add anything at the present time to what he said on that occasion. It is my intention to ask one of the members of the government to move that the

Great Lakes Fisheries
bill be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries when it receives second reading.

subtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER 10, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the bill not only involves the great lakes area but also involves the federal governments of two countries and the governments of the province of Ontario and eight states in the United States, I should like to make a few observations. The parliamentary assistant has just said that he is going to ask that the bill be referred to the standing committee; therefore I am going to limit my remarks and make them as brief as possible. We on this side of the house welcome the convention and regret that it did not come into existence years ago.
I am one of the members of the house who happen to live on the shores of the great lakes. I live on the shore of lake Huron, and in front of where I live the fisheries are carried on which are the concern of this parliament and are involved in this proposed legislation. Having lived there for some 25 or 30 years I must say that I am a bit more familiar with the difficulties that have been encountered by the fishermen than many hon. members of the house. Figures already placed on the record have revealed a condition that must be corrected, and only through research and co-operation among the higher levels of government will that result be attained.
People have the idea that all a man needs to do is obtain a fishing boat, set out a few nets, haul in the fish and sell them. I have become very well acquainted with some of these fishermen over the period I have lived there, and I know from experience that fate has not been very kind to the fishermen of lake Huron because of the damage caused by the sea lamprey which we are now attempting to overcome. I noted from the minister's statement of last March that some research work has been done. I think it was done around Manitoulin island as a joint co-operative effort of the federal government and the Ontario government, and I believe some degree of success was achieved. I thought the amount of money spent on the project was terribly small for the task involved, because the annual loss to fishermen is in the millions.
I think no one will disagree with me when I say that the fishermen and the two governments had plenty of notice of the condition, and that some measures should have been undertaken at least 15 years ago. The condition is becoming worse. I do not intend to put a lot of figures on the record because I know the department in Ottawa,
through its research facilities, has all the figures available over the years as to the catch of the respective types of fish in the different lakes. But there is one point I should like to mention here. In looking at the figures I have seen it seems to me that some lakes and some particular species of fish are affected more than others. It would seem that the fishermen of lake Huron and lake Superior-no doubt lake Michigan too, though 1 do not know anything about it- have suffered more than the fishermen on the other lakes.
Fishing is not a highly paid profession to begin with. I recall that years ago the fishermen made good money when they could get a decent price. The unfortunate part about the industry is that while there are certain times of the year when they get high prices, immediately after Lent, for instance, whitefish or pickerel for which the fishermen have been getting 55 or 60 cents a pound drop to 5, 10 or 15 cents a pound, and at times cannot be sold at any price. This is startling but true. You cannot see the result of that in the retail stores, but there it is. The fish caught by the fishermen of the great lakes go to great centres such as New York and Chicago. I know that a lot of lake Huron fish goes to New York.
This is an interwoven picture, but I want to deal with Ontario. I believe the Ontario government grants licences to the fishermen and tells them how many nets they may set out. I believe such licences cost about $50 per net and entitle the fishermen to lawfully fish these waters. The minister made a statement that can probably be clarified in committee, because I do not understand it. He said that in Canada fisheries are the responsibility of the federal government. I suppose in so far as the great lakes are concerned that might apply to the distance from our shore United States fishermen may come, and things of that sort. I cannot quite grasp what the statement really means.
I am going to place two or three figures on the record to substantiate the argument that this convention should be operative just as soon as possible. I cannot give the name of the newspaper that was the source of this clipping, but apparently it is from some reliable newspaper. I believe the figures have been reported before in this house. No doubt the department also has figures which substantiate the fact that there has been a severe drop in the catch over the last few years. I recall that years ago we did not have anything preying on these fish, but now each year the catch seems to get less and less. These figures corroborate what the minister said, and certainly substantiate completely the

Great Lakes Fisheries facts put on the record by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. McBain) in his fine presentation during the resolution stage.
I believe the house will be alarmed to note that in the Georgian bay area, which is part of lake Huron, there was a decrease of 38 per cent in the catch in 1954 as compared to 1953. Certainly this is an alarming situation that commercial fishermen in that area are facing. There was a drop of 41 per cent in the catch of whitefish and that is the fish which, along with pickerel, brings the best price. I am quoting the figures for 1954 as compared with 1953. In northern inland waters there has been a reduction of 10 per cent. In other parts of lake Huron one special type of fish shows a reduction of 8 per cent, and there are greater reductions in the catch of other types of fish.
I just wish to emphasize that these are figures which I know the department will have, together with a great many more. I am satisfied, and I know the department is too, that over the years the figures will show that this curse of the fishing industry has been increasing. I know that today some fishermen even hesitate to set their nets.
There is another item I wish to mention, Mr. Speaker. I realize it is something that probably should be mentioned in a provincial legislature, but because the province is tied in with this government through this convention I think I will make this observation in order that it may be on the record. It is this. Down where lake Huron flows into the river St. Clair at Sarnia or Point Edward we have an alarming situation which is a proper matter for research. These big boats, sandsuckers I think they are called, are allowed to suck up sand and gravel from the bottom of the river. Many people may think that a few boatloads of sand or gravel would not amount to very much. I can only tell you what the fishermen tell me, and they have two complaints about it.
In the first place they say it takes the sand off the beaches in that area for probably 20 miles. It so happens that the only good sand beaches are on the Canadian side and there is a good deal of shale on the other side, so it is our area that is affected. Coupled with the high water we have a terrific erosion problem which is costing the people of this country millions of dollars a year. On other occasions I have mentioned the erosion damage caused by the high lake level, and I have maintained there should be some correction because this high water is caused in part by man-made diversions into lake Superior.
In some areas I have noticed that the fishermen have registered complaints about


these sandsuckers with the Ontario government. It is said they are doing a great deal of damage to the shore line. I say this subject is related to the fulfilment of the desire expressed in this convention. The subject matter may be connected with civil rights and may be under provincial jurisdiction, but since through this convention the provincial government are agreeing to having the federal government act for them in this connection, I am mentioning the matter in the hope that it will be discussed.
There is another matter which is also connected with research that the fishermen in my area complain about. I do not know whether it is the whitefish or trout or pickerel that spawn in the shallow waters along this area, but they are affected by the large amount of sand removed every year by these sandsuckers. Instead of the fish roe being kept in a position where it would hatch, we lose the resultant new fish for lake Huron and other places every year. This process is seriously affected by the removal of this sand and gravel. There are companies who operate fleets of these boats and remove millions of tons of sand and gravel every year. One can readily understand the concern of these fishermen when they see it causing a disturbance to their successful fishing operations.
Everyone would concur in what the minister had to say when he introduced this resolution on March 21, as reported at page 2242 of Hansard. He said that the principal duties of the commission are as follows:
(1)	to formulate a research program with a view of determining the need for conservation measures in respect of any stock of fish of common concern to the fisheries of Canada and the United States;
I think what I have just now said would be concerned with this particular research program. I continue to quote:
(2)	to co-ordinate research and to undertake any research by the commission where necessary;
(3)	to recommend appropriate measures to the contracting governments based on such research;
(4)	to formulate and implement a comprehensive program for the purpose of eradicating or minimizing the sea lamprey menace.
There is no use enlarging upon what the minister said. The facts speak for themselves. I am sure we shall have some further information when we go into committee. I am sure that, because of these paragraphs I have just referred to, this act will bring about more co-operation between the government and the fishermen. I need give only one illustration. The success of this legislation will depend to a great extent on the co-operation of the shore fishermen in distributing small fry, and so on.
In my area we have an unfortunate situation. In Lambton the shore fishermen do not

have proper facilities for launching their boats. We do have there quite a wide stream. This convention will deal properly with the plight of the fisherman, particularly with regard to streams that may have polluted water, and I hope that will include the one to which I refer and have mentioned in previous debates. Some consideration must be given to this branch of our economy so that something is done to provide aid in the areas where the fishermen do not have proper access to the lake. It is feasible and I know the economics will stand it, so I am sure that problem can be solved so the fishing industry of this country may be encouraged. We must provide for them the same facilities that we provide ordinary businesses, that is, access to their business operations. I hope that when this convention becomes operative this one stream, which is very wide and which at one time carried down sugar beet disease, will be kept open as part of the program for promoting a better and healthier fishing industry, not only in Ontario but in all Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES SIGNED SEPTEMBER 10, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my appreciation of the provisions of this bill. Perhaps I should read into the record one of the sections of the bill so that hon. members who are not informed will know what we are talking about. Article I of the convention reads:
This convention shall apply to Lake Ontario (including the St. Lawrence river from Lake Ontario to the forty-fifth parallel of latitude) Lake Erie, Lake Huron (including Lake St. Clair), Lake Michigan, Lake Superior and their connecting waters, hereinafter referred to as "the convention area". This convention shall also apply to the tributaries of each of the above waters to the extent necessary to investigate any stock of fish of common concern, the taking or habitat of which is confined predominantly to the convention area, and to eradicate or minimize the populations of the sea lamprey (petromyzon marinus) in the convention area.
It will not be necessary for me to place on Hansard the figures with respect to the depletion of the trout and whitefish in lake Huron; they have already been placed on the record by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. McBain), as may be seen at page 2242 of Hansard for March 21. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) also spoke on the resolution, and a few minutes ago the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), who is situated right on lake Huron, also dealt with the matter.
I do want to inform the house how important it will be to the fishermen of lake Huron if the provisions of this bill are carried out. For the benefit of those who are not acquainted with the county of Huron, may I say that we have between 75 and 100 miles of shore line bordering the county on the southwest side. We have several small
Canadian National Railways harbours that are used especially for refuge by small craft in time of storm. As the hon. member for Elgin has already told the house, lake trout and whitefish have almost disappeared owing to the presence of sea lamprey in these waters, as mentioned in the bill. No doubt they destroy all kinds of fish, but the fact that trout and whitefish have almost disappeared is evidence that the lamprey prefer the best we have, namely trout and whitefish.
With the assistance mentioned in the bill and the agreements to be entered into by the dominion and the province of Ontario, hundreds of Huron fishermen in a very short time, we hope, will be able to get a creditable catch of trout and whitefish in lake Huron.
We in Huron need a lot of money spent on our harbours, but that has nothing to do with this bill. At a later date, I shall have something to say on that. Men in Huron depend on fishing to make their living. This bill will help them greatly. I sincerely hope that when the bill goes to committee, if amendments are found necessary the minister will give careful consideration to them. Like our forests, we must conserve our fish if we are to continue to enjoy them as a necessary part of our diet.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the primary purpose of this proposed legislation is to consolidate the legislative provisions relating to the Canadian National Railways. These provisions are to be found in a number of statutes, the Canadian National Railways Act, Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act, and various other laws which include

Canadian National Railways legislation relating to railway financing and construction of branch lines, and even old acts relating to the Grand Trunk Railway. As it is often found necessary to refer to these provisions in order to determine powers and obligations of the company, the management has represented to the government that it would be of great assistance if these statutes could be consolidated into one. I am sure the advantages of such a step are so obvious to all hon. members that it is unnecessary for me to make any argument to convince them.
I should perhaps add that the decision to effect this consolidation does not result from any change in government policy concerning the Canadian National Railways. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the primary purpose of this legislation is to consolidate the various legal provisions relating to the Canadian National Railways.
I should like to explain that it is intended also to effect the following changes in the various enactments applying to the company. First, it is proposed to give the Canadian National Railways authority to operate a telecommunication system. At present these powers are exercised by the railway through its subsidiaries, and it is thought it would be desirable if these powers were given to the parent company.
Second, it is proposed to authorize officers and employees of the Canadian National Railways to act as directors of partially-owned subsidiaries. Third, it is proposed to give the railway the power to construct short branch lines without specific parliamentary authority. Fourth, it is proposed to establish a simple procedure to extinguish the charter of any company comprised in the Canadian National Railways. Fifth, it is proposed to give to the railway the power to operate motor vehicles in conjunction with or in substitution for rail services under their management or control. At the present time this power is exercised through subsidiaries of the railway.
As I think it is manifestly in the interests of the railway that its charter be consolidated and that these additional powers as outlined should be given, I urge the committee to adopt this resolution forthwith.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister's
statement has made it clear that considerable study will be required in order to consolidate these various statutes, and I am wondering whether he has in mind referring the bill to a committee of the house. It would seem that the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines would be a suitable committee to undertake this task. It js quite obvious that witnesses from the

company should be called to explain at least some of the implications of this consolidating statute, and that of course can be done only if the bill is considered by a committee.
The minister has said that the railway company is to be given the power to construct short branch lines without coming to parliament. I would ask him to explain what is meant by a short branch line. In recent years several branch lines have been constructed by Canadian National Railways and also one by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and in all cases the proposal was brought to the house. I think that is a very wise course to follow.
For example, there was the extension from Sherridon to Lynn Lake in northern Manitoba, and another from Terrace to Kitimat on the British Columbia coast. Then last year there was the extension to Chibougamau. Probably the minister has read or has been told that there was a great deal of controversy over the branch line from Beattyville to Chibougamau. Parliament also granted the power to build an extension from Chibougamau to St. Felicien in the Lake St. John area, and many of us felt that the railway should have completed the line right through to Lake St. John rather than merely going to Chibougamau in the first stage and then taking the position that it may be able to build the Lake St. John half of this branch line at a later date.
There was considerable feeling in the Lake St. John area against that proposal, and I think rightly so, because the plan of the government had the effect of tapping the Chibougamau district by the line from Beattyville, whereas I believe that area is served at the present time by a highway from Lake St. John. The question of access to the port of Chicoutimi was also involved.
The government faced some rather difficult questions over this proposed branch line, and there was considerable debate in the house and in the committee. I think the government was under some difficulty in justifying its policy with regard to that branch line in so far as it did not contemplate completion right through to St. Felicien at the time the line was extended to Chibougamau.
I am wondering whether the proposal to do away with the requirement that the Canadian National Railways come to parliament for approval of the building of branch lines is the result of the criticism last year. If that is so the proposal is without justification, because I believe it is wise to have both railways come to parliament for approval of the building of branch lines. Otherwise they would have the power to expropriate in order to put a line through an area

without the consideration of parliament. I think that coming to parliament is the practice which has been followed in Canada for many years.

The short lines to which I referred a moment ago, as he will see in due course, are lines intended to serve industrial customers. Perhaps the minister will
explain to the committee why parliament should not sanction the building of branch lines even though they are only six miles in length. Surely the railways should come to this house for approval of the extension of their lines. As I said before, they have the right to expropriate property and six miles of line may be of extreme importance to many people, particularly if it is in a metropolitan area and I presume that that is the type of extension the minister has in mind.

I should like to have an explanation as to why it is felt the railways should be given this right to build such lines without getting parliamentary approval.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION
subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister was correct when he said that the advantages of consolidating these various enactments into one statute are so obvious that he did not need to spend much time trying to convince the house that this step should be taken. I am sure we all agree it would be a good idea to have all the legislation respecting the Canadian National Railways in one place, at least so far as that is possible.
Canadian National Railways
I was glad to hear the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, to which the minister has agreed, namely that after second reading this bill should be referred to one of the committees of the house so that it might be thoroughly studied.
I also was a bit concerned over the phrase in the resolution which suggests that short lines might be constructed without parliamentary approval. I confess that the minister has removed my concern to a considerable extent by making it clear that there will be a specific limitation in the bill as to what constitutes a short line.
The minister, in speaking to this resolution, said that it involved no change in government policy so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned. It seems to me that there is one matter of policy, whether it be government policy or Canadian National Railways policy, which does need to be reviewed at the present time. I refer-and the minister knows that many of us in this house feel strongly about it-to the employment situation on the Canadian National Railways. This legislation is designed to take a look at the whole picture so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, and I suggest that one of the things sorely needed at the present time is some positive kind of assurance to those who work for this railway and are its mainstay that the terrible cloud of insecurity and uncertainty that hangs over them will be removed.
I am not asking merely for the kind of statement we have had from the minister and his predecessor from time to time, namely the hope that we are at the end of lay-offs on the Canadian National Railways. In fact I have upstairs a letter from one C.N.R. employee in Winnipeg who says that every time the Minister of Transport assures us there will be no further lay-offs, all the employees of the C.N.R. tremble. So often has that been said only to be followed by another lay-off that they do not want that kind of statement made again.

The minister placed that statement on the record in response to a request of mine that he give the assurance

Canadian National Railways that we were at the end of the lay-offs. However, what is required is not just the settling of a debating point between the minister and myself. What is required is not just another ministerial statement or vicepresidential statement or presidential statement. What is required is a policy with respect to this matter.
It used to be thought that if a man got a job with one of the railways in this country and got in a few years of employment and a few years of seniority and did a good job, he had a reasonable measure of job security. Now it turns out that even men who have 10 years' service on the railway, and who thought there was that measure of job security, face every week the uncertainty as to whether that employment will be continued.
We recognize that changes are taking place. We recognize in particular that there is a dieselization program now in progress, but surely something could be done, whenever a change-over such as that is being pursued, to recognize the rights of the men. After all, some of us feel that their rights are just as important as the concern which some people feel for capital investment, for the maintenance of equipment and for all the other factors which go into the running of the railway. It is our feeling that there is something lacking in government policy and in Canadian National Railways policy with regard to the employees of this great system. I strongly urge that this matter be gone into in the consideration of this legislation.
I am glad to know, as I have already said, that after second reading the bill will be referred to a committee. I note that the minister proposes that it go to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, rather than to the committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government. That means that a group of members different from those who generally look at Canadian National matters in committee will have a look at this situation. I hope some policy can be worked out in

that committee, when it is considering this bill, which will protect in a way that is not now effective the rights of the employees of this railroad.
In addition to the lay-offs which are taking place and the insecurity which arises because of that fact, there are certain other matters of policy in relation to the railway that I think call for review at this time. Perhaps I had better suggest that you call it ten o'clock so I can go into those other matters the next time this resolution is called.

Before I leave the chair, I was going to ask hon. members to consider between now and the next time this committee meets on this resolution the wording of the resolution. I am making no ruling at the moment, but I am of the opinion that there may be a large number of matters connected with the operation of the Canadian National Railways which are not appropriate subjects for discussion under a resolution which says that it is expedient to consolidate the existing statutes and to make certain other provisions. I am not undertaking to rule at the moment. I am suggesting to all hon. members that because this resolution consolidates the statutes dealing with the Canadian National Railways, it may not necessarily open for discussion every phase of the operation of the Canadian National Railways system.
Progress reported.
